## 2026-09-02 (latest) — ONE STATUS CHANGE, **EIGHT** STALE CLAIMS, AND A LITERAL-STRING GREP FOUND ONLY FIVE

**Symptom.** Wiring §Ch21 into `_play()` falsified one sentence — "the chapter is not wired yet".
That sentence turned out to exist, in eight different phrasings, across THREE files. Two independent
Tier 1 passes plus three of my own greps were needed to clear them, and each pass found ones the
previous had missed:
* Tier 1 round 1 found 3 (the "60-SECOND VERSION" block, a punch-list cell contradicting *itself*,
  and a banner clause I had half-patched).
* My own re-grep of that round's instruction found 3 more — including **two that gated a promotion
  decision on now-false premises** ("`sootopolis.py` … leg 5 missing, not wired … so it is not a
  promotion candidate").
* Tier 1 round 2 found a 7th: the **opening clause of the banner** — the literal first sentence a
  cold reader sees — still said *"what is LEFT is the `_play()` WIRING"*.
* A SEMANTIC sweep then found an 8th, in `12-STORYMODE-DESIGN.md`, **a file neither Tier 1 pass had
  looked at**, because both were scoped to `04-HANDOFF.md` + `03-PUNCH-LIST.md`.

**Root cause.** Two distinct failures, and it is worth separating them.
1. **My greps were LITERAL.** I searched `"NOT wired into"`, `"does NOT exist yet"`,
   `"no orchestrator"`, `"NEXT ACTION IS TO WIRE"` and reported "UNMARKED SURVIVORS: 0" — while
   *"what is LEFT is the `_play()` WIRING"* sat in the banner's first sentence. ⛔ **A literal-string
   grep cannot prove the absence of a CLAIM; it proves the absence of a SPELLING.** The fix that
   worked was a proximity search — a topic word (`wiring|orchestrator|_play()`) within ~240 chars of
   a staleness cue (`is LEFT|what remains|still not|not yet|does not exist|NOT wired|NOT built`) —
   which found the two the literal patterns could not.
2. **The pair check was SCOPED to two files.** P1–P5 name `04-HANDOFF` and `03-PUNCH-LIST`, so a
   reviewer who does exactly what is asked never opens `12-STORYMODE-DESIGN.md`. The checklist
   protected exactly what it enumerated — the same shape that added P5 in the first place.

**Prevention rules.**
⛔ **SWEEP BY MEANING, NOT BY SPELLING.** When a status flips, the sweep is
`<topic word> NEAR <staleness cue>`, not a list of exact phrases you happen to remember writing. You
did not write them all, and the ones you did write you paraphrased.
⛔ **AND SWEEP THE WHOLE TREE, NOT THE PAIR LIST.** Before declaring a status change complete, grep
EVERY `PROJECT KNOWLEDGE/*.md` for the topic — Tier 1's P1–P5 are a floor, not a ceiling, and a
reviewer told to check two files will check two files. ⇒ **the enumeration is the reviewer's scope;
the sweep is yours.**
‼ *Second-order note worth keeping: the banner clause fixed here carried, in its own parenthetical,
the warning "when the next leg/wiring ships, THIS SENTENCE is the one to grep for first" — written by
me, one commit earlier. A note that predicts its own staleness still does not prevent it. Only a
sweep does.*

**Symptom.** I recorded, in `04-HANDOFF.md`, `03-PUNCH-LIST.md`, `12-STORYMODE-DESIGN.md` and a
commit message, that the §Ch22 start fixture "ENDS chipped — one member fainted, lead 25/115". An
adversarial refuter reviewing an unrelated recon flagged the arithmetic; re-measuring settled it:
**`post_hm07.ss1` is SIX ALIVE at 629/694 (91%), lead 52/115. Nothing is fainted.**

**Root cause — and it is subtler than a typo.** BOTH numbers are real measurements I took the same
day, from **two different runs**:
* `post_hm07.ss1` was captured by the **leg-5** drive, which started from `post_rayquaza_gone.ss1`
  (already at 91%) — so it inherited a healthy-ish party.
* The **chapter** drive ran legs 1→5 from `post_ch20.ss1` and ENDED with Zigzagoon 0/44 and the lead
  at 25/115 — a genuinely harder handover, and one that was **never captured to a fixture**.
I read the chapter drive's `PARTY end=` line, and wrote it down as a property of the FIXTURE.
‼ The tell was there and I did not look: `probe_anchor_inventory.py` reported `HP 629/694 (91%)` for
`post_hm07.ss1` in the same session. **A fixture's party is a property of the RUN THAT CAPTURED IT,
not of the last run I happened to read.**

**Why it mattered rather than being cosmetic.** §Ch22 is a readiness problem — the fight is not
winnable as-is — so the start party is the planning input. A "revive first / restructure the party"
design premised on a faint would have solved a problem that is not in the save, while the real
problems (no Dragon move, one Potion, zero Revives, `allow_escaping: false`) went unaddressed.

**The fix that worked.** Re-measured directly, corrected all four sites, and — the part worth
keeping — **recorded BOTH states**, because they are both real: the pinned fixture is healthier than
a live §Ch21 handover, and **§Ch22 must be built for the WORSE one**.

**Prevention rules.**
⛔ **A FIXTURE'S PARTY/STATE IS A PROPERTY OF THE RUN THAT CAPTURED IT.** Before writing any state
claim about a save, measure THAT SAVE (`probe_anchor_inventory.py` / `probe_box_contents.py`) — never
transcribe it from a drive log that happens to be on screen, however recent.
⛔ **WHEN TWO RUNS PRODUCE TWO END STATES, RECORD BOTH AND NAME WHICH IS WHICH** — and plan for the
worse. A fixture captured mid-arc is systematically healthier than a full playthrough's handover, so
"the fixture says 91%" is an optimistic floor, not the design input.

## 2026-09-02 (final) — THE LIVE-GRID INSTRUMENT THAT SOLVED §Ch21 IS A **FALSE NEGATIVE BY CONSTRUCTION** IN THE NEXT GYM

**Symptom (caught in recon, before any code).** Planning §Ch22 I reached for `_live_collision_grid`
and `probe_live_mapgrid.py` — the instruments that cracked KI-73 for §Ch21 and are described in
`02-ARCHITECTURE.md` as *"the oracle for can the bot actually step there"*. In the Sootopolis Gym
they would have reported **0 differences and PASS** over a model that is catastrophically wrong.

**Root cause, verified at all three links myself:**
1. `sootopolis.py:934` — our grid keeps `(block & 0x0C00) >> 10`, i.e. **collision bits only**.
2. `src/scrcmd.c:2044-2047` — `ScrCmd_setmetatile` ORs `MAPGRID_IMPASSABLE` **only** when its 4th
   argument is TRUE.
3. `SootopolisCity_Gym_1F/scripts.inc` — **every** gym `setmetatile` passes **FALSE**.
⇒ The gym rewrites its floor as you walk, and **not one of those writes touches the bits our reader
looks at.** The ice cracking under the bot is invisible to it.

**The fix (specified, not yet built).** Read the METATILE ID (`block & 0x03FF`) rather than the
collision bits — a two-line variant of the existing helper, reusing its already-calibrated
`offset = 7` — and/or gate on `get_event_var("ICE_STEP_COUNT")`, which exists today and must
increment by exactly 1 per step.

**Prevention rule.** ⛔ **AN INSTRUMENT IS VALID FOR THE FIELD IT READS, NOT FOR THE QUESTION YOU ARE
ASKING.** Before reusing a probe on a new map, ask *which bits does it actually compare, and does the
mechanism I am worried about write those bits?* A green result from a probe that cannot see the
failure is worse than no probe — it is a certificate of correctness for an untested claim.
‼ And note the shape: this instrument did not become wrong; **it was always collision-only**, and
§Ch21's hazard happened to be a collision change. *Success on one map is not validation for the
class of problem.*

## 2026-09-02 (latest) — I VIOLATED MY OWN SKILL'S RULE IN THE NEXT DRIVER I WROTE, HOURS AFTER WRITING IT

**Symptom.** A Tier 1 reviewer found that `Ch22ProbeMode`'s grade could return
`ACCEPTANCE: PASS` on a run that measured nothing: `self.probes_run.append("P3")` ran
**unconditionally**, including on the branch where no ice tile is found and the branch where the
step raises. `passed` then only checked that the label was present — never `stepped`, never whether
the metatile grid actually moved. The headline measurement the whole probe exists for was not in its
own predicate.

**Root cause.** The exact shape this project calls **"A CANDIDATE IS NOT AN ATTEMPT"** — instrument
the ACTION, never the input to it. ‼ And the aggravating fact: I had written that rule into
`.claude/skills/unlazy/SKILL.md` **earlier in the same session** ("Did the thing actually RUN, or did
a guard skip it? … ⛔ A CANDIDATE IS NOT AN ATTEMPT"), and into `story-drive` ("a VACUITY conjunct in
the grade"). I then wrote the violating driver a few hours later.
⇒ **A rule filed as a SKILL does not fire either.** Writing it down improves the odds for the next
reader; it did not stop the author. What stopped it was an independent reviewer reading the diff.

**The fix that worked, and the arm that proves it.** P3 is recorded only when `stepped and mt_moved`;
`passed` requires both. `POKEBOT_CH22_FAULT_NOSTEP=1` suppresses the step and the run now goes
`P3 NOT RECORDED` → `probes run: ['P0','P1','P2','P4','P5']` → `ACCEPTANCE: FAIL`. **Before the fix
that arm would have PASSED.** The clean arm was re-run byte-identical (`frames=3958`, PASS), proving
the change touched only the failure path.
⛔ Note the polarity choice: `col_moved` is deliberately NOT a pass condition. It is the FALSIFIER —
if the collision grid ALSO moved, the static analysis was wrong and KI-73's new paragraph is what
needs correcting. A falsifier must never be a pass condition, or it silently becomes an escape hatch.

**Prevention rules.**
⛔ **A GRADE MUST NAME THE MEASUREMENT, NOT THE CODE PATH.** "Did block P3 execute" and "did P3
measure anything" are different predicates, and only the second is a grade. Concretely: every label
appended to a readings list must be appended INSIDE the success branch, never after the `if/except`
that could have skipped it.
⛔ **AND THE TEST FOR THIS IS MECHANICAL, SO RUN IT: add the arm that suppresses the measurement and
confirm the grade goes FAIL.** If you will not write that arm, you do not know your grade works.
‼ Meta-rule, earned here: **writing a rule into a skill/doc does NOT protect the author who wrote
it.** Skills help the next reader; the only thing that caught this was an independent reviewer given
the diff. ⇒ **keep Tier 1 mandatory even when the author is the person who wrote the rulebook.**

## 2026-09-03 — MY OWN REACHABILITY BFS WALKED THROUGH WALLS, AND I NEARLY PUBLISHED IT AS A REFUTATION

**Symptom.** Measuring whether §Ch22's ice leg ends STRANDED, my live BFS reported
`live_reachable=372, live_reaches_exit=True, live_reaches_ladder=True` — apparently REFUTING the
recon's "once the ice is cracked, Juan's platform is a 20-tile island, and the only way out is a
deliberate fall". I was one sentence from writing that up.

**What stopped it.** The number was implausible on its face: 372 of a 17×26 = 442-tile map. A gym
that is mostly ice and wall does not have 84% of its tiles mutually reachable.

**Root cause.** My walkable set was
`{t for t, mt in metatiles.items() if t not in blocked and mt not in THIN_ICE}` — it filtered ice,
cracked ice and locked stairs, and **never checked collision at all**, so it walked straight through
walls. With `collision.get(t, 1) == 0` added, the answer is **20 tiles, exit False, ladder False** —
matching an independent decomp BFS *exactly*, and CONFIRMING the recon rather than refuting it.

**The deeper error, and it is one I had already written the rule for.** I had just spent a day
establishing that in this gym `_live_collision_grid` is *blind to the ice*, and I over-generalised
that into treating the collision bits as useless. They are not: they are blind to the ICE and
**correct about WALLS** — the gym's `setmetatile`s never touch them, which is exactly why both
things are true at once. ⇒ **each grid answers its own question**; the metatile grid says "is this
ice and what state", the collision grid says "is this solid". Neither substitutes for the other.

**Prevention rules.**
⛔ **A REACHABILITY/REFUTATION RESULT MUST PASS A PLAUSIBILITY CHECK BEFORE IT IS BELIEVED, AND
ESPECIALLY BEFORE IT IS PUBLISHED.** Ask "what fraction of the map is this, and does that make
sense for this map?" A number that would be remarkable if true is a number to re-derive, not to
report. ‼ Refuting a prior finding is exactly when to be *most* suspicious of your own instrument —
the reward for a dramatic result is what makes it dangerous.
⛔ **AND DO NOT LET "INSTRUMENT X IS BLIND TO Y" COLLAPSE INTO "INSTRUMENT X IS USELESS".** State
what each instrument measures and use it only for that. Here the correct answer needed BOTH grids;
using either alone gives a confidently wrong map.

## 2026-09-03 — I ANSWERED A BINARY QUESTION AND SHIPPED IT AS AN OPTIMUM: "FIVE FORCED BATTLES" WAS REALLY THREE

**Symptom.** I committed, in a research note, the punch list, the handoff and a commit message, that
§Ch22's gym exit "costs FIVE forced battles". An adversarial refuter said the minimum was THREE; I
re-derived it myself and it is **three (Andrea, Bethany, Connie), in 19 tiles**.

**Root cause — methodological, not arithmetic, which is why review would not have caught it.** I
asked a BINARY question: *"is there a trainer-free route from the fall tile?"* The answer was no, so
I fell back to reporting the SHORTEST route — which happens to cross five sight lines — and wrote
that up as what the exit COSTS. **The right question was never "is there a free route" but "what is
the CHEAPEST route"**: a Dijkstra weighted by battles, not a BFS weighted by distance.
⇒ **WHEN THE IDEAL IS UNAVAILABLE, MINIMISE. Do not fall back on the metric you happen to have
already computed.** "No perfect option exists" and "here is the best option" are different findings,
and only the second one is planning.

**A second, compounding error: my walk model was wrong in the pessimistic direction.** B1F has **six
`MB_SLIDE_SOUTH` tiles** ((8,10)(8,11)(8,15)(8,16)(8,20)(8,21)) that carry the player south for free
— *past sight lines* — and my 4-connected BFS did not model them at all. It also missed **six
DOUBLE-battle tiles** where two trainers see the same square and a 2v2 starts.
‼ Note the direction: I had just been burned by an optimistic bug (a BFS walking through walls) and
this one was pessimistic. **A wrong model is not reliably conservative — it is just wrong**, so
"erring on the safe side" is not a reason to skip verifying it.

**The fix that worked.** A battle-weighted Dijkstra with slide chains modelled, re-derived by me
after the refuter flagged it. The refuter independently found a *different* 3-battle route (35 tiles
vs my 19) — **two derivations agreeing on the COUNT while disagreeing on the PATH is exactly the
corroboration to want**, and far stronger than agreeing on both.

**Prevention rules.**
⛔ **A ROUTING/COST ANSWER MUST NAME ITS OBJECTIVE, AND THE OBJECTIVE MUST BE THE ONE THAT MATTERS.**
Before reporting "it costs N", state what was minimised. If the answer came from a shortest-path
search but the cost that matters is battles/damage/time, the number is not an answer to the question
asked.
⛔ **AND MODEL THE MAP'S OWN MOVEMENT MECHANICS BEFORE ROUTING ON IT.** Slide tiles, ice, currents,
warps and one-way ledges all break a plain 4-connected walk. Census the behaviour bytes of every
walkable tile FIRST — one line of code — and only then route. *(`{0x0: 116, 0x47: 6, 0x61: 1}` would
have told me in seconds.)*


## 2026-09-03 — A DAMAGE CALCULATION BECAME A PUBLISHED CLAIM IN SIX FILES, AND THE FIGHT WAS WON FIRST TRY

**Symptom.** For a full day, `04-HANDOFF.md`, `03-PUNCH-LIST.md`, two research notes, the production
module `sootopolis_gym.py` and the `ch22juan` driver's own docstring all said, in bold, that the
party **could not win** the Juan fight — several of them with the word *MEASURED* attached. The
first live drive won it: `BADGE08_GET`=True, `SOOTOPOLIS_CITY_STATE=6`,
`outcomes=['BattleOutcome.Won']`, **5 of 6 survivors**, 32,891 frames, zero whiteouts.

**Root cause — and it is NOT "the numbers were wrong".** Every input fact was correct and is still
correct: Kingdra L46 really is Water/Dragon, so the party's Grass, Electric and Ice are all
**neutral**; nothing in the party has a Dragon move; Juan really does restore it three times
(Rest + Chesto Berry, then two Hyper Potions); Sceptile's Leaf Blade really is a 3HKO on 138 HP
while Ice Beam 2HKOs Sceptile. From those premises I computed that **Sceptile loses the 1v1** —
which is *true* — and then published the conclusion **"the party cannot win"**, which does not
follow. The battle is **six versus five**. Five other party members, five of Juan's own mons to
grind down, switch-ins (Swellow is *immune* to Whiscash's Earthquake — an adversarial refuter had
already corrected me on exactly that), and the AI's own move choices are all outside the
calculation. ⇒ **I solved a sub-problem and reported it as the problem.**

**The compounding error was the WORD.** Writing "MEASURED not to win" made a calculation
indistinguishable from a reading, in the one project whose whole method is that those are different
things. Nothing in the docs told a later reader which it was — and I was the later reader.

**The near-miss this created.** The build spec's §1 recommended, on the strength of that
conclusion, a *readiness programme*: take the ten B1F trainers for XP, buy a full stock at the
Mart, and **grind if still short**. Had I built that first, it would have "worked" — the bot would
have won after grinding — and the grind would have looked load-bearing forever. The cheap
discriminator (one drive, ~33k frames, ~4 minutes, fully reversible because a whiteout respawns at
the Poké Center and the ice puzzle resets on every entry) was available the whole time.

**The fix.** All 12 stale claims corrected in place (the two in `07-CHANGELOG.md` are append-only
and are corrected forward), each one keeping the typing analysis — which is still the right input
to any future re-balancing — and marking only the CONCLUSION as withdrawn.

**Prevention rules.**
⛔ **NEVER WRITE "MEASURED" OVER SOMETHING THAT WAS COMPUTED.** If no run produced the number, the
word is *calculated*, *derived*, or *predicted*. This project already refuses to let a Gemini recall
pass as verification and refuses to let a candidate list pass as an attempt; a damage calculation
passing as a measurement is the same offence with a new coat.
⛔ **A CONCLUSION ABOUT A WHOLE SYSTEM MAY NOT BE DRAWN FROM A CORRECT ANALYSIS OF ONE PART OF IT.**
Before publishing "X cannot work", name what the analysis left out. Here: five party members, five
opposing mons, switching, and the AI. If the omitted set is non-empty, the honest headline is
*"here is the hard part of X"*, never *"X cannot work"*.
⛔ **AND WHEN A CHEAP DISCRIMINATOR EXISTS, RUN IT *BEFORE* WRITING THE PREDICTION INTO SIX FILES.**
Pre-registering a prediction is good practice and I did it — but I also promoted the prediction to
a finding across the tree, so the pre-registration bought nothing and the retraction cost six files.
‼ **Pre-register in ONE place (the driver docstring or the PREDICTIONS note); publish only results.**


## 2026-09-03 — I TRIED TO MEASURE RELIABILITY BY RE-RUNNING A DETERMINISTIC HARNESS (my own rule, violated in the experiment's DESIGN)

**Symptom.** Having won the Juan fight once, I wrote — correctly — that *"one win is not a
reliability measurement"* and launched two more runs of the same driver against the same fixture to
get an N/3. All three came back **byte-identical**: `frames=32891`, `SURVIVORS 5/6`, `won=True`.
I was one keystroke away from reporting **"3/3 wins"**, which would have been a fabricated
confidence interval over a single trajectory.

**Root cause.** `story_harness.py` replays a save state through a deterministic emulator with a
deterministic driver. Same save + same code + same button sequence ⇒ **the same 32,891 frames,
every time.** A repeat is a REPLAY, not a draw. This is written down, in this project's own
`CLAUDE.md`, as SESSION DISCIPLINE **#8**: *"IDENTICAL OUTPUT ACROSS RUNS IS A DETERMINISM CHECK,
NEVER A REPLICATION. Say 'one trajectory, replayed' — never 'measured twice'."*
‼ **I had quoted that rule earlier the same day.** It did not fire, because #8 is filed as a rule
about *reading results* and this was a failure of *experimental design*: the moment to apply it was
when I typed the `for` loop, not when the output came back. **A rule that only fires at
interpretation time cannot stop you spending the frames.**

**Why the §Ch20 precedent misled me.** `ch20room9`'s Archie fight really is **2W/1L** — so I had a
live example of a stochastic boss fight in this very harness and generalised from it. But those
three runs differed in *code*: they were taken across driver revisions and route changes. ⇒ **the
outcome is deterministic for a fixed (save, driver, code) triple, and re-rolls when ANY of the
three changes.** That is a materially different — and much more useful — statement than "boss
fights are stochastic".

**What the wasted runs actually bought (they were not wasted).** They are the first *measurement*
in this tree that the harness is deterministic end-to-end across a 33k-frame run containing a full
gym-leader battle. That re-prices a reflex this project has: *"run it again to be sure"* buys
**nothing** here unless something is perturbed.

**The fix that worked — perturb the RNG, and prove the perturbation.** `gRngValue` is readable
(`read_symbol("gRngValue")`; the tree already ships `wait_for_unique_rng_value()`). `Ch22JuanMode`
now takes `POKEBOT_CH22JUAN_JITTER=N`, idles N frames on Juan's front tile, and **prints the RNG on
both sides of the idle**, so a run that failed to perturb announces itself instead of being counted.
✅ Verified before spending the sample: with `N=181` the value moves `0x008c33fa → 0xfbf1b389` — a
~30-second, 6,500-frame probe that answered "does idling even advance the RNG?" before any 33k-frame
arm was run.
*(Cheap sub-lesson from that probe: it died at f0 with `NameError: name 'os' is not defined`,
because my patch script's guard was `"import os" in text` — which matched an unrelated
`import os.path`. **A substring is not an import.** Same shape as "a candidate is not an attempt".)*

**Prevention rules.**
⛔ **BEFORE RUNNING THE SAME THING TWICE, NAME WHAT DIFFERS BETWEEN THE RUNS.** If the answer is
"nothing", you are buying a determinism check — which is worth having ONCE, and is worth nothing
after that. Write the perturbation into the instrument, not into the hope.
⛔ **A SAMPLER MUST PRINT THE THING IT PERTURBED**, on both sides of the perturbation, so a
no-op sampler is visible in its own transcript. (Same shape as INSTRUMENT THE ACTION, NOT THE INPUT.)
⛔ **AND STATE THE SCOPE OF A DETERMINISM CLAIM AS A TRIPLE:** deterministic *for a fixed (save,
driver, code)*. ⇒ **the §Ch22 chapter drive will re-roll the Juan battle**, because it arrives by a
different route with a different frame count — so the assembled chapter is an independent sample and
must not be assumed to inherit this win.


## 2026-09-03 — I MEASURED A LEG'S COST IN A PREMISE THE PRODUCTION RUN WILL NEVER BE IN

**Symptom.** `--driver ch22exit` measured the §Ch22 escape as **3 forced trainer battles** costing
**629/694 → 332/694 (~48% HP)**, and I wrote that number into the handoff, the punch list, the
changelog and a production comment as *the readiness cost of the chapter*. It also drove the leg
ORDER: "the fall goes AFTER the badge, because the exit costs half the party's HP."

**Root cause.** The driver runs from `post_hm07.ss1`, where `BADGE08_GET` is **False**. The Juan
victory script sets it — and, in the same script, runs
`setvar VAR_0x8008, 8` + `call Common_EventScript_SetGymTrainers`, which `settrainerflag`s **all
ten** B1F trainers as already defeated (`data/scripts/set_gym_trainers.inc`). ⇒ **in the assembled
chapter the descent happens AFTER the badge and costs ZERO battles.** The 3-battle, −297-HP figure
is real, reproducible, and describes a state the production run never enters.

**Why the numbers being *correct* is the trap.** Nothing about the measurement was sloppy: the
route was battle-weighted, the sight lines were decomp-verified, the tiles were predicted before
the run and matched. A wrong number gets caught. A **right number attached to the wrong premise**
propagates, because every check it meets — the driver's own grade, the pair checks, the gates —
compares it against itself.

**What it nearly cost.** A whole leg. The refuted "the party cannot win" claim had already produced
a plan to *"take the ten B1F trainers deliberately for XP"*; this measurement then looked like its
supporting evidence, and the two together were about to justify a pre-clearing descent that the
game performs for free. Two independent-looking artifacts agreeing — which is exactly what this
project has measured to be worthless as a confidence signal.

**How it was actually caught.** Not by any gate and not by re-reading my own docs: by asking a
decomp agent the flat question *"what EXACTLY happens in the Juan victory script?"* and then
re-reading the two quoted blocks myself. The refuter, working from our code alone, could not have
found it — it is not in our code.

**Prevention rules.**
⛔ **A COST MEASURED FROM A FIXTURE IS A COST *FOR THAT FIXTURE*. Before quoting it as the
chapter's cost, name the flags and vars that differ between the fixture and the production run,
and say which of them the measured path depends on.** Here the whole finding hung on one flag the
fixture had False and production has True.
⛔ **WHEN A LEG IS DRIVEN OUT OF ITS PRODUCTION ORDER, WRITE THE ORDER IT WAS DRIVEN IN NEXT TO THE
NUMBER.** "3 battles" is not wrong; "3 battles (measured pre-badge; the chapter runs this leg
post-badge)" is what a later reader needs, and it is one clause.
⛔ **AND READ THE SCRIPT THAT SETS YOUR GRADING FLAG, ALL THE WAY THROUGH.** `BADGE08_GET` was
treated as a boolean to grade on; it is a line in a script that also hides five NPCs, moves an NPC
in front of the Cave of Origin, enables a Match Call, and clears ten trainer flags. **A flag is an
event, not a value.**


## 2026-09-03 — TWO TIER-1 REVIEWS IN A ROW FOUND STALE TEXT, EACH IN A PLACE THE PREVIOUS ONE HAD NOT LOOKED

**Symptom.** One retraction ("the party cannot win Juan" → it won, 4/4) had to be chased through the
tree **four separate times**:
1. My own first sweep found 12 occurrences and fixed them.
2. **Tier 1 pass 1** found three more: the NEXT ACTIONS queue head still opened *"NEXT ACTION: §Ch22
   — GYM 8, JUAN"*; the leg count said THREE in one file and FOUR in two others over the same four
   items; and `2026-09-02-ch22-PARTA-RESULTS.md` still said *"sample it before calling the fight
   solved"* — a caveat **discharged in the same round that wrote it**.
3. **Tier 1 pass 2**, run specifically to check *where* those fixes landed, found four more — the
   worst being `04-HANDOFF.md`'s own **YOU ARE HERE banner**, line 10, still reading *"THE LIVE WORK
   IS NOW §Ch22 (GYM 8 — JUAN)"* while the queue head 300 lines below had already been corrected.
   ⇒ **the fix landed in the half a reviewer had pointed at, and not in the half a cold agent reads
   first.** It also found a punch-list bullet contradicting the header **two lines above it** that
   the same edit had just fixed, and the same discharged caveat surviving verbatim in the sibling
   note that `04-HANDOFF.md` explicitly tells readers to go and read.
4. My own sweep after that still found one more ("all four legs" in `12-STORYMODE-DESIGN.md`).

**Root cause.** My sweeps were **literal**: I grepped the retracted phrase I remembered writing
("not winnable", "expected to lose") and fixed the hits. Every survivor was a **paraphrase of the
same claim** — *"THE LIVE WORK IS NOW §Ch22 (GYM 8 — JUAN)"* contains none of my search terms and
says the same wrong thing. ‼ And the highest-value survivors clustered in exactly two places a
literal grep is worst at: **a banner** (which states the claim as framing, not as a sentence about
Juan) and **a file the corrected file points AT** (so a reader following the fixed pointer lands on
the stale text — the fix and the staleness are one hop apart and never appear in the same grep).

**What actually worked.** Independent reviewers given the FACT and asked to sweep for its
*negations*, not for a phrase. Pass 2 was told explicitly to check *where* the fixes landed, and
that instruction is what found the banner.

**Prevention rules.**
⛔ **A RETRACTION IS NOT DONE WHEN THE PHRASE IS GONE. IT IS DONE WHEN THE *CLAIM* IS GONE.** Write
the corrected fact as one sentence, then sweep for things that CONTRADICT that sentence — including
paraphrases, framings and titles that never contain your original wording.
⛔ **SWEEP THE BANNER AND THE POINTERS FIRST, NOT LAST.** The two places a stale claim survives a
grep are (a) the headline that frames it rather than states it, and (b) the file the corrected file
cites. Both are one hop from the fix and neither shares its vocabulary.
⛔ **WHEN AN ITEM RAISES A CAVEAT AND THEN DISCHARGES IT IN THE SAME ROUND, GREP FOR THE CAVEAT'S
OWN WORDING BEFORE COMMITTING.** "One win is not a reliability measurement" was written by me, made
false by me, and then survived in two files.
⛔ **AND RE-RUN TIER 1 AFTER FIXING TIER 1** — not to re-check the same pairs, but because the fix
itself creates a new inconsistency between the half that was corrected and the half that was not.
Two passes here found *disjoint* sets of defects; one pass would have shipped the banner.
‼ Filed as `#24-retiredclaimgate`: this is enforceable and therefore belongs in a gate, not here.


## 2026-09-03 — THREE CONJUNCTS IN ONE ACCEPTANCE LINE WERE SATISFIABLE **BY NOT DOING THE THING**

**Symptom.** The §Ch22 chapter driver's grade contained `battles_b1f == 0`, `isinstance(cont, int)`
and `whiteouts == 0`. All three looked like tightening. All three were wrong, and the runs — not a
review — exposed them one at a time:

1. **`battles_b1f == 0`** was the chapter's HEADLINE DISCRIMINATOR (does the post-badge B1F descent
   cost zero trainer battles?). Drive 1 lost the Juan fight, never reached B1F, and printed
   **`battles_on_B1F=0`** — the exact number that would have "confirmed" the finding. **Zero
   battles for zero opportunities.**
2. **`isinstance(cont, int)`** was the can-continue check — the conjunct this project added because
   §Ch15, §Ch18 and §Ch19 each PASSED while stranded. Drive 1 returned `cont = 0`, because **a
   whiteout respawns the player standing ON the Poke Center apron the path is measured to.** So the
   check was satisfied by the very failure it exists to catch.
3. **`whiteouts == 0`** graded a **successful recovery as a failure**. Drive 2 lost the fight,
   cleared the abort latch, walked out, re-entered, walked virgin ice, won, took the fall, cleared
   B1F and walked out — and got `ACCEPTANCE: FAIL`. Production tolerates forty whiteouts.

**Root cause, and it is one cause with three faces.** Every one of these conjuncts asserts the
*absence* of something. An absence is satisfied both by "the thing was tried and did not happen"
and by "the thing was never tried" — and only the first is evidence. This is the same shape as this
project's own **"A CANDIDATE IS NOT AN ATTEMPT"** rule, which is written down for *inputs to an
action*; it had never been written down for **grades**.

**The fix.** Every absence conjunct is now paired with a presence conjunct that proves the
opportunity existed: `battles_b1f == 0` **and** `b1f_steps > 0`; `cont` an int **and** `cont > 0`;
and `whiteouts == 0` replaced by `recoveries <= 2` with the raw count REPORTED beside it. The log
lines print the pair together so the number can never be read alone.

**Prevention rules.**
⛔ **AN ACCEPTANCE CONJUNCT THAT ASSERTS AN ABSENCE MUST BE PAIRED WITH ONE THAT PROVES THE
OPPORTUNITY EXISTED.** "No battles" needs "and it walked the floor". "No errors" needs "and it ran
the step". Ask of every `== 0` and every `not`: *what else makes this true?*
⛔ **AND A GRADE MUST NOT PUNISH A RECOVERY THE DESIGN REQUIRES.** If production tolerates a failure
mode and recovers from it, a driver demanding zero occurrences grades the healthy system as broken.
Grade the BOUND, report the COUNT. *(A cold-start audit once found this project's KI-80 arm inverted
the same way — expecting PASS from a command whose FAIL was the proof the fix worked.)*
‼ **AND NOTE WHAT FOUND THESE: not a reviewer, and not a re-reading — a run that took a branch I had
rated unlikely.** Two of the three were only visible because a HIGH-confidence prediction missed.
The pre-registered prediction is what turned a bad run into three measurements.


## 2026-09-03 — A CHRONOLOGICAL APPEND-LOG INSIDE A CURRENT-STATE FILE ROTS FROM THE MIDDLE

**Symptom.** `04-HANDOFF.md`'s NEXT ACTIONS queue head had become a **single 14,476-character
line**: every §Ch22 finding appended to the end as it was made, newest last. By the time the
chapter shipped — the same day — that one line still carried, as plain live text:

* *"SO THE NEXT ACTION IS NOW §Ch22 CHAPTER ASSEMBLY"* (it shipped)
* *"a descent helper is still owed"* (`_descend_to()` was written)
* *"NO DRIVER HAS EVER RUN `walk_the_ice → fight_juan → fall_to_b1f` COMPOSED"* (three had)
* *"SAMPLED — 4 WINS OUT OF 4"* (it became 5W/1L)
* *"the chapter must be heal → stock → ice → Juan → fall/B1F/out"* (no stock leg; the order changed)

**Five statements the same day's work had falsified**, all of them true when written.

**Root cause.** Append-only is the right discipline for `06`/`07`/`08` — files whose whole purpose
is *what was true then*. `04` is a CURRENT-STATE file, where the rule is the opposite: **edit in
place, remove stale content.** I was appending to it as though it were a log, and each new clause
was correct at the moment of writing, so nothing ever triggered a re-read of the ones above it.
‼ **This is why it survives a pair check.** P1 compares the banner with the queue head; both said
"§Ch23 next" and AGREED. The rot was 2,000 characters *inside* the queue head, below its own
corrected opening — a place no named pair points at.

**The fix.** Retire a chapter's build log the moment the chapter ships: summarise, point at
`07-CHANGELOG.md` and the notes, and keep only the facts the NEXT chapter inherits. Here that is
three sentences (the fight is stochastic and the chapter recovers; KI-47 can freeze it and is not
§Ch22's to fix; the ladder is 23 of 24). 14,476 → 2,273 characters.

**Prevention rules.**
⛔ **DO NOT APPEND TO A CURRENT-STATE FILE. WHEN A NEW FACT ARRIVES, EDIT THE SENTENCE IT
CONTRADICTS.** If that feels like losing history, the history belongs in `07-CHANGELOG.md`, which
exists for exactly that and is never trimmed.
⛔ **AND RETIRE A CHAPTER'S QUEUE ENTRY IN THE COMMIT THAT SHIPS THE CHAPTER**, not later. §Ch21's
entry had the same shape and was retired for the same reason a day earlier — twice is a pattern.
‼ **A pair check cannot see this**: both halves of P1 can be freshly correct while the body under
one of them is stale. ⇒ when an item ships, re-read its queue entry TO THE END, not just its first
sentence — the first sentence is the half everyone remembers to fix.

**A SECOND, MECHANICAL VERSION OF THE SAME SHAPE, FOUND IN THE SAME PASS.** Filing a new
`### #24-retiredclaimgate` item into `03-PUNCH-LIST.md` by inserting it *before* an existing
anchor line **silently reparented the last bullet of `#24-ch22chapter`** — a `- [x]` bullet about
§Ch22's preflight ended up sitting under the new item's heading, where it read as a done sub-task
of a gate that has not been written. Nothing flagged it: the text was unchanged, the file linted
clean, and both headings were individually accurate.
⛔ **INSERTING A HEADING IS A STRUCTURAL EDIT, NOT A TEXT EDIT. After adding a `###` item, list
every bullet under the NEW heading and under the one ABOVE it, and confirm each belongs.** A
two-line check (`^### ` and `^- \[` in order) catches it; reading the diff does not, because the
diff shows only the inserted lines and never the bullet that moved.
‼ Related and worth the same care: this project's headings are load-bearing claims (pair P2), so a
bullet under the wrong heading is a false claim even when every word in it is true.


## 2026-09-03 — ⚠ A PREVENTION RULE IN THIS FILE NAMES A MECHANISM THAT THE CODE CONTRADICTS

**This entry corrects the CAUSE of an earlier entry, not its fix.** The 2026-09-02 §Ch21-leg-5
entry says a msgbox was parked for 20,000 frames because *"`press_button` on EVERY frame … HOLDS
the button"*, giving Gen 3's `waitbuttonpress` no `JOY_NEW` edge; the fix was a `frames % 4` duty
cycle, and **the fix demonstrably worked**.

⛔ **But the stated mechanism does not match the emulator wrapper.** ✅ Read by me,
`sandbox-pokebot/modules/libmgba.py:476`:
```python
self._pressed_inputs |= (self._prev_pressed_inputs & input_map[button]) ^ input_map[button]
```
with `self._prev_pressed_inputs = self._pressed_inputs; self._pressed_inputs = 0` each frame
(`:588-589`). If the button was pressed last frame, `(prev & mask) ^ mask` is **0** — so it is NOT
pressed this frame. ⇒ **calling `press_button` every frame produces a 1-on/1-off alternation, i.e.
a clean `JOY_NEW` edge every two frames — not a hold.** `hold_button` is a separate method.

**Why this matters more than a wording nit.** A prevention rule is only worth its accuracy: the
next person to meet a parked msgbox will apply a duty cycle *because of the holding story*, and if
holding is not the mechanism the duty cycle may be treating a symptom of something else (a wrong
button choice, a predicate that opened the loop in the wrong state, or a printer state the press
lands in the wrong half of). **This project has an explicit rule that a fix must be attributed, and
one whose attribution is wrong is a fix nobody can generalise from.**

⛔ **WHAT IS AND IS NOT CLAIMED HERE.** Claimed: the wrapper auto-releases, and the entry's stated
cause therefore cannot be right as written. **NOT claimed:** that I know the real cause. The
§Ch21-leg-5 fix landed together with a predicate change (`not ...is_active`), so two variables
moved at once and neither was isolated.
⇒ **Filed as `#24-pressbuttoncause`:** the discriminating A/B is one arm with the duty cycle
removed and the predicate kept, on the §Ch21 leg-5 fixture. Until that runs, the §Ch21-leg-5
entry's FIX stands and its CAUSE is marked UNVERIFIED — ‼ **not deleted**, because a wrong
recorded cause that is flagged is far safer than a silent one.
‼ Found by an agent diagnosing an unrelated freeze, which is the second time this session that a
sourced, quoted contradiction arrived from a direction nobody was looking.


## 2026-09-03 — MY CONTROL PASSED WHILE THE MODEL IT DID NOT TEST WAS BROKEN

**Symptom.** An agent claimed Victory Road needs no Strength and no Rock Smash — a scope cut worth
two side-quests. I refused to take it on trust and re-derived it myself in a committed tool
(`solve_victory_road.py`): decoded the decomp layouts, **asserted every byte length**, ran a
**negative control** (0 of 1,388 collision tiles reachable), ran a **fault arm** (ignoring collision
made a wall reachable, proving the refusal came from the collision model), and got **71 steps**. I
reported the scope cut as independently confirmed, and wrote it into `chapters.py`, the handoff
banner-adjacent queue head, and a research note.

**It was wrong.** An adversarial review refuted it, and my own corrected tool now reproduces the
refutation exactly: **the exit is UNREACHABLE on 1F alone**, and the route needs BOTH field moves.

**Root cause — the elevation model, which my controls never touched.** Gen 3 gives the player a
**carried elevation**; an elevation-15 tile **preserves** it rather than setting it. This repo
already implements exactly that (`map_path.py:859` and `:1039`). My tool compared **tile-to-tile**
elevations and treated any 15 as a free pass, so on 1F's multi-level bridge — an elevation-3
corridor passing under an elevation-4 one — it changed levels for free and welded two regions
together. ‼ **Our own planner would have refused the route**, so the number could never have driven;
the tool disagreed with production and nothing noticed.

**⛔ THE ACTUAL LESSON, AND IT IS NOT "CHECK YOUR ELEVATION".** My control was real, it was correct,
and it passed — *about collision*. The bug was in elevation. **A control tests the failure mode it
was written for and no other, and a passing control creates exactly as much false confidence as its
scope is narrower than the model.** This project already knows the neighbouring half of this rule —
*"a positive control proves a scan is not BLIND; it says NOTHING about over-reporting"* — and this
is its twin: **one control does not certify a model with two independent parts.**

**The fix.** `solve_victory_road.py` now keys its search by `(x, y, CARRIED elevation)` — collapsing
that to the tile is what allowed the free level change — and its `--self-test` carries **one control
per model, each with its own fault arm**: collision leak + collision fault, **elevation leak +
elevation fault**, plus an off-grid raise. The new elevation control fires on **169** open tiles the
elevation rule alone refuses. The tool also prints its answer **with and without** the elevation
rule, side by side, so the artifact that fooled me is visible in every future run.

**Prevention rules.**
⛔ **COUNT THE MODELS BEFORE YOU COUNT THE CONTROLS.** A reachability search over this game has at
least three independent gates — collision, elevation, and objects. One control per model, each with
a fault arm that disables only that model. A single "the search doesn't walk through walls" control
certifies one third of the thing.
⛔ **WHEN A TOOL ANSWERS A QUESTION PRODUCTION ALSO ANSWERS, DIFF THEM.** `map_path.py` implements
this exact rule and disagreed with my tool. **Ten minutes reading the shipped planner would have
caught it, and I had already cited that file twice the same day.** ⇒ before writing an offline model
of something the bot does at runtime, read the runtime one and copy its rule verbatim.
⛔ **THE BIGGER THE SCOPE CUT, THE HARDER IT MUST BE REFUTED BEFORE USE.** I called this "the single
biggest scope reduction available on this chapter" in the same note that got it wrong. A finding
that deletes work is the one with the most incentive to be believed and the least resistance in its
path — it earns an adversarial pass, not a confirmatory one.
‼ **And note what DID work:** the adversarial agent was told to attack, given the byte-length trap
in advance, and required to state what it asserted. It refuted a claim I had already "verified".
That is the second time this session an adversarial pass overturned something I was confident in.


## 2026-09-03 — I FIXED "MY CONTROL DIDN'T TEST THE MODEL" BY ADDING A MODEL WITH NO CONTROL

**Symptom.** Yesterday's entry records that `solve_victory_road.py` v1 was wrong because its
control tested COLLISION while the bug was in ELEVATION-ENTRY. I rewrote it, added an elevation
control, and shipped v2 with the docstring *"⛔ ONE CONTROL PER MODEL … a control for EACH model,
and a fault arm for each, independently."*

**An adversarial review fault-injected every gate and asked v2's own self-test whether it noticed:**

| gate | injected fault | self-test |
|---|---|---|
| collision decode | wrong shift | **fails ✓** |
| elevation ENTRY | always `True` | **fails ✓** |
| v1's exact bug | tile-to-tile, keyed by tile | **fails ✓** |
| ⛔ **elevation CARRY (`_carry`)** | `return map_elev` | ⛔ **PASSES** — while the answer went 477 tiles → 32 and the B1F ladder became UNREACHABLE |
| ⛔ object model | `blockers()` → `set()` | ⛔ **PASSES** |
| B1F / B2F | — | ⛔ **no controls ran at all** — `_self_test(floors["1F"])` |

⇒ **`_carry` — the single rule the entire v2 rewrite existed to add — had no control and no fault
arm.** Break it and the script printed a different world *and* `SELF-TEST PASSED — one control per
model, each with its own fault arm.`

**Root cause. This is not "I forgot a control".** It is the identical failure one layer up: v1
controlled the model it *had* while the bug was in the model it *added*; v2 did exactly the same.
**A lesson recorded about old code does not automatically apply itself to the new code written to
fix it** — and the new code is precisely where nobody has looked yet.

**Two subtler defects in the same review, both worse than a missing control:**
* ⛔ **The elevation fault arm was a TAUTOLOGY.** `elev_blocked` was *defined* as "refused normally
  AND reachable with elevation ignored", and the fault line sat in the same `else` restating that
  definition. **It could not fail independently.** A control that cannot fail is not a control; it
  is a sentence that says "PASS".
* ⛔ **The docstring's safety promise was FALSE.** *"UNREACHABLE verdicts are conservative"* holds
  only for the OBJECT model ("the obstacle is gone"). On TERRAIN the script UNDER-approximates —
  it models no surf, no waterfall, no ledges — and **B2F is 238 tiles of `MB_OCEAN_WATER`**. So its
  UNREACHABLE verdicts were not safe to act on, and that sentence is the one a future reader would
  have acted on.

**The fix, and it is a design change rather than three patches.**
1. A control **and an independent fault arm per gate**: collision, elevation-entry, elevation-carry,
   objects, start-elevation, off-grid. Breaking `_carry` now loses 445 tiles on 1F and 180 on B1F,
   and the arm is anchored to a tile **the route actually depends on** (the B1F ladder), not to
   "some tile".
2. Controls run on **all three floors**, not just the one whose answer was already known.
3. ⭐ **A control that CANNOT discriminate now says so (⚠) instead of failing OR passing.** B1F's
   entry rule gates nothing from that start — a MAP PROPERTY, not a defect — and the script now
   proves that by checking whether `_carry` still discriminates there before deciding which it is.
   ‼ **Failing on a map property teaches the next maintainer to weaken the control, which is
   strictly worse than having none.**
4. The summary line no longer claims "one control per model"; it says every control that *could*
   discriminate did, and the rest said so.

**Prevention rules.**
⛔ **THE CONTROL FOR A NEW RULE IS PART OF THE NEW RULE.** When a fix adds a model, the fix is not
done until that model has a fault arm that fails when it is broken. Ask, mechanically: *for each
gate, what single-line change would corrupt it, and does the self-test go red?* If you cannot name
the injection, you do not have a control.
⛔ **A FAULT ARM MUST BE COMPUTED FROM DIFFERENT DATA THAN THE CONDITION IT VALIDATES.** If it is
derived from the same expression, it restates a definition and can never fail.
⛔ **AND A SAFETY CLAIM IN A DOCSTRING IS A LOAD-BEARING ASSERTION.** *"UNREACHABLE verdicts are
conservative"* is the sentence a reader acts on; it was false for two of the three models and had
no test at all. Either prove such a claim or delete it.
‼ **What worked, again:** an adversarial agent told to attack, given the tooling trap in advance,
and required to fault-inject rather than reason. It confirmed all four headline numbers AND found
that the controls certifying them were hollow. **Third time this session that an adversarial pass
overturned something I was confident in.**


## 2026-09-03 — I REFUTED A TRUE CLAIM TWICE BY TESTING BOARD STATES THE GAME CAN NEVER REACH

**Symptom.** An agent audit said two boulder pushes seal Victory Road B1F and the minimum solution is
2 pushes + 1 smash. I wrote `probe_vr_b1f_claims.py` to check it myself. Its geometry sections were
right and valuable — they independently confirmed the boulder/rock positions, both shaft walls, both
push destinations, and the 23-tile arrival chamber, settling the coordinate-space worry that was the
likeliest way the audit could have been worthless. Then two further sections reported, confidently:

* *"PUSH WEST (4,7) is REDUNDANT — the ladder is reachable without it"* — **WRONG.**
* *"pushing (4,7) SOUTH does not seal the floor — 297 tiles still reach the ladder"* — **WRONG.**

Two independent solvers (one built from scratch with no sight of the first) both return minimum cost
**3** with that push required, and both return SEALED when (4,7)-south is forced as the first push.

**Root cause — and ⛔ MY FIRST DIAGNOSIS OF IT WAS ALSO WRONG, which is half the lesson.** I blamed
the missing directional edge-blocker rule (B1F has 178 `MB_IMPASSABLE_NORTH` tiles and my model
ignores them), and wrote that into the note as the explanation. The independent solver then PROVED
that rule is **vacuous on this map**: all 13 *passable* such tiles have a collision-1 wall directly
north, so 0 passable→passable crossings are blocked by it, and its fault arm changes nothing.
⇒ **I had produced a plausible mechanism and presented it as a cause.** A cause needs the same
evidence bar as the claim it explains.

**The actual, single cause of both false findings: I BUILT BOARD STATES THAT ARE UNREACHABLE.**
* The seal test asked *"with this boulder parked here **and every other obstacle cleared**, is the
  ladder reachable?"* — but you cannot clear the other obstacles **from** the sealed state. That is
  what "sealed" means. The premise assumed away the conclusion.
* The necessity test dropped push 1 and kept push 2 — but **push 2 is impossible without push 1**:
  the only route to (8,10), the tile you must stand on to push (9,10) east, is (4,7)→(4,10)→(8,10),
  and push 1 is what opens (4,7).

**The fix.** Both sections were DELETED from the probe rather than repaired, and replaced with a long
comment naming the trap, because the approach cannot be made correct by being more generous. The
probe now answers geometry only and says so in its docstring, its section 6 banner and its verdict.
The note (`ai-research-notes/2026-09-03-ch23-VICTORY-ROAD-B1F-B2F.md` §E2) records the false findings
rather than quietly dropping them.

**Prevention rules.**
⛔⛔ **APPLYING A SUBSET OF ACTIONS DOES NOT PRODUCE A REACHABLE STATE.** Before a counterfactual
board, config or fixture is allowed to refute anything, **prove it is reachable, in order.** A query
over an impossible premise is vacuous, and it does not announce itself — it returns a clean,
confident number.
⛔ **A "NECESSITY" TEST THAT REMOVES STEP k AND KEEPS STEP k+1 ASSUMES THE STEPS ARE INDEPENDENT.**
When the steps are order-dependent, that test measures nothing. ‼ *I had already written "pushes are
ORDER-DEPENDENT and a tile graph cannot express them" into the same document, and then tested as
though it were false.* **A constraint you have documented is not thereby in force in your next test.**
⛔ **AN EXPLANATION FOR YOUR OWN ERROR IS A CLAIM AND NEEDS EVIDENCE.** "My model lacks rule X" is a
hypothesis until you show rule X would have changed the answer. Mine would not have.
✅ **WHAT WORKED, AND IT IS THE ONLY REASON NO CODE WAS BUILT ON THIS:** I filed the disagreement as
a DISAGREEMENT — "my instrument says otherwise AND my instrument is known to be weaker here" — instead
of as a refutation, and wrote *"until it is adjudicated, take the UNION of both answers: forbid BOTH
south pushes and perform all THREE actions."* That union was the correct behaviour under both the
true and the false model. ⇒ **when two instruments disagree on a safety property, ship the
intersection of what they permit, and let the adjudication catch up.**
‼ **Fourth adversarial overturn in this session.** The pattern is now unambiguous: a fresh agent told
to ATTACK, given the tooling traps in advance and required to fault-inject rather than reason, finds
things I do not — including errors in the corrections I made to my own earlier errors.


## 2026-09-03 — TWO FACTS, BOTH RECORDED, WHOSE *CONJUNCTION* WAS THE HAZARD — AND NOTHING JOINED THEM

**Symptom.** `saves/FIXTURES.md5`'s entry for §Ch23's start fixture said, in one sentence,
*"61% HP with one member fainted — heal first"*, and in another sentence,
*"WAILMER IS THE SINGLE POINT OF FAILURE FOR THE WHOLE CHAPTER — sole carrier of Dive (the only exit
from the Sootopolis crater) AND of Waterfall (the only way up)."*
Both true. Both written by me. **Neither says which member is fainted.** Measured with a driver:
`Wailmer#FA51ECF3 hp=0/160 ⛔ FAINTED`. ⇒ **the chapter's irreplaceable Pokémon starts it dead**, and
a bot that departed before healing would have tried to leave the crater on a corpse — into an ocean
leg with `allow_escaping: false` and no Poké Center for its entire length.

**Root cause — a doc-consistency shape the pair checks P1-P5 cannot see.** Every existing pair check
asks *"do these two statements AGREE?"* These two agreed perfectly. The defect is that **the hazard
lives in their CONJUNCTION and no sentence performs it.** Consistency checking is blind to a fact
that is only dangerous when combined, because there is no contradiction to find.
‼ A second cause made it invisible: **no instrument in the tree could answer the question.**
`probe_anchor_inventory.py` reports "1 FAINTED" without saying which; `--driver partypids` reported
PIDs without HP. The one question that mattered — *"is the fainted one the mon we cannot lose?"* —
was unanswerable, so it was never asked.

**The fix.**
1. `--driver partypids` now reports **HP by identity** and prints an explicit
   `FAINTED BY IDENTITY: [...]` line. The gap is closed for every future fixture, not just this one.
2. The finding is recorded at all three places a reader could arrive: the fixture registry entry,
   `04-HANDOFF.md`'s queue head, and `#24-ch23victoryroad`.
3. §Ch23's preflight requirement is upgraded from "assert Wailmer BY PID" to **"assert Wailmer is
   ALIVE by PID"**, and the opening heal from hygiene to a **hard precondition**.

**Prevention rules.**
⛔⛔ **WHEN A DOCUMENT NAMES A SINGLE POINT OF FAILURE, IT MUST ALSO STATE THAT COMPONENT'S CURRENT
STATE.** "X is irreplaceable" and "something is broken" in the same file, without joining them, is
worse than either alone — it reads as two handled risks.
⛔ **A HAZARD CAN LIVE IN A CONJUNCTION THAT NO SENTENCE PERFORMS.** Pair checks find
contradictions; they cannot find a dangerous AND. When you write a criticality claim, immediately
ask "and what is its state RIGHT NOW?" — then measure it rather than assuming.
⛔ **IF THE DECISIVE QUESTION IS UNANSWERABLE BY ANY EXISTING INSTRUMENT, THAT IS THE FINDING.**
Build the instrument first. The question "which member is fainted?" went unasked for a day because
nothing could answer it, not because anyone judged it unimportant.
✅ **And the generic form of the rule this project keeps re-learning: ASSERT IDENTITY, NEVER A COUNT.**
Six alive and six-with-one-down both report `party=6`.


## 2026-09-03 — MY "IS THIS ITEM CLOSED?" HEURISTIC WOULD HAVE RETIRED TWO ITEMS WITH LIVE WORK IN THEM

**Symptom (caught before any damage).** `03-PUNCH-LIST.md` went over its 3,600-line budget, so I
searched for a fully-closed item to archive. My detector was *"the item contains no `- [ ]` and no
`- [~]` checkbox"*. It nominated **`#26-manualderails` (105 lines)** and **`#26-surfteachchain`
(38 lines)** as the two biggest closed items.
⛔ **Both have live work.** `#26-manualderails` carries **D4, one of the three ripe USER DECISIONS**
named in `04-HANDOFF.md` (the post-wind repeat burn). `#26-surfteachchain` carries **D3, which is
OPEN and specifically ARMED on the §Ch23 route I am building right now** — its hazard is re-entry
into `_select_forget_slot`, and the clean §Ch23 leg-1 run never re-entered it, so D3 *did not fire*
rather than being fixed.

**Root cause.** These items track state in PROSE with sub-item markers (`D1`, `D2`, `D3`, `D4`),
not with checkboxes. **A structural test for openness is only valid where the structure is
enforced** — and nothing enforces the checkbox convention here. My detector measured a proxy for
"closed" and would have reported a confident, clean answer while deleting a user decision.

**Why it was caught.** Only because I recognised both slugs from this session's own reading and
stopped to check. ‼ **That is not a control — it is luck**, and it would not protect an agent with
no prior context, which is exactly who does budget retirements at session end.

**The fix applied instead.** I retired nothing and compressed **my own** newly-added verbose text —
the §Ch23 guard spec, which was duplicating a ruling now stated in full in `06-DECISIONS-LOG.md`.
Duplicating a decision across two current-state files is itself how halves drift apart.

**Prevention rules.**
⛔⛔ **NEVER RETIRE AN ITEM ON A STRUCTURAL TEST ALONE. READ IT.** "No open checkbox" is a proxy;
open work also hides in prose, in `D<n>` sub-items, and in "AWAITING A USER RULING". ‼ Before
archiving, `grep` the item's slug across `04-HANDOFF.md` and `05-KNOWN-ISSUES.md` — if the handoff
names it as a live decision, it is not closed no matter what its checkboxes say.
⛔ **WHEN OVER BUDGET, COMPRESS YOUR OWN NEWEST TEXT FIRST.** It is the text you understand best,
it is the most likely to be verbose, and it is the only text whose removal cannot lose someone
else's finding. Retirement of an OLD item is a bigger decision than a line budget should force.
✅ **And prefer de-duplication to deletion:** a full ruling belongs in `06-DECISIONS-LOG.md` once,
with a pointer from the punch list — not stated twice in two current-state files.


## 2026-09-03 — I ASSERTED A PROPERTY OF MY OWN INSTRUMENT IN A COMMENT, THEN READ EVERY RESULT THROUGH IT

**Symptom.** `Ch23RouteMode`'s R6 block carried this comment, written by me, as the justification for
how to interpret its Victory Road B1F readings:

> *"On a map the bot is NOT standing on, `active_objects` is empty, so production does not block live
> boulders — its answer is therefore the 'Strength and Rock Smash both spent' case, which is exactly
> the question worth asking of the terrain."*

**Measured FALSE, at zero cost, by a query I only ran because something else looked odd.** On
`ROUTE128` — a map the bot is not standing on — `calculate_path` **REFUSED** to path to **(101,29)**
and **(101,22)**, the template tiles of the trainers Carlee and Harrison, while pathing happily to
**(101,26)** and **(100,29)** right beside them (32 and 34 wp). ⇒ **production DOES block on object
events on a non-active map.**

**How it surfaced, which is the part worth copying.** A route query refused, and instead of recording
*"Route 128 is obstructed"* I ran a discriminator: the same journey in two hops. The LONGER half
succeeded (79 wp) while the SHORTER one refused — so it was not a path budget. That asymmetry
(pathing FROM (101,29) works, pathing TO it fails) is the signature of an occupied DESTINATION with an
exempt START, which named the hypothesis; two more queries confirmed it.

**Root cause.** I wrote a confident claim about how the planner behaves, in a comment, and then read
every downstream result through that claim. Nothing tested it. It was not a guess about the game —
it was a guess about **my own instrument**, which is the kind that hides best, because the instrument
is the thing you are using to check everything else.

**What it actually changed — and it is GOOD news, which is why it could have gone unnoticed for a
long time.** R6's B1F answers are the **"boulders STILL PRESENT"** case, not the "both moves spent"
case. So R6a/R6b/R6c refusing is a genuine corroboration that the arrival chamber is SEALED until the
pushes happen — a **stronger** reading than the comment claimed, not a weaker one. B2F has no
boulders, so R6d/R6e are unaffected; 1F's R8 queries aimed at bridge tiles and warps, not object
tiles, so they stand. ‼ **A false premise that happens to make your conclusions look better is the
hardest kind to notice.**

**Prevention rules.**
⛔⛔ **A CLAIM ABOUT YOUR INSTRUMENT NEEDS THE SAME EVIDENCE BAR AS A CLAIM ABOUT THE SUBJECT.** "The
planner does not model X here" is a testable assertion, not a framing device. Test it in the same
run, especially when it is doing interpretive work for every other reading.
⛔ **WHEN A PATH QUERY REFUSES, ASK *WHICH TILE* YOU ASKED FOR BEFORE CONCLUDING ANYTHING ABOUT THE
TERRAIN.** A refusal to a tile an object stands on says "something is standing there". ⇒ **never aim
a path at an object's tile**; aim beside it.
⭐ **THE DISCRIMINATOR THAT WORKED, WORTH REUSING: split the journey.** If the whole refuses and both
halves succeed, it is a budget. If the LONGER half succeeds and the SHORTER refuses, it is not — and
the from/to asymmetry then tells you it is the destination.


## 2026-09-03 — I AVOIDED THE DOCUMENTED IMPORT TRAP AND WALKED INTO ITS SIBLING, THEN INTO ITS COUSIN

**Symptom.** `--driver ch23depart` printed `ACCEPTANCE: PASS` and then died:
`NameError: name 'pathlib' is not defined` — in the fixture-capture block, three lines after the
verdict. **The run reported success and captured nothing.**

**The trap, and why knowing about it did not help.** The build spec carries this warning, and I had
just written it into the punch list myself:

> *"`story_harness.py` imports **`os as _os`**, so a bare module-level `os` in a new driver is a
> `NameError` on frame 1 … it has already cost a 25-minute drive."*

I honoured it exactly — every `os` reference in my driver is `_os`. **And then I wrote
`pathlib.Path(...)`.** The harness has `from pathlib import Path`, so the *module* name `pathlib` is
not bound at all. ⇒ **the rule named ONE SYMBOL when the hazard is a CLASS**, and a rule phrased as
"use `_os`" is silent about every other stdlib name.

⛔ **AND THE FIX WAS THE SAME BUG AGAIN.** I saw existing capture blocks using `_pathlib`, changed
mine to match — and `_pathlib` is a **function-local** import in every one of those blocks
(`:8967`, `:9237`, `:9317`), not a module-level alias. So the "fix" was a third `NameError`,
avoided only because I checked where `_pathlib` was bound before re-running instead of assuming the
grep hit meant module scope.

**Root cause.** A prevention rule written as an instance (*"use `_os`"*) instead of a property
(*"this file's import bindings are not what you assume"*) protects exactly the instance it names. I
followed the letter of a rule I had personally re-typed into the docs an hour earlier, and the
letter did not cover the case.

**What worked, and it is a design property rather than luck.** The capture is gated on the full pass
and **the fixture's EXISTENCE is the acceptance record**. The NameError landed after the verdict but
before the write, so **no file was created and no false record existed** — the failure was loud
(a traceback) and left nothing behind to mislead the next session. ‼ *A convention that refuses to
record a thing that did not happen survives its own tooling crashing mid-record.*

**Prevention rules.**
⛔⛔ **A RULE THAT NAMES A SYMBOL PROTECTS THAT SYMBOL AND NOTHING ELSE. WRITE THE PROPERTY.** The
correct rule here is: **check EVERY stdlib name your new code references against this file's actual
bindings — module scope AND function scope — because `story_harness.py` aliases some, `from`-imports
others, and imports several only locally.**
⛔ **AN EXISTING USAGE IS EVIDENCE OF A NAME, NOT OF ITS SCOPE.** `grep _pathlib` finds the idiom; it
does not tell you the binding is local. Read the line above the usage.
⭐ **SMOKE-TESTING WITH A TINY `--frames` WOULD NOT HAVE CAUGHT THIS**, and that is worth knowing:
the smoke test passed cleanly, because the capture block is reached only on a FULL PASS with the env
var set. ⇒ **a code path gated on success is not exercised by a failure-free smoke test** — exercise
the capture path deliberately, or accept that its first real run is its first test.


## 2026-09-03 — I FIXED THE INSTANCE AND NOT THE CLASS, TWICE IN ONE FILE, ON THE SAME DAY

An adversarial review of §Ch23 legs 2-3 (the CODE, after a separate review of its design) returned
two BLOCKERS. Both were mine and both are the same shape.

**BLOCKER 1 — a precondition narrower than the leg it guards.** `assert_ch23_preflight` accepted only
the island-side maps and ROUTE126, while `leave_the_crater` has explicit phase branches to resume from
`UNDERWATER_SOOTOPOLIS_CITY` and `UNDERWATER_ROUTE126`. A fresh run from a savestate taken mid-leg-3
would raise in the preflight, **before the phase selector built to handle it ever ran.**
‼ **AND I HAD ALREADY FIXED THIS EXACT BUG EARLIER THE SAME DAY**, in the orchestrator, and written it
up: *"a precondition for one leg must not be able to fail the next."* I fixed the gate I was looking
at and never asked whether it had siblings. It had one, eight lines away.
⇒ **PREVENTION: when a precondition is found wrong, `grep` for the OTHER places answering the same
question.** A predicate duplicated across two call sites is the code form of the P5 doc shape, and
fixing one copy is the most dangerous state — the bug survives while feeling resolved.
✅ Fixed by introducing `_RESUMABLE_MAPS` (every map the chapter can start OR resume on) as a set
distinct from `_ISLAND_SIDE_MAPS` (where leg 2's work can happen). They answer different questions;
conflating them was the bug.

**BLOCKER 2 — a fault arm that switched off its own detector.** The only HP-completion check in the
entire chapter read `if could_rise and not _fault("NOHEAL")`. Nothing else in leg 2, leg 3 or the
driver inspects HP before departure. So `POKEBOT_CH23_FAULT_NOHEAL=1` would have printed
**`ACCEPTANCE: PASS` with the party at 61% and the sole Dive carrier still fainted.**
‼ This is the purest form of *"an arm that cannot fail is a sentence that says PASS"* — a rule I had
re-typed into the punch list hours earlier, violated inside the code written under it.
✅ **FIXED AND FAULT-PROVEN BY A/B:** clean arm gives `ACCEPTANCE: PASS`; `NOHEAL=1` gives
**`ACCEPTANCE: FAIL`**, naming the two members that did not rise (Swellow 5/118, Wailmer 0/160) and
stating that the raise IS the arm firing. **Before the fix that run passed; after it, it fails.**
That is the difference between a claimed guard and a proven one.

**AND A THIRD THING, WHICH IS A LESSON ABOUT READING RESULTS RATHER THAN A BUG.** The `NOPIN` arm also
returns `ACCEPTANCE: FAIL` — but on `missing=['R-PIN']`, i.e. the *reading* was not taken, while
`ended_on_r126=True`, `dived=True` and `can_continue=True`. **The run still succeeded.** So the arm
proves the readings check works; it does **NOT** prove the layout pin protects anything. The pin only
bites in a full `_play()` run where §Ch21 left a stale pin behind, and no such run has happened.
⛔ **AN ARM CAN FAIL FOR THE WRONG REASON, AND A FAILING ARM IS NOT AUTOMATICALLY A PROVEN GUARD.**
Read WHICH conjunct failed before claiming the arm demonstrated the hazard.

**PROCESS NOTE THE REVIEWER RAISED, AND IT IS FAIR.** I edited both files *while* the review was
running, so its first and second reads disagreed. It caught this itself and re-read. ⇒ **freeze the
artifact under review, or tell the reviewer it is moving** — a reviewer racing the author can deliver
findings that are already stale.


## 2026-09-03 — I REPORTED A GATE SUITE AS GREEN BY READING `tail`'s EXIT CODE

**Symptom.** I told the user *"the full gate suite exited 0"*. It had **FAILED 2 of 33**.

**Cause.** The command was
`run_gates.py > gates.txt 2>&1; echo "GATES_EXIT=$?"; tail -5 gates.txt`, run in the background. A
`;`-chain gives the harness the exit status of the **last** command — `tail` — which succeeds
whatever the suite did. The true status went to stdout as `GATES_EXIT=1`, into the *task output*
file, while I read the *gate log* file. **The verdict and the evidence ended up in two different
places and I read the one without the verdict.**

**Why it slipped.** The notification said "completed (exit code 0)" in the same sentence shape as
every successful command all session, so it looked like confirmation rather than a different
measurement. I then quoted it onward without opening the file that held the real answer.

**Prevention rules.**
⛔⛔ **PUT THE EXIT CODE WHERE THE READER WILL LOOK.** `echo "EXIT=$?" >> the_same_file`, so the
verdict and the evidence cannot be separated. Never let a redirect split them.
⛔ **A `;`-CHAIN LAUNDERS FAILURE.** The harness reports the LAST command's status. End the chain on
the command under test, or use `set -o pipefail`/`&&`, or check the status explicitly.
‼ **AND A HARNESS "exit code 0" IS A MEASUREMENT OF WHATEVER YOU ACTUALLY RAN**, not of what you
meant to run. Quoting it onward is a claim; treat it like any other claim and check the artifact.
✅ **What caught it:** re-reading the gate log for a different reason and seeing the word `FAILED`
in a suite I had already called green.


## 2026-09-04 — MY OWN PUNCH-LIST HEADER SAID "PRODUCTION CODE IS ZERO" WHILE THREE LEGS SHIPPED FROM IT

**Symptom.** `#24-ch23victoryroad`'s heading read *"RECON IS DEEP, **PRODUCTION CODE IS ZERO**"* and
its first bullet *"⛔⛔ `sandbox-pokebot/modules/story/victory_road.py` **DOES NOT EXIST**"* — for a
full day after legs 2, 3 and 4 shipped **from that very file**, each with a passing drive and a
pinned fixture. A cold reader arriving at the live work item would have been told the chapter had no
code at all.

**Why it survived.** I updated the item's BODY every time a leg landed — adding "LEGS 2-3 ARE BUILT",
then "LEG 4 IS SHIPPED" — and never re-read the two lines above them. The pair check I keep applying
(P1 banner↔queue, P5 item↔handoff) is about agreement BETWEEN documents; this was a contradiction
*within a single item*, between its heading and its own newest sentence. **Nothing in the routine
looks upward from the line being edited.**

**And the line budget hid it.** Every time the item grew I trimmed the NEWEST text to fit, which is
the correct rule — but it meant the oldest, most stale lines were the ones never touched. ⇒ **a
"compress your newest text" rule protects fresh content and preserves stale headers.** The two rules
need each other: compress the newest, but re-read the OLDEST before declaring the item current.

**The fix.** The item was rewritten whole rather than patched again: 103 lines → 47, header and body
both true, all analysis pointed at the build spec instead of duplicated. The rewrite ALSO paid the
line budget it had been fighting — a stale narrative is usually the cheapest space available.

**Prevention rules.**
⛔⛔ **P2 APPLIES *WITHIN* AN ITEM, NOT ONLY BETWEEN DOCUMENTS.** A heading is a claim about every
line beneath it — including lines added months later. When appending a status to an item, **re-read
its heading and first bullet in the same edit**, or the append is what makes them false.
⛔ **WHEN AN ITEM HAS BEEN APPENDED TO THREE TIMES, REWRITE IT INSTEAD OF APPENDING A FOURTH.** The
signal is the append count, not the length.
‼ **AND THE STALEST TEXT IS WHERE A LINE-BUDGET RULE POINTS AWAY FROM.** "Trim your newest text" is
right for authorship and wrong for accuracy; pair it with "re-read the oldest".


## 2026-09-04 — THE SAME TRAP THREE TIMES IN ONE CHAPTER: AIMING A PATH AT A **WARP** TILE

**The shape.** `navigate_to` OVERRIDES ITS OWN DESTINATION when the plan's last waypoint is a warp
(`walking.py:446-448`). So asking to walk to a door, a ladder or a stair does not park you in front
of it — **it takes you through it**, onto a different map. Any grade asserting `_at(thisMap, thatTile)`
then FAILS a perfect run, and the leg silently does the NEXT leg's job.

**It has now happened three times in §Ch23 alone, on three different kinds of warp:**

| # | the tile aimed at | what the plan actually ends on |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Sootopolis Poké Center **door** (43,31) | inside the building — caught in design |
| 2 | Victory Road **door** (18,41) | `VICTORY_ROAD_1F (15,40) is_warp=True` — **measured** |
| 3 | the B1F **ladder** (9,14) | `VICTORY_ROAD_B1F (8,3) is_warp=True` — **measured** |

⇒ #3 would have dropped the bot into B1F's **sealed 23-tile arrival chamber**, whose only two exits
are the boulders that can permanently seal the floor — i.e. the most dangerous tile in the chapter,
reached by a leg that had no business being there.

**Why it kept recurring.** Each time it was recorded as a fact about *that tile* — "(18,41) is a
door" — rather than as a property of the primitive. A fact about one tile does not generalise; a
property of `navigate_to` does. The first two were caught by review and measurement; the third I
asked about **before writing the code**, and that is the only reason it cost seconds instead of a
drive.

**Prevention rules.**
⛔⛔ **NEVER AIM A PATH AT A WARP TILE. AIM AT ITS APRON.** Doors, ladders, stairs, arrow warps and
dive spots are all destinations that *move you*. The apron is the tile you can stand on and still be
where you think you are. Name the pair explicitly in code (`PC_DOOR`/`PC_APRON`,
`VR_DOOR`/`VR_APRON`, `B1F_LADDER`/`B1F_LADDER_APRON`) so the distinction survives the next edit.
⛔ **AND ASK THE PLANNER BEFORE AIMING AT ANY TILE ADJACENT TO A WARP.** One `calculate_path` call,
dumping the last waypoint's `(map, coordinates, is_warp)`, settles it in seconds — versus a
30-minute drive that ends on the wrong map and reports a confusing failure.
✅ **THE CHECK IS NOW ROUTINE, AND THAT IS THE POINT.** `ch23route` R11/R12 exist precisely to ask
this before each leg is written. ‼ *A trap that recurs is not bad luck — it is a rule written at the
wrong level of generality.*


## 2026-09-04 — I WROTE A DIAGNOSTIC THAT RULED OUT THE TRUE CAUSE, THEN BELIEVED IT FOR SIX DRIVES

**Symptom.** §Ch23 leg 5 reached Wally's trigger tile (3,23) and `DEFEATED_WALLY_VICTORY_ROAD` stayed
clear. I spent **six diagnostic drives** proving the coord-event mechanic was intact.

**The mechanic was never broken.** `WallyEntranceBattle` ran, and the log carried
`BattleScript_LocalBattleLostEnd` **twice**, with two `WhiteoutListener` hand-offs. ⇒ **the trigger
fired and the bot LOST THE BATTLE.**

**⛔⛔ THE ROOT CAUSE IS THE MESSAGE I WROTE MYSELF.** The raise read:

> *"a clear flag here means the trigger was never stepped on — **not** that the battle was lost
> (a loss whites out instead)."*

Every clause is wrong in the case that happened, and the sentence **ruled out the true cause by
name**. Worse, the disconfirming evidence was printed in the same output the whole time: the driver's
own `whiteouts=2` line, two lines below the failure text. I read past it six times because my
message had already told me what the answer was not.

‼ **A DIAGNOSTIC THAT SAYS WHAT THE FAILURE *ISN'T* IS A CLAIM — AND A WRONG ONE IS WORSE THAN NO
MESSAGE**, because it redirects the reader with authority. ⇒ **state what was OBSERVED and let the
reader weigh it.** The rewritten raise now prints the three diagnostics and ends: *"If all three are
good, the trigger fired and the BATTLE WAS LOST."*

**Three more errors inside the same chase, each worth its own line:**

1. ⛔ **AN INSTRUMENT THAT CHANGED WHAT IT MEASURED.** I added `on_battle_started` to count battles —
   but that hook is the **strategy provider**, and I returned `None`. `Ch23CrossMode` (leg 4) has no
   override at all and battles worked fine, so my counter *introduced* a defect into the thing it was
   measuring. ⇒ **before overriding a hook to observe something, check whether its RETURN VALUE is
   load-bearing.**
2. ⛔ **I MEASURED A VALUE ADJACENT TO THE LOAD-BEARING ONE AND CALLED THE QUESTION SETTLED.** I read
   `MapLocation.elevation` (the tile's grid elevation) and reported "elevation 4 — matches". The
   value the game actually compares is `gObjectEvents[player].previousElevation`, a *different
   number* that merely happened to agree. Same class as reading `tail`'s exit code for the gate
   suite's.
3. ⛔ **I MISAPPLIED MY OWN RECON.** I treated "Hope is an unavoidable sight battle" as proof that
   *any* 1F traversal must fight her, so `battles=0` looked like a second broken mechanic and I built
   a "two mechanics, one shared cause" theory on it. The recon says her cone is unavoidable on the
   route to **the ladder (44 steps)**; leg 5 walks to **the trigger (29 steps)**, which never enters
   it. **Zero battles was the CORRECT result.** ⇒ *a claim scoped to one route is not a claim about
   the map.*

**⭐ THE TECHNIQUE THAT FINALLY SETTLED IT, AND IT IS REUSABLE.** `GAME_STAT_STEPS` is incremented at
`field_control_avatar.c:157`, **inside the same `if (input->tookStep)` block and two lines above** the
call that runs coord events — and nothing else increments it. So the step-count DELTA across a walk
is a perfect proxy for *"did the step gate open on every step?"*. Measured **23491 − 23462 = 29**
against a 29-waypoint walk ⇒ the gate opened every time and the lookup ran with correct arguments.
That one number eliminated the entire mechanic-is-broken family in a single drive.

**Prevention rules.**
⛔⛔ **NEVER WRITE "THIS IS NOT X" INTO A FAILURE MESSAGE UNLESS X IS DISPROVEN *AT THAT MOMENT* BY A
VALUE IN THE MESSAGE.** Diagnostics enumerate observations; they do not adjudicate.
⛔ **WHEN A FAILURE PERSISTS, RE-READ THE FULL RUN OUTPUT BEFORE FORMING THE NEXT HYPOTHESIS.** The
counters that contradicted me were always on screen. A hypothesis built without re-reading is built
on the last thing you happened to notice.
⛔ **FIND THE GAME'S OWN COUNTER FOR THE GATE YOU SUSPECT.** A step counter, a flag, a stat — an
incrementing value adjacent to the branch under test converts "is this code path running?" from an
argument into a measurement.


## 2026-09-04 — I DELETED THE WORKING CODE BECAUSE A PROXY SAID IT SHOULDN'T BE NEEDED

**Symptom.** §Ch23 leg 5 contained a "re-entry" loop that walked between Wally's two trigger tiles.
A decomp analysis gave me a decision rule: `GAME_STAT_STEPS` is incremented inside the very
`if (input->tookStep)` block that runs coord events, two lines above the call, so *"a step delta
matching the walk length proves the gate opened and the re-entry cannot help."* I measured
**delta = 29 across a 29-waypoint walk**, concluded the loop was dead weight, and deleted it —
writing a confident comment about deleting refuted experiments.

**The very next drive refuted ME:**

| | battles | whiteouts | `WallyEntranceBattle` | steps_delta |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **with** the re-entry | 5 | 2 | **RUNS** | 29 |
| **without** it | 0 | 0 | never fires | 29 |

**The delta is identical in both.** So the proxy cannot distinguish them, and the loop is the only
thing that makes the battle fire.

**Root cause.** The step counter proves a step **completed**. It does *not* prove the coord-event
lookup ran **with the arrival position on that frame**. Those are different claims, and I let the
cheap one settle the expensive one because it came with a decomp citation and a clean number.
‼ **A citation makes a premise credible; it does not make it the same claim as your conclusion.**

**What made it recoverable.** I re-drove after deleting, rather than committing on the inference —
so the deletion and its refutation were one run apart, and the comparison was accidentally a clean
A/B: same fixture, same code except the block, same step delta.

**Prevention rules.**
⛔⛔ **A PROXY THAT SAYS "THIS SHOULD NOT BE NECESSARY" NEVER OUTRANKS AN A/B SHOWING THAT IT IS.**
Direct evidence about the behaviour beats an inference about the mechanism, even a well-cited one.
⛔ **BEFORE DELETING CODE AS UNNECESSARY, RUN THE ARM WITHOUT IT.** This project already had the
rule in the other direction — *"a claim of the form 'without X the bug survives' is a CLAIM, and the
only currency is an arm with X removed"* — and the converse holds exactly as hard: *"X is redundant"*
is a claim, and its currency is an arm with X removed. I had that arm available and reasoned instead.
