left "NOT mechanically defended". **This instance settles that call with evidence:**
* the deleted gate compared *"next step"* declarations **per line**. These two clauses are not two next-step
  declarations — one is an imperative and one is a *diagnosis*. ⇒ **it would have returned PASS.**
* the independent Tier 1 reviewer quoted both halves and rejected the commit. ⇒ **it returned KICK-BACK.**
⇒ ⭐ **DELETING THE GATE WAS RIGHT, AND THE REVIEWER IS THE CONTROL THAT ACTUALLY WORKS FOR THIS CLASS.**
The failure is *semantic contradiction between neighbouring sentences*, which is not a string property.
A regex can catch a duplicated marker; only a reader can catch "these two sentences cannot both be true".
‼ **So do not re-attempt the gate.** Spend the effort on making sure Tier 1 actually runs, and on giving
it the diff plus a claim paragraph — that is what let this reviewer find it in one pass.

**⇒ PREVENTION RULES (three).**
1. ⛔⛔ **WHEN YOU CORRECT A CONCLUSION, SEARCH FOR THE CONCLUSION — NOT FOR THE TOPIC AND NOT FOR THE
   SLUG.** I searched "next action" and "leg-9". The stale text said *"the wall moved from a BOT DEFECT
   to a GAME PROBLEM"* and matched neither. ⇒ **grep for the WORDS OF THE CLAIM YOU ARE RETRACTING**,
   verbatim, tree-wide, and read every hit.
2. ⛔ **A CORRECTION PLACED NEXT TO THE ERROR DOES NOT REPLACE IT — AND ADJACENCY HIDES THIS.** Nine
   instances now, and this is the first where both halves were in one paragraph. ⇒ after editing a
   paragraph, **re-read the WHOLE paragraph as a stranger would**, not just the sentence you inserted.
3. ⭐ **RETRACT IN PLACE, WITH THE OLD WORDS QUOTED.** Every fix here uses the form *(this read "X" —
   SUPERSEDED: Y)*. That is strictly better than deleting X, because a future reader who half-remembers
   X can see it was considered and why it lost — and a grep for X still lands somewhere truthful.

‼ **Corollary about my own checkers, earned twice today:** the verification script I wrote to prove the
retraction landed **failed on correct text**, twice — once because its window regex knew "this read" but
not "this stub briefly read", once because the retraction word sat on the previous line and the window
was line-scoped. ⇒ ⭐ **WHEN A CHECK FAILS, READ THE FAILING LINE BEFORE TOUCHING THE SUBJECT.** Both
times the document was right and the instrument was wrong.


## 2026-09-05 — I overrode an agent AND our own reachability rule with a homemade BFS, and built on it

**Symptom.** I specified, documented and implemented a pre-exit heal for §Ch23 leg 9 (106 lines, a
fault arm, a registry row). The first drive failed at the first navigation:
`UnreachableDestinationError: Could not find a path from (21/32 @ VICTORY_ROAD_1F) to (15/39 @
VICTORY_ROAD_1F)`. The fix was impossible; it has been fully reverted.

**Root cause.** A decomp research note said 1F's entrance corridor "is in the **entrance** component,
not the exit component". That is the single fact that kills the design, and **it was in front of me**.
I doubted it, wrote a BFS over our cached layout, got "one 652-tile component", and treated my own
result as decisive — going so far as to write *"REACHABILITY IS MEASURED, NOT ASSUMED"* into the new
function's docstring, citing the BFS. My flood-fill allowed a step whenever either tile's elevation was
0 or 15, which is not Emerald's rule; the real planner disagrees.

**⭐ WHAT IT COST, AND WHY IT WAS STILL CHEAP.** One 120k-frame drive (~7 minutes) and a revert. It was
cheap **only because the drive came before the next build step**. Had I stacked the bypass work on top
first, the same refutation would have invalidated two features instead of one.

**⇒ PREVENTION RULES (three).**
1. ⛔⛔ **REACHABILITY IS `calculate_path` FROM A REAL CAPTURED POSITION. NOTHING ELSE COUNTS.** This is
   already the project's rule (`ai-research-notes/00-READ-THIS-FIRST.md` names it explicitly) and I
   substituted a homemade instrument for it *while quoting the rule*. ⇒ **a flood-fill over cached map
   data is a HINT, at the same tier as an agent's recall — never the tier above it.**
2. ⛔ **PER-TILE WALKABILITY IS NOT CONNECTIVITY.** The tile table I produced was CORRECT — every
   collision and elevation value matches. The *conclusion drawn from it* was wrong. ⇒ when a cheap
   check succeeds, be precise about which claim it actually licenses; "all these tiles are walkable"
   does not license "a path exists between them".
3. ⭐ **WHEN A SOURCE YOU ARE ABOUT TO OVERRIDE IS THE ONLY ONE THAT WOULD STOP YOU, THAT IS THE MOMENT
   TO SPEND MORE, NOT LESS.** The agent's component remark was the single load-bearing claim against my
   design. I refuted it with the weakest instrument available instead of the strongest. ⇒ **rank
   instruments by authority, and let the load-bearing claim be settled by the top one.**

‼ **The genuinely valuable output is the NEGATIVE result:** `calculate_path` has now MEASURED that from
the leg-8 landing (21,32) the entrance arrow warp is unreachable ⇒ **there is no heal of any kind
between leg 8 and leg 10.** That permanently removes "heal before the traverse" from the option set and
leaves only the routing levers. A refuted design that returns a durable measurement is not a wasted
drive.


## 2026-09-05 — the 10th instance: I retracted a claim's BODY and left its HEADLINE announcing it

**Symptom.** Fixing the ninth instance of "I edited the half I named", I retracted the refuted
pre-exit-heal design inside the handoff's `➡➡➡` marker — and left the marker's own bolded headline
reading **"NEXT ACTION — `#24-ch23chain` STEP 4: WIRE THE HEALING THAT IS ALREADY BUILT."** The very
next clause said *"THE HEAL IS REFUTED — MEASURED IMPOSSIBLE."* A Tier 1 reviewer caught it: a skimmer
reading only the bold queue head is sent to build the exact thing the body proves impossible.

**Root cause.** I treated "retract the claim" as an operation on the SENTENCE that states it. The
headline is a second assertion of the same claim, in the position most likely to be acted on — and it
is not phrased like the sentence, so no search for the claim's wording finds it.

**⇒ PREVENTION RULES (two).**
1. ⛔⛔ **RETRACTING A CLAIM MEANS REWRITING EVERY HEADLINE THAT ANNOUNCES IT.** Headings, bold queue
   heads, table cells and list labels each ASSERT; a retraction buried under one of them does not
   reach the reader who acts on it. ⇒ after any retraction, **re-read the enclosing block from its
   nearest heading downward** and ask whether the heading is still true.
‼‼ **AND THE 11th INSTANCE HAPPENED WHILE THIS ENTRY WAS BEING WRITTEN.** The reviewer named the handoff marker's headline; I fixed THAT headline and left its identical twin — the step-4 heading in `03-PUNCH-LIST.md`, still reading *"THE LIVE STEP IS NOW (4): HEAL BEFORE LEG 9"* — untouched, in the other half of the very pair this project defines as P1/P5. My own self-check grep caught it, one command after I wrote rule 1. ⇒ ⭐⭐ **RULE 1 IS INCOMPLETE AS STATED: "rewrite every headline that announces it" MUST mean *in every file*, and the pair definition already says which files.** A reviewer names the instance it found; it does not enumerate the twins. ⇒ **when a finding is about a headline, immediately grep the OTHER half of the pair for the same headline before fixing anything.**

2. ⭐ **THIS ONE WAS WRITTEN *DURING* THE FIX FOR THE PREVIOUS ONE.** Nine instances of the same class
   did not stop the tenth, and the tenth occurred inside the remediation of the ninth. ⇒ **the moment
   of highest risk for this error is while you are correcting it** — you are focused on the sentence
   you came to change, which is exactly the wrong granularity. ‼ And note which control caught it:
   not a gate (the deleted one would have passed — this is one imperative and one diagnosis, not two
   next-step declarations), but an independent reviewer reading for meaning. That is now three catches
   for Tier 1 in one session and zero for any mechanical check.


## 2026-09-05 — my probe called `calculate_path` FROM A BRIDGE TILE and published the false negative to four documents

**Symptom.** `--driver ch23leg9probe` reported `bypass_to_exit = {'reachable': False, 'why':
'PathFindingError'}`, and I concluded **"the (33,17) bypass is DEAD"** — writing it into
`07-CHANGELOG.md`, `03-PUNCH-LIST.md`, `04-HANDOFF.md` and a research note, and using it to eliminate
the option. A research workflow challenged it. **It was an artifact of my own call**, and re-measuring
correctly showed the bypass is not merely alive but **FREE**.

**Root cause, verified in our own code before believing the workflow.**
```
map_path.py:916   open_queue.put(PathNode(source_tile, source_tile.elevation, ...))
map_path.py:859   if tile.elevation not in (0, 15) and from_elevation != 0
                  and tile.elevation != from_elevation: return False
```
The search is seeded with the **source TILE's** elevation. (33,17) sits on the elevation-**15** bridge,
so the search began as a phantom player carrying 15 and was then forbidden from stepping onto every
normal elevation-3 tile. ⇒ the refusal described **my call**, not the map.
‼ **A real player never carries 15** — it keeps its own elevation while crossing a multi-level tile.

**What the corrected measurement says** — same probe, source moved one tile north to **(33,16)**
(elevation 3, off the bridge):
```
to_bypass_33_16        reachable  44 wp   enters_cones []   SAFE
bypass_33_16_to_exit   reachable  18 wp   enters_cones []   SAFE      44 + 18 = 62
direct route           reachable  62 wp   ENTERS the cone at (31,17)
CONTROL from (33,17)   PathFindingError  ← the artifact, reproduced beside the fix
```
⇒ ⭐⭐ **THE BYPASS COSTS EXACTLY WHAT THE DANGEROUS ROUTE COSTS — 62 WAYPOINTS EITHER WAY — AND
AVOIDS BOTH TRAINERS.** The decomp note's original "+0 steps" claim was RIGHT; I refuted it with a
broken instrument and then recorded my refutation as measured fact.

**⇒ PREVENTION RULES (three).**
1. ⛔⛔ **`calculate_path` FROM A TILE THE BOT IS NOT STANDING ON IS ONLY VALID WHEN THAT TILE'S
   ELEVATION MATCHES THE BOT'S.** Off-elevation sources — bridges (15), water (1), stair/ledge
   transitions — produce refusals that say nothing about the map. ⇒ **when probing a hypothetical
   waypoint, seed from a tile of the elevation the bot will actually carry**, and say which that is.
2. ⛔ **A REFUSAL IS ONLY A MEASUREMENT IF THE QUESTION WAS ASKABLE.** I had written into the probe's
   own docstring that *"a refusal IS the reading"* — true for a genuine query, false for a malformed
   one. ⇒ **before recording a negative result, ask what would have to be true for the tool to refuse
   for an uninteresting reason** — and where cheap, include a CONTROL that would expose it. This probe
   now keeps the bad (33,17) call, labelled, precisely so the artifact stays visible.
3. ⭐ **THE THIRD WRONG REACHABILITY ANSWER IN ONE SESSION, AND THE FIRST TWO WERE MY BFS.** Twice I
   trusted a homemade flood-fill over the planner; the third time I trusted the planner but **fed it
   an invalid question**. ⇒ the lesson is not "use `calculate_path`" — it is **"state the elevation
   and the standing tile your reachability claim assumes"**, because both instruments fail silently on
   exactly that axis.

‼ **And note what caught it:** not a gate, not my own re-reading — an adversarial research agent told
to REFUTE the plan, which went and read `map_path.py`. That is four catches this session for
independent adversarial review and zero for any mechanical check.


## 2026-09-05 — the SUMMARY LINE of an option list has now been wrong three times

**Symptom.** `#24-ch23chain`'s step 4 carries a one-line summary of its options. Today it read, in
sequence: *"(a) is the fix; (b)/(c) are cheap force-multipliers — DO (a) FIRST"* → *"(a) AND (b) ARE
BOTH REFUTED. (c) IS THE WHOLE OPTION SET"* → and now *"(b) IS SELECTED"*. **Each rewrite was itself
made stale by the next measurement, and twice I updated the option BLOCKS and left the summary.**

**Root cause.** A summary is a DERIVED claim: it restates the status of every item beneath it. Editing
any one option silently invalidates it, and it does not contain the words of the option it summarises,
so a grep for the changed option's text never finds it.

**⇒ PREVENTION RULES (two).**
1. ⛔ **A SUMMARY OF N THINGS IS N CLAIMS, AND IT ROTS WHEN ANY ONE OF THEM MOVES.** ⇒ when you change
   an option, a step, or a status, **immediately re-read the nearest sentence that summarises the
   group** — it is the half most likely to be stale and the least likely to be found by searching for
   what you changed. This is the same failure as heading-vs-body (instances 10 and 11), one level up.
2. ⭐ **PREFER A SUMMARY THAT NAMES THE MEASUREMENT, NOT THE VERDICT.** *"(b) is dead"* rots; *"(b):
   44+18=62 wp, cone-free"* stays true even when the choice changes, because a measurement is not a
   decision. Where a verdict is genuinely needed, put it in exactly ONE place and point at it.

‼ **And a note on gates, earned the same hour:** the run that caught this also produced a RED from
`probe_closed_item_refs.py` that was a **false positive** — it read *"step 1 DONE 2026-09-04"* in an
open item's header as a closed-status marker. ⇒ ⭐ **WHEN A GATE GOES RED, ESTABLISH WHETHER THE
SUBJECT OR THE INSTRUMENT IS WRONG BEFORE EDITING EITHER.** I have now had this cut both ways in one
session: three times the instrument was wrong (two BFS runs, one malformed `calculate_path`), and the
temptation each time was to believe the reading and rewrite the subject.


## 2026-09-05 — I swept for the SENTENCE I wrote, not for the CLAIM, and five live copies survived

**Symptom.** Having established that "the (33,17) bypass is dead" was false, I swept the tree and
reported it clean. A Tier 1 reviewer then found **five live copies still asserting it**, three of them
in sections this session never opened — including the handoff's **STATE table**, which is the canonical
"where are we" cell and was still commanding the superseded split-singles plan.

**Root cause.** My sweep grepped the phrases I remembered writing: `bypass is DEAD`, `MEASURED DEAD`,
`61 steps`, `+0 steps`. The survivors said *"dead end"*, *"NOT reachable from it"*, *"reachable 43 wp"*,
*"(measured dead)"*. **Same claim, different words** — so the sweep returned clean while the claim
stood in five places.

**⇒ PREVENTION RULE — and this one supersedes the weaker version I wrote two hours earlier.**
⛔⛔ **SWEEP BY THE FACT-BEARING TOKEN, NEVER BY YOUR OWN SENTENCE.** A claim is *about* something —
a coordinate, an identifier, a number, a filename. Those tokens appear in **every** phrasing because
they are the data; prose is rewritten freely around them. Here, `grep -E "33,17|43 wp"` found all five
instantly, including the three I had never read.
⇒ Practically: before declaring a retraction complete, **grep the one token the claim cannot be stated
without**, and read every hit. ‼ Expect noise — that sweep flagged ten lines of which nine were neutral
geometry or correct retractions. **A coarse token sweep is for finding CANDIDATES; the reading is still
yours.** Noise is the correct trade: a sweep that only matches your own wording is silent exactly where
you most need it.

‼ **Corollary about summaries, now confirmed twice in one hour:** the reviewer noted my own rule
("re-read the nearest sentence that summarises the group") should have caught these — and it did not,
because I applied it only in the files I was editing. ⇒ **the summary sentence and the status cell live
in EVERY file that mentions the item, not just the one you have open.** The STATE table is the highest-
value instance and the easiest to forget, because it is a table cell and reads nothing like prose.


## 2026-09-05 — my A/B passed on BOTH arms, because the fixture was healthier than production

**Symptom.** I built the leg-9 bypass and ran a clean A/B: arm A (bypass) `battles=1`, arm B
(`NOBYPASS=1`) `battles=2` with the extra fight at exactly **(31,17)** — the tile the chain drive died
on. The discriminator is exact and the mechanism is proven. **But both arms returned
`ACCEPTANCE: PASS`, `whiteouts=0`** — the direct route WON the fight that killed the chain.

**Root cause.** `post_return.ss1` enters that fight with **Mightyena at 141/141 (100%)**; the real
chain arrives with **Mightyena at 23/143 (16%)** after eight battles and no heal. Same tile, same
trainers, materially different party. ⇒ the fixture is **healthier than production at the same point**.

**Why this matters more than it sounds.** Had I not compared the two entry states, the natural write-up
was *"the bypass fixes the leg-9 loss — A/B proven."* It does not. It provably removes an ENCOUNTER;
whether that converts the chain's loss into a win is a different claim, and only the full chain drive
can settle it.

**⇒ PREVENTION RULES (two).**
1. ⛔⛔ **BEFORE GRADING AN A/B, COMPARE THE FIXTURE'S ENTRY STATE TO PRODUCTION'S AT THE SAME POINT.**
   If the fixture is healthier/richer/further along, the control arm may survive something production
   cannot, and **a PASS on both arms is then uninformative about the outcome** — even when the
   discriminator is perfect. ⇒ quote both entry states in the write-up.
2. ⭐ **NAME WHICH CLAIM THE A/B SUPPORTS: "removes an encounter" or "converts a loss into a win".**
   They need different evidence. The first needs a discriminator; the second needs the control arm to
   actually FAIL. Mine had the first and I nearly wrote the second.

‼ **Related, same run:** I predicted the bypass would meet NEITHER trainer and it met one — **Edgar
(33,22)**, a MANDATORY sight battle already documented in the handoff's own recon. The code was right;
my forecast was careless. ⇒ **when predicting a count, enumerate from the map data you already have**,
not from the two actors you happen to be thinking about.


## 2026-09-05 — I costed a routing change as "free" and it cost ₽4,128

**Symptom.** Leg 9 was re-routed around two trainers to stop the party being wiped. I priced the detour
carefully — **62 waypoints either way, exactly the direct route's cost** — and recorded the trade-off
as *"forfeits their EXP"*, weighed against the Elite Four level gap. The chain then cleared Victory
Road for the first time and failed at leg 11, **₽2,387 short** of the basket.

**Root cause.** I enumerated ONE of the things a skipped encounter produces. A trainer battle yields
**EXP, PRIZE MONEY, sometimes an item, and sometimes a flag**. The arithmetic is exact and I could have
computed it in advance: ₽56,041 (drive with the fight) − ₽51,913 (drive with the bypass) = **₽4,128**
= 2 × ₽2,064 = 2 × (`48 × level 43`) for two Cooltrainers.

**⇒ PREVENTION RULES (two).**
1. ⛔⛔ **"THE DETOUR IS FREE" IS A CLAIM ABOUT STEPS ONLY. ENUMERATE EVERY YIELD OF WHAT YOU SKIP.**
   For a trainer that is EXP, money, items and flags; for an item ball, the item and its flag; for a
   scripted event, whatever it sets. ⇒ **write the list before calling anything free** — the cost that
   bites is the one not on the list.
2. ⭐ **A COST THAT APPEARS TWO LEGS LATER STILL BELONGS TO THE CHANGE THAT CAUSED IT.** The failure
   surfaced at leg 11 as a shopping problem, which is exactly where a future reader would NOT look for
   a leg-9 routing decision. ⇒ the leg-11 refusal message now names the cause out loud (*"if this
   appeared after a ROUTING change, check what payouts the new route skips: ₽2,064 per Cooltrainer"*).
   **When you accept a trade-off, put the pointer at the place the bill will arrive, not only at the
   place you made the choice.**

‼ **What went RIGHT and is worth copying:** the leg-11 guard refused to buy a thinner basket silently.
That turned an invisible §Ch24 defeat five fights later into a loud, precise, early failure with the
exact shortfall in the message. ⇒ **a guard that refuses to degrade quietly is worth more than the
feature it blocks.**


## 2026-09-06 — my retraction convention FIGHTS a measuring gate, and the gate is right

**Symptom.** After the promotion, `audit_doc_consistency` flagged nine docs claiming `drift=14` when
the measured drift was 0. I fixed all nine using this project's standard retraction form — *(this read
"Drift is 14")* — and **four still failed**, because the gate matched the number inside my own
quotation.

**Root cause.** The retraction convention exists for PROSE claims, where quoting the old wording helps
a reader who half-remembers it. But `audit_doc_consistency` does not read prose — it **MEASURES** drift
by running the comparison, then greps for numeric claims. A quoted stale number is indistinguishable
from a live one to a grep, and *should* be: the gate cannot know my parenthesis means "formerly".

**⇒ PREVENTION RULES (two).**
1. ⛔ **WHERE A GATE MEASURES A FACT, DO NOT PRESERVE THE STALE VALUE VERBATIM IN A CURRENT-STATE
   FILE.** State the new value and point at the append-only log for the history. ⇒ **retract prose by
   quoting; retract MEASURED NUMBERS by deleting and pointing.** They are different operations and I
   had one habit for both.
2. ⭐ **PREFER A GATE THAT DERIVES GROUND TRUTH OVER ANY SWEEP OVER PROSE.** This gate found all nine
   sites in one pass, including two saying *"promotion is the USER's call"* after the promotion had
   happened — which no token sweep of mine would have connected. ‼ My own sweeps this week only worked
   once I guessed the right token. **Wherever a fact is mechanically measurable, measure it and check
   the docs against the measurement**; that is strictly stronger than checking documents against each
   other.


## 2026-09-06 — I cited two evidence files without opening them. BOTH were empty of evidence.

**Symptom.** The promotion's DIVERGENCE-LOG entry cited
`evidence/2026-09-06-PROMOTION-{BEFORE,AFTER}-custom.*` as the proof. I had created both with
`... | tail -N | tee <file>`. **Neither contained a single line of the evidence it was cited for** —
no `ACCEPTANCE`, no `ModuleNotFoundError`. I was one commit from shipping a promotion record whose
proof was shutdown noise.

**Root cause, two compounding halves.**
1. **I captured the wrong STREAM.** The harness writes its verdict to the `--log` file; stdout's tail
   is emulator shutdown chatter. `tee` faithfully captured what I pointed it at, which was not the
   thing the claim rests on. ⇒ **the same shape as "instrument the ACTION, not the input to it"**,
   now applied to evidence capture.
2. **The raw `.log` that DID hold the verdict is GITIGNORED** (`tools/story-dev/.gitignore:2  *.log`).
   So even the correct file would not have travelled to another machine — the identical trap as the
   `stalls/` saves, which this project has already paid for once (`ki90_double_absent_seed.ss1`).

**⇒ PREVENTION RULES (three).**
1. ⛔⛔ **READ AN EVIDENCE FILE BEFORE CITING IT.** One `grep` for the string the claim depends on. I
   wrote the citation, the summary and the log entry without ever opening either file.
2. ⛔ **A TRANSCRIPT MUST BE CHECKED FOR THE CLAIM'S OWN KEYWORD, NOT FOR EXISTENCE.** "The file is
   there and is 3 KB" proves nothing. The check that works is `grep -c ACCEPTANCE <file>` — and it is
   cheap enough to be unconditional.
3. ⛔ **BEFORE CITING A PATH AS DURABLE EVIDENCE, ASK WHETHER GIT WILL KEEP IT** — `git check-ignore -v
   <path>`. An evidence directory can still be covered by a `*.log` rule two lines long.

‼ **What caught it:** not a gate and not the reviewer — I went to confirm the cited files existed
before committing, and found them empty. ⇒ ⭐ **the habit of verifying your own citation is worth more
than the citation**, and it is the third time this session that opening the artefact refuted the
sentence about it.


## 2026-09-06 — a GREEN GATE let ten stale copies through, and I trusted the green

**Symptom.** After the promotion, `audit_doc_consistency` flagged nine docs claiming `drift=14`. I
fixed all nine, re-ran it, got **PASS**, and treated the sweep as complete. A Tier 1 reviewer then
found a **10th** live claim inside `04-HANDOFF.md`'s banner — and my own follow-up sweep found **two
more** phrased as *"PROMOTION IS THE USER'S CALL"*, which the gate does not check at all because it is
not a numeric claim.

**Root cause, two parts.**
1. ⛔ **I read a green gate as "no instances remain" when it means "no instances THIS GATE CHECKS
   remain".** The gate checks numeric drift claims; "promotion is the user's call" is a STATUS claim in
   prose and outside its contract entirely.
2. ⛔ **The gate is genuinely blind at that position** — fault-proven, filed as `KI-92`: a stale claim
   injected 17,400 chars into a 39,825-char line passes.

**⇒ PREVENTION RULES (three).**
1. ⛔⛔ **A GREEN GATE BOUNDS ITS OWN CONTRACT, NOT THE WORLD.** Before treating a sweep as finished,
   ask *what shape does this gate NOT check?* Here: prose status claims, and anything its unit logic
   cannot reach. ⇒ **pair every mechanical check with one sweep in a DIFFERENT shape** — I found the
   remaining two by grepping the STATUS phrase, which no gate owns.
2. ⭐ **WHEN A REVIEWER FINDS WHAT A GATE MISSED, FAULT-TEST THE GATE.** Re-injecting the exact claim
   turned "the reviewer was luckier" into "the instrument is blind, here is the repro" — a filed,
   reproducible defect instead of an anecdote. That took two minutes.
3. ⭐ **A 39,825-CHARACTER LINE DEFEATS EVERY PER-LINE INSTRUMENT, INCLUDING MINE.** My token sweeps
   print `file:line`, which is useless when the file has one line holding years of history. ⇒ report
   `file:line@offset` when a line is huge, and treat "the longest line in the file" as the **last**
   place a stale fact will be found and therefore the **first** place to look.


## 2026-09-06 — two §Ch24 notes and a 4-agent workflow all computed damage from an assumption nobody measured

**Symptom.** §Ch24 planning has produced careful damage tables since 2026-09-04: which Elite Four
attack OHKOs which of our mons, which fight ends the run, which TM fixes it. **Every one of those
numbers assumed IV 31 / EV 0.** Measuring the party today gives implied `(IV + EV//4)` contributions
ranging **1 to 54** — and for Sceptile, the mon the whole plan hinges on, a special attack of **20**
where 31 was assumed.

**Root cause.** The assumption was made once, early, in a note that was then CITED rather than
re-checked. Each later analysis inherited it as a premise and did rigorous work on top — and **the
rigour is what made it convincing.** Nobody re-derived the premise because the conclusions looked
carefully argued.

**⇒ PREVENTION RULES (three).**
1. ⛔⛔ **AN UNMEASURED INPUT DOES NOT BECOME MEASURED BY BEING USED IN A CAREFUL CALCULATION.** The
   more elaborate the arithmetic downstream, the more authoritative a guessed input looks. ⇒ before
   trusting a damage/threshold/timing table, **name its inputs and mark each measured or assumed** —
   and check whether the tool to measure it already exists. Here it did: the probe already read
   `mon.stats.speed`; adding five more fields took minutes.
2. ⭐ **THE AGENT THAT DOUBTS ITS OWN NUMBERS IS THE VALUABLE ONE.** Three angles produced confident
   damage analysis; one said *"every damage number in this report rests on an unmeasured estimate,
   measure it before you trust my level target."* That single caveat was worth more than the three
   confident reports, and it is why the adversarial angle is always briefed to attack.
3. ⛔ **WHEN A PREMISE FALLS, RE-GRADE THE CONCLUSIONS — DO NOT DELETE THE NOTES.** The ROSTER and
   ROUTING sections of both §Ch24 notes are independent of this assumption and remain sound. Only the
   DAMAGE sections are now unsourced. ⇒ **mark the affected sections rather than discarding the
   document**, or the good half is lost with the bad.


## 2026-09-06 — my probe abandoned a live battle and produced a signature that looked like a bot hang

**Symptom.** The first §Ch24 probe run ended in `HANG CONFIRMED` with
`state=BATTLE ctrl=<none>` and `BattleScript_SelectingTormentedMove` in the no-progress signature. It
looked exactly like a Torment defect in our move chooser.

**It was my instrument.** The probe's battle wait was **4,000 frames**. When it expired the probe fell
through to its report and called `set_manual_mode()` — **abandoning a live battle**, which then waited
forever for a move selection that no controller was left to make. The party EXP was frozen for 10,000
frames because *nothing was driving the fight at all*.

**⇒ PREVENTION RULES (two).**
1. ⛔⛔ **AN INSTRUMENT THAT ABANDONS THE THING IT MEASURES PRODUCES A SIGNATURE THAT LOOKS LIKE A
   FINDING.** The stall state it reports is wherever the subject happened to be standing, and it will
   name a real mechanic — Torment, here — which makes the false finding *plausible and specific*. ⇒
   before reading a hang signature, **prove the instrument was still attached**: look for
   `no controller on the stack` and check the wait budget against the frame it stopped at.
2. ⭐ **A TIMEOUT MUST REFUSE, NOT FALL THROUGH.** The probe now raises with an explicit message
   ("do NOT read this as a bot hang until you have checked the controller was still attached") instead
   of quietly finishing. ⇒ **a bounded wait that ends silently converts an unfinished measurement into
   a confident wrong one** — the same shape as a gate that passes without printing a verdict.

‼ **The second run, with a 90,000-frame budget, shows the controller dropping at ~f19,363 — so there
IS a real defect underneath (`KI-93`).** But the first run's evidence is VOID and is recorded as void:
had I filed KI-93 from it, the diagnosis would have rested on a measurement of my own bug.


## 2026-09-06 — my A/B instrument silently swapped the subject, three different ways

**Symptom.** Building the turn recorder that the KI-93 fix's ordinary-case A/B depends on, it produced
no output file. Three separate defects, found one at a time, and **not one of them announced itself**:
1. `_TurnRecorder` did not subclass `BattleStrategy`, so `_listeners.py:110`'s `isinstance` check
   discarded it and the trainer battle ran on `DefaultBattleStrategy()` instead.
2. `NameError: pathlib` (the harness imports `Path`, not the module) — absorbed, run continued.
3. `__getattr__` delegation does not cover methods the BASE CLASS defines; `BattleStrategy`'s stubs
   `raise NotImplementedError`, so the wrapper passed `isinstance` and then broke everything it had
   not explicitly overridden.

**⇒ PREVENTION RULES (three).**
1. ⛔⛔ **AN INSTRUMENT THAT FAILS DOES NOT GO QUIET — IT SUBSTITUTES THE SUBJECT.** Each of these
   produced a *running bot* on a *different code path* than the one under test. Had the file happened
   to be written, the A/B baseline would have come from the wrong strategy and been believed. ⇒
   **before trusting any wrapper/probe, prove the observed run is UNCHANGED** — here, that the
   recorded run returns the same `ACCEPTANCE`/`battles`/`whiteouts` as the un-instrumented one. That
   check is what makes a recorder evidence rather than decoration.
2. ⛔ **A DELEGATING WRAPPER MUST DELEGATE THE WHOLE SURFACE, NOT RELY ON `__getattr__`.** `__getattr__`
   fires only for attributes Python cannot find, so any method the base class DEFINES — including
   abstract stubs — silently wins. ⇒ install delegates by introspection over the base class, so a
   method added upstream is covered without anyone remembering to.
3. ⭐ **THE MISSING OUTPUT FILE WAS THE ONLY SIGNAL.** No exception surfaced for (1); (2) and (3) were
   absorbed into a continuing run. ⇒ **give an instrument a mandatory artefact and check for it
   FIRST** — "did the thing I built actually write anything?" is the cheapest possible test and it
   caught a class of bug that produces confident, plausible, wrong evidence.


## 2026-09-06 — I copied the right precedent into the wrong place, and one log line proved it

**Symptom.** The KI-93 Torment fix was modelled on a SHIPPED precedent sitting 12 lines above it in
the same function — the `BattleScript_SelectingMoveWithNoPP` fork that overrides a bounced pick. Same
shape, same file, observed-refusal, and it **passed the ordinary-case A/B byte-identically**. It also
did not fix the bug.

**Root cause.** The fork sits AFTER the branch dispatch, so it only runs when a decision is being
COMMITTED. The Torment loop never reaches that point — it cycles
`HandleInputChooseAction` → refusal → `HandleInputChooseMove` → "press B" → `continue`, short-circuiting
first. The PP precedent works because ITS refusal leaves the game somewhere that does reach the commit
path. **The precedent was right about the shape and wrong about the location**, and the two are easy to
conflate because the code looks identical.

**⇒ PREVENTION RULES (three).**
1. ⛔⛔ **"THE FIX IS WRONG" AND "THE FIX IS NEVER REACHED" ARE DIFFERENT ANSWERS.** A fix that changes
   nothing looks exactly like a fix that is incorrect, and they need opposite next steps. ⇒ **before
   theorising about why a fix failed, log that it RAN.** One line, one drive, and the answer was
   unambiguous: zero hits.
2. ⭐ **COPYING A PRECEDENT COPIES ITS PRECONDITIONS, NOT JUST ITS SHAPE.** The PP fork's precondition
   is "the game bounced us into the commit path". I matched the code and inherited an assumption I had
   never checked. ⇒ when reusing a pattern, **ask what state the original relies on and prove the new
   case reaches it.**
3. ⭐ **A PASSING A/B PROVES HARMLESSNESS, NEVER EFFICACY.** The ordinary-case A/B was byte-identical
   — which was true, valuable, and said nothing about whether the bug was fixed. ⇒ keep the two
   questions separate and answer both: *does it break anything?* and *does it do anything?*

‼ **The dead fork was REVERTED, not left in place.** It was provably harmless, which makes it tempting
to keep as "groundwork" — but dead code in the most safety-critical loop in the codebase teaches the
next reader that the case is handled. The corrected design is recorded in `KI-93` instead.


## 2026-09-06 — I guessed three fix locations before reading the stack the harness had already printed

**Symptom.** Fixing `KI-93` (the Torment freeze) I implemented, drove and reverted **three** candidate
fixes in a row. Each was disproved cleanly — I instrumented whether the code RAN rather than theorising
— but each cycle excluded exactly ONE location and cost a full build-drive-revert.

**Root cause.** The harness prints a **generator stack** on every no-progress event, and it was in the
log the whole time. It shows the deepest frame as `handle_battle.<locals>._watch`
(`battle_handler.py:314`) with `handle_battle_action_selection` **not on the stack at all** — which
excludes all three of my guesses simultaneously and names the frame to read instead. I reached for it
only after the third failure.

**⇒ PREVENTION RULES (three).**
1. ⛔⛔ **WHEN SOMETHING HANGS, READ THE STACK BEFORE CHOOSING A FIX SITE.** This harness prints one
   free with every `NO-PROGRESS` line. A stack excludes a whole class of hypotheses at once; a
   drive-and-revert excludes exactly one and costs minutes. ⇒ **the order is stack → hypothesis →
   change**, and I ran it backwards three times.
2. ⭐ **"THE FIX DID NOT WORK" IS NOT A LOCATION.** Each attempt was disproved correctly and I still
   had no idea where the freeze WAS — because eliminating a site tells you nothing about the right
   one. The stack is the only artefact that points forward rather than backward.
3. ⭐ **A PASSING ORDINARY-CASE A/B IS NOT PROGRESS TOWARD A FIX.** All three attempts passed it
   byte-identically. That was genuinely valuable — it proved each was harmless enough to test safely
   — but it is a SAFETY result, not an EFFICACY one, and it made three dead ends feel like progress.

‼ **What went right and is worth keeping:** every attempt was reverted, none left dead code in a
shared battle path, and each was disproved by instrumenting that it RAN rather than by argument. The
discipline was sound; the ORDER was wrong.


## 2026-09-06 — I committed three "eliminated by measurement" verdicts produced by a logger that never wrote

**Symptom.** Chasing `KI-93` I implemented, drove and reverted three candidate fixes, and recorded each
as ELIMINATED because its diagnostic "fired zero times". I committed that to `05-KNOWN-ISSUES.md` as a
table of excluded locations. **All three verdicts were void.** The diagnostics called
`debug_logger.log(...)`; `modules/debug_logger.py` exposes `event()`, not `log()`. The resulting
`AttributeError` was swallowed by **my own `try/except: pass`**, so nothing was ever written.

**Root cause.** I wrote the guard clause reflexively — "a diagnostic must never break the run" is a
good instinct — and it converted a broken instrument into a silent one. "Zero hits" then read as
evidence about the SUBJECT when it was evidence about the INSTRUMENT.

**⇒ PREVENTION RULES (three).**
1. ⛔⛔ **AN INSTRUMENT NEEDS A CONTROL THAT MUST FIRE.** Add one unconditional line that has to appear
   on every pass. If the control is silent, the instrument is broken; only if the control fires and the
   detector does not have you learned anything about the subject. Adding a CONTROL is what finally
   distinguished "not reached" from "not logging" — in one drive, after three wasted cycles.
2. ⛔ **`try/except: pass` AROUND A DIAGNOSTIC IS THE MOST DANGEROUS PLACE TO PUT IT.** It protects the
   run and destroys the measurement. ⇒ let a diagnostic RAISE, or at minimum verify the API exists
   before relying on its silence.
3. ⭐ **"ZERO HITS" IS NEVER EVIDENCE ON ITS OWN.** It is one of: the code did not run, the logger did
   not work, or you are reading the wrong file. ⇒ **rank those three and rule them out in that order**
   — the cheapest first, which is proving the logger writes.

‼ **And the cost was not just the three cycles:** I published the false verdicts to a permanent record
where a future session would have trusted them and skipped the right location. **The correction matters
more than the original finding**, which is why `KI-93` now leads with the retraction rather than
burying it.


## 2026-09-06 — I drove §Ch24 from a fixture whose own note says "NOT READY", all session

**Symptom.** Every §Ch24 probe and all four `KI-93` fix attempts started from
`post_league_shop.ss1`. That fixture's note opens: **"⛔ THE BOT IS NOT READY TO ATTEMPT §Ch24."** The
tell was visible in every drive — `Wailord L47: Dive, Surf, Water Spout, Waterfall`, no Ice Beam,
while a CLOSED punch-list item says Wailord knows it. I read that moveset line a dozen times.

**Root cause.** I picked the fixture by POSITION ("the bot is at the League door") and never read
what state it was in. The §Ch24 prep is a separate lineage — four move changes, Fly, TM13, the teach —
that ends at ROUTE108 and **captures no combined fixture**, so nothing carries it to the League.

**⇒ PREVENTION RULES (three).**
1. ⛔⛔ **A FIXTURE'S NOTE IS A PRECONDITION, NOT DECORATION.** `FIXTURES.md5` entries in this project
   routinely open with what the save is NOT ready for. ⇒ **read the note before the drive**, and treat
   a "NOT READY" as a refusal to start, not a caveat to remember.
2. ⛔ **A CLOSED ITEM CLAIMS A CAPABILITY, NOT A SAVE.** `#24-icebeamteach` is correctly closed — the
   teach works. It does not follow that any fixture HAS the taught move. ⇒ **when a closed item's
   result must persist, ask which fixture holds it**, and if none does, that is an open gap
   (now `KI-94`).
3. ⭐ **THE ANOMALY WAS IN EVERY LOG.** The moveset dump printed on every single drive and contradicted
   a closed item. ⇒ when a routine dump disagrees with a doc, that is the cheapest possible signal —
   **read the dumps you already print** before building instruments to find what they were telling you.

‼ **Cost:** a session of §Ch24 measurement against a party the bot will never field. **Not wasted
entirely** — the routing, `KI-93` and the doc fixes all stand — but the readiness and winnability
numbers must be re-taken.

## 2026-09-06 — I shipped a scale-mixing bug INTO MY OWN FIX for a ranking bug (caught before commit)

**Symptom.** None observed — caught by re-reading the diff I had just written, before any commit and
before the reviewer I had already dispatched came back.

**Root cause.** `rank_replacement`'s legacy fallback was written as:
```python
best_index, best_key, ok, failed = None, None, 0, 0    # ok initialised OUTSIDE the candidate loop
for index, mon, mon_types in candidates:
    ...
    if ok == 0:            # ...but TESTED INSIDE it
        outgoing = legacy
```
`ok` accumulates across candidates, so the fallback was decided **per candidate, in candidate order**:
a candidate measured before the first successful estimate was scored with the legacy multiplier
(0–4) while a later one was scored in damage (0–300) — and the sort key then compared them as if they
were the same quantity. The reverse order did something different again (a later failing candidate
kept `outgoing = 0.0` and got no fallback at all). ⇒ **the winner could depend on party order.**

**What makes this worth writing down:** the prose above the code said *"if every damage estimate fails,
fall back to legacy"*. The code said *"if no estimate has succeeded SO FAR"*. I wrote both, minutes
apart, and the comment made the loop LOOK right on re-reading. This is the same shape as the standing
rule that **a diagnosis and a prescription are two separate claims** — here the docstring was the
prescription and nothing had checked it against the loop.

**The fix that worked.** Two passes: measure every candidate (recording BOTH the damage estimate and
the legacy multiplier), then choose ONE metric for the whole ranking and score every row with it.
Plus `report["metric"]` naming which one decided, so a log line can never leave it ambiguous.

**⭐ PREVENTION RULE — A RANKING IS ONLY MEANINGFUL IF EVERY ROW IS SCORED IN THE SAME UNITS, SO THE
CHOICE OF UNITS MAY NEVER BE MADE INSIDE THE LOOP THAT SCORES THEM.** If a comparison has a fallback
metric, decide the metric in a pass that completes BEFORE any comparison happens. A state variable
that accumulates across iterations must never be read as though it were per-iteration.

**⭐ SECOND PREVENTION RULE, from the same hour — WRITE THE TEST CASE THAT MAKES THE TWO VERSIONS
DISAGREE, or you have not tested the change.** My first three attempts at a regression case for this
bug all returned the SAME winner under the old and new code, so they would have passed over the defect.
Case C6 only became a test once it was built so old→A and new→B. *This is the `08-MISTAKES.md` entry on
vacuous A/Bs arriving in a new costume: an arm that cannot distinguish the arms is not an arm.*

---

## 2026-09-06 — I nearly cited an A/B that CANNOT EXECUTE THE CHANGED CODE as proof of a hot-path fix

**Symptom.** `KI-95`'s own entry, and my overnight plan, both named the ordinary-case turn-recorder A/B
(`POKEBOT_RECORD_TURNS` vs `evidence/ki93_ordinary_BASELINE.turns`) as the gate this fix had to pass.

**Root cause.** The turn recorder records what `decide_turn` RETURNS. The code I changed lives in
`choose_new_lead_after_faint`, **which is not called unless something faints.** In an ordinary battle
the recording is byte-identical whether the fix is present, absent, or actively broken.

**Why it is dangerous rather than merely useless:** it would have come back GREEN, and a green arm gets
quoted. The entry would then have carried "A/B passed" beside a change the A/B never touched.

**The fix that worked.** Ask *"does this run execute the changed line?"* before choosing the
instrument — then build one that does: a pure-function probe (gate #39) whose fault arm proves it goes
RED on the defect.

**⭐ PREVENTION RULE — BEFORE QUOTING AN A/B, NAME THE LINE IT EXECUTES.** *A passing A/B over a code
path the run never reaches is not weak evidence, it is NO evidence* — and it is worse than none,
because it reads as proof. This is the playbook's *choose the instrument by the question* rule applied
one level earlier: not "which question?" but "does the instrument reach the subject at all?"

## 2026-09-06 — my citation "fixer" wrote THREE IMPOSSIBLE LINE RANGES (`2861-2772`), and the gate passed

**Symptom.** An independent Tier 1 reviewer found `story_mode.py:2861-2772`, `story_mode.py:1404-1356`
and `story_mode.py:364-313` in the docs — spans whose START is AFTER their END. All three were created
by the script I wrote to REPAIR citations, minutes earlier, in the same session.

**Root cause.** The repair replaced the token `story_mode.py:2758` with `story_mode.py:2861`. But that
citation was a RANGE — `story_mode.py:2758-2772` — so the substring matched its FIRST HALF and the
end line was left behind pointing at the old file. ⇒ **a line number is not always a line number; it
can be the opening half of a span.**

**Why nothing caught it.** `audit_doc_citations.py` checks that a cited line falls INSIDE the symbol's
span. `2861` does fall inside `_guard`, so the gate went green over a citation that cannot exist. **The
gate validated the half I changed and had no opinion about the half I broke.**

**The fix that worked.** Re-derive the WHOLE span from the source with `ast` (start AND end), keyed on
the symbol named on the same line, and sweep for `start > end` as a standalone invariant.

**⭐ PREVENTION RULE — WHEN REWRITING A NUMBER THAT MAY BE PART OF A COMPOUND TOKEN, MATCH THE WHOLE
TOKEN, NEVER ITS PREFIX.** And after any mechanical doc rewrite, run a cheap self-consistency sweep
over the SHAPE it produced (`start > end`) rather than trusting the gate that motivated the rewrite —
*a green gate bounds its contract, not the world*, and an automated edit is exactly where a
contract's edges get found.

**⭐ SECOND RULE, and the reason the reviewer was worth its cost — ⛔ DO NOT EDIT THE SUBJECT WHILE AN
INDEPENDENT REVIEW OF IT IS IN FLIGHT.** I dispatched two reviewers and then rewrote the file under
them. One correctly refused to certify: *"I cannot certify a diff that mutates under me while the
self-report describes a version that no longer exists on disk."* That is the right call, and the wasted
pass was mine to prevent. **Freeze the tree, or dispatch the review only when you are done editing.**

## 2026-09-06 — three self-inflicted bugs in one hour of `KI-93` work, all in the BOOKKEEPING, not the fix

The `KI-93` dismiss half worked on its FIRST drive — gating on `TextPrinterState.WaitForButton` and
pressing B ended the park every time (`[KI93-WAIT] ENDED after 257 frames`, repeatedly). **Every
failure that followed was in the memory that decides which slot not to re-pick.** Three distinct bugs,
each of which produced a *plausible-looking* log.

### 1. A STALE SIGNAL, READ EVERY FRAME, MANUFACTURES EVIDENCE

I recorded "the slot we last committed was refused" on **every frame** the printer was parked with a
refusal script on screen. But `get_current_battle_script_instruction()` still reads
`SelectingTormentedMove` during the *next* park, so each freshly re-picked slot was marked refused
although the game had never rejected it. Measured: `refused={0: {0, 1, 2, 3}}` — **all four slots** —
after which the re-pick found no alternative and the livelock returned.

**⭐ PREVENTION RULE — SAMPLE A LEVEL ONCE PER EDGE, NEVER CONTINUOUSLY.** A signal that stays true
after the event it describes is a LEVEL, not an event. Reading it in a loop does not gather more
evidence; it manufactures duplicates of one observation and disguises them as many.
⭐ Corollary that caught it: **a derived set that can be complete is telling you it is wrong.** Torment
forbids exactly ONE move, and the engine takes the Struggle path when nothing is usable — so a
"refused everything" state is impossible in the game and therefore a bug in the bookkeeping. Assert the
impossible state and collapse it rather than acting on it.

### 2. A GUARD MADE THE CLEARING BRANCH ITS FALL-THROUGH

The fix for (1) was a once-per-park latch, written as:
```python
if _instr_now in REFUSAL_SCRIPTS and not _ki93_recorded_park:   # ⛔ WRONG
    ...record...
elif _instr_now:
    _ki93_forget()          # "the turn moved on"
```
On the frame after banking a refusal, the first test goes False, the `elif` sees a perfectly truthy
`SelectingTormentedMove`, and **the memory is wiped**. Measured: `refused={}` on every line and
`KI93-REPICK: 0` — the exact opposite failure to (1), from the fix for (1).

**⭐ PREVENTION RULE — A CONDITION'S `elif` INHERITS EVERY TERM YOU ADD TO ITS `if`.** When a guard is
about *whether we have already acted*, it must nest INSIDE the test about *what state we are in*, never
be `and`-ed into it. Adding a term to an `if` silently widens its `elif`.

### 3. `ls -t` SORTS BY MODIFICATION TIME, SO I READ THE WRONG RUN'S LOG

I started a second ROM drive while the first was still running, then picked "the newest log" with
`ls -t | head -1` — which returned the OLDER run, because it was still being appended to and therefore
had the later mtime. I read the previous experiment's numbers as the new one's result.

**⭐ PREVENTION RULE — IDENTIFY AN ARTEFACT BY ITS IDENTITY, NEVER BY ITS RECENCY.** These logs carry
their start time IN THE FILENAME; that is the identity. `ls -t` answers a different question than "which
run produced this".
**⭐ AND: NEVER START A SECOND ROM DRIVE WHILE ONE IS RUNNING.** Beyond the wrong-log trap, they contend
for CPU — which silently corrupted the throughput measurement I took at the same time (see
`ai-research-notes/2026-09-07-emulator-throughput-MEASURED.md`). Wait for the completion signal.

## 2026-09-06 — I broke `CLAUDE.md`'s OWN rule #3 ("assert IDENTITY, never position") and declared the result clean

**Symptom.** An independent adversarial reviewer read my `KI-93` diff and the drive log I had just
called "driven clean", and found that a **fainted** Pokémon's move vetoes were being applied to its
**replacement**:
```
f4348916  Swellow (battler 0) Tormented; refused={0: {0,1,3}}
f4349501  Swellow FAINTS; Castform is sent in to battler 0
f4349924  [KI93-REPICK] battler=0 slot 0 was REFUSED -> 2     ⬅ no preceding [KI93-WAIT]
f4373734  battle_text='NICK whited out!'
```
Castform was forced into Sunny Day for two consecutive turns having been refused nothing, in the
battle that then whited out.

**Root cause.** `_ki93_refused_slots` was keyed by **`battler_index`** — a POSITION. The thing that
earns a refusal is a POKÉMON. `CLAUDE.md` SESSION DISCIPLINE #3 states this in capitals: *"Assert
IDENTITY, never position or count. PIDs — never slot indices."* **I had read that rule this session,
quoted it in another document the same night, and still wrote position-keyed state.**

**What makes this the expensive kind of mistake:** I had already READ that log. I grepped it for
`KI93-DISMISS`, `KI93-REPICK` and `KI-47`, saw healthy-looking counts, and reported success. The
evidence of the defect was in the lines I counted but did not read — **a `[KI93-REPICK]` with no
preceding `[KI93-WAIT]` is an override with no refusal behind it**, and that is visible only if you
look at the sequence rather than the totals.

**The fix that worked.** (1) `_ki93_owner[battler_index]` records the `personality_value` that owns the
memory, checked before every read and write. (2) The memory expires when a turn actually executes —
because Torment forbids the LAST MOVE USED, which changes every turn, so a veto is true only for the
selection episode that produced it.

**⭐ PREVENTION RULE — A COUNT IS NOT A READING. When a log is the evidence for a fix, grade the
SEQUENCE, not the totals.** Name, in advance, the ordering invariant that must hold (here: *every
`REPICK` is preceded by a `WAIT … ENDED` in the same episode*) and grep for its VIOLATIONS, not for the
presence of the happy lines. Healthy counts are exactly what a partially-working fix produces.

**⭐ SECOND RULE — WHEN A RULE EXISTS FOR A BUG CLASS, CHECK THE NEW CODE AGAINST IT BY NAME BEFORE
CALLING THE WORK DONE.** `08-MISTAKES.md` and SESSION DISCIPLINE are not background reading; they are a
checklist with entries like "position vs identity" that can be mechanically applied to a diff. A rule
I had quoted hours earlier did not fire when I wrote the code it governs — which is the precise failure
mode SESSION DISCIPLINE's own preamble warns about: *"a rule filed as 'the lesson from bug X' does not
fire when you are building Y."*

## 2026-09-06 — the grader I wrote to catch my bug PASSED the bug, twice, for two different reasons

Having been caught grading a drive by its totals, I wrote `tools/story-dev/grade_ki93_drive.py` to
grade by SEQUENCE. It then failed its own fault test twice — and both failures are more instructive
than the tool.

### v1 — the invariant was keyed on POSITION, so it flagged CORRECT behaviour

C2 armed on a refusal and disarmed on the next `COMMIT`. That marked **6 re-picks RED that were
right**: `handle_battle_action_selection` is re-entered per selection phase, so a mon's own veto
legitimately survives a commit — that persistence is the entire point of the fix. Keyed by slot, a
mon's carried-over veto and a **fainted mon's veto inherited by its replacement** are the same shape.

**⭐ PREVENTION RULE — AN INVARIANT ABOUT AN ENTITY MUST BE KEYED ON THAT ENTITY.** I fixed the
production code to assert identity and then wrote the CHECKER against position. *The instrument needs
the same discipline as the subject, and it is easy to grant it less because it is "just a script".*

### v2 — it returned PASS on the known-bad log, because it could not SEE identity

With C2 keyed on `owner=`, I re-ran it against the drive that contains the real defect. It printed
**`C2 PASS — 0 REPICK(s) with no refusal behind them`** and `ACCEPTANCE: PASS`. That log predates the
`owner=` field, so every lookup returned `"?"`, the arming degenerated, and **the grader cleared the
exact defect it was written to catch.**

**⭐ PREVENTION RULE — A CHECK THAT CANNOT SEE ITS INPUT MUST SAY "INDETERMINATE", NEVER "PASS".**
Missing evidence is not absence of the defect. The grader now detects that its `REPICK` lines carry no
identity and refuses to grade C2, exiting non-zero. ⇒ **a gate that passes its own fault case is worse
than no gate** — this project already had that rule for false POSITIVES (they teach the reader to
bypass), and this is the mirror image: a false NEGATIVE teaches the reader to trust.

**⭐ THIRD RULE, re-learned the same hour — `EXIT=$?` AFTER A PIPE REPORTS THE PIPE.** I printed
`EXIT=0` from `... | grep -E "C2|ACCEPTANCE"` and briefly read the grader as passing; run without the
pipe it exits 1. `run_gates.py`'s own docstring warns about exactly this, which is why that runner
reads `returncode` directly.

## 2026-09-07 — a PERFECT 30-minute grind wrote NOTHING, and I had reproduced a trap this very file records

**Symptom.** `--driver ch24grind` took all four battlers from L47/51 to **L60** — 623 battles, 0
whiteouts, 1806 s — printed `ACCEPTANCE: PASS`, exited 0, and **left no fixture**. Every level died with
the process.

**Root cause, from the run's own log:** `*** EXCEPTION: name 'pathlib' is not defined`.
`story_harness.py` imports `from pathlib import Path`, not the module, and my capture block wrote
`pathlib.Path(...)`. The exception fired AFTER the ACCEPTANCE line, so the run still looked clean.

**‼ THIS FILE ALREADY CONTAINED THAT TRAP, IN THAT FILE.** The turn-recorder entry records:
*"`NameError: pathlib` — the harness imports `Path`, not the module. The exception was absorbed and the
run continued on the fallback strategy."* I read that entry earlier the same session.

**⭐ BUT THE IMPORT IS THE SHALLOW CAUSE. THE REAL ONE: I VALIDATED THE GRIND AND NEVER THE CAPTURE.**
The L49 validation run was deliberately careful — estimate first, short target, check the levels moved —
and it ran with `GRIND_CAPTURE` **unset**. So the single line that converts 30 minutes of work into a
durable artefact was the one line the validation never executed.

**⭐⭐ PREVENTION RULE — VALIDATE THE PATH THAT KEEPS THE RESULT, NOT ONLY THE PATH THAT PRODUCES IT.**
A rehearsal that skips the save step has not rehearsed the run. When a long job ends in a write, the
write is the part most worth testing first, because it is the only part whose failure costs everything
that came before it. ⇒ **exercise the persistence path on a 90-second run before spending 30 minutes.**

**⭐ SECOND RULE — A LONG JOB MUST CHECKPOINT, NOT COMMIT EVERYTHING TO ITS LAST LINE.** The capture now
runs after EVERY step (~3 min each), so a failure costs one step rather than the night. All-or-nothing
persistence turns any late error into total loss.

**⭐ THIRD RULE — LOG THE DECISION, NOT JUST THE SUCCESS.** "No capture requested" and "the capture
raised" were the same silence. `_checkpoint` now logs on every path, including `NOT REQUESTED` and
`⛔ CAPTURE FAILED`, and confirms a write by RE-READING the file's size. *A guard that cannot tell "no"
from "I broke" is worse than no guard* — the rule `repro_no_silent_except.py` enforces, which I had
just spent an hour satisfying elsewhere in the same file.

## 2026-09-07 — grinding to L60 "broke" §Ch23's chain, and that framing is wrong in a way worth naming

**Symptom.** §Ch23's chain PASSES at L47-52 (`done=True`, `battles=16`, `whiteouts=0`, 2026-09-05).
Driven from the new L60 fixture it **wedges** in the in-battle party menu at ~f27k and never reaches
the League. The obvious reading — *the grind broke the chain* — is false.

**What actually happened.** Production's own `[TURN]` telemetry shows the lead badly poisoned and
falling 118 → 98 → 69 → **31/307**, at which point the strategy correctly chose `RotateLead` — and the
switch hung. ✅ A/B'd with the entire `KI-93` change reverted: **the hang reproduces identically**, so
it is not a regression from that night's work either.

⇒ **At L47 the chain never got that far.** It lost, or ended, before a rotate was ever attempted. The
stronger party did not introduce a defect; it **survived long enough to execute code no drive had ever
executed.**

**⭐ PREVENTION RULE — MAKING THE BOT STRONGER MOVES THE FAILURE, IT DOES NOT REMOVE IT.** Every level
gained, every fix that lets a run continue, pushes execution into paths that have never run. So a
"regression" that appears immediately after an improvement deserves the A/B **before** the blame: revert
the improvement and re-drive. If the bug survives the revert, the improvement was the MESSENGER.
‼ The corollary matters for planning: *a green chain is only green over the states it reached.* §Ch23
passing at L47 was never evidence that §Ch23 passes — only that it passes when the party is too weak to
reach the party menu.

**⭐ SECOND RULE — WHEN A LONG-RUNNING IMPROVEMENT LANDS, EXPECT THE NEXT WALL AND BUDGET FOR IT.** I
priced the grind (30 min) and treated the §Ch24 measurement as the payoff. The real outcome was a new
blocker (`KI-96`) standing between the two — which is the normal shape of unblocking work, not a
surprise. Say so in the plan, so a night that ends at a NEW wall reads as progress rather than failure.

## 2026-09-07 — Tier 0 was GREEN while the STATE table named a dead frontier and a drift figure 7× the truth

**Symptom.** After a night of work and a Tier 1 review and a Tier 2 audit and fixing everything they
found, a Tier 2 **RE-audit** found FIVE more defects — all in `04-HANDOFF.md`'s STATE table, and all
invisible to every mechanical gate:
* the §Ch24 row: *"§Ch24 remains gated on the LEVEL GAP, not on a hang — the party is L48-53"* —
  **both halves false**: the party was L60 and the blocker was a hang (`KI-96`);
* the *"if stopped mid-task"* row — **the row that says of itself it is what a resuming session reads
  FIRST** — named `#24-ch23chain` / `KI-90` as the live frontier (both closed), claimed **drift 14**
  where `promote.py --check` measures **2**, and cited a superseded pushed commit;
* an instruction to *"RE-READ … THE 60-SECOND DIGEST IN THE SAME EDIT"* — **no such section exists**,
  so the instruction was unobeyable;
* a fixture ladder written `post_grind_L{49..59}.ss1`, implying 11 files where SIX exist;
* the daily upstream check three days overdue.

**Root cause.** I edited the parts of the handoff my work TOUCHED — the banner, the queue marker, the
KI entries — and never re-read the STATE table, because nothing I did that night changed it. But the
world it describes had moved underneath it.

**⭐ PREVENTION RULE — A GREEN TIER 0 MEANS "NO CONTRADICTION IT CAN COUNT", NOT "TRUE".**
`lint_docs` and `audit_doc_consistency` check line budgets, gate counts, drift NUMBERS, citation
targets and flag registration. **None of them can see a stale FACT** — "the frontier is X" and "the
party is L48-53" are sentences no gate parses. Every one of these five passed both gates.
⇒ **The cold-start pass is not ceremony; it is the only instrument that reads MEANING.** And this is
exactly why the rule says *re-run Tier 2 after fixing Tier 2* — the first pass found four defects and
the second found five DIFFERENT ones, in a region the first never reached.

**⭐ SECOND RULE — WHEN AN ITEM SHIPS, RE-READ EVERY ROW THAT DESCRIBES THE WORLD, NOT ONLY THE ROWS
YOU EDITED.** The dangerous rows are the ones your change made stale WITHOUT touching: a STATE table, a
"live frontier" note, a "if stopped mid-task" resume pointer. Grepping for the item's own slug (the P5
rule) does not find them, because they never mention the slug — they describe the situation the slug
just changed. ⇒ after shipping, ask *"which sentences in this file are now false?"*, not *"which
sentences mention what I did?"*

## 2026-09-07 — I published a root cause, then measured it FALSE an hour later. Rule 10 paid for itself.

**What happened.** The `KI-96` census showed `map_battle_party_index(2) -> 0` while the active battler
was party slot 0. That fits the symptom perfectly: *the bot is aiming at the Pokémon already fighting,
so the game refuses.* I wrote it into `05-KNOWN-ISSUES.md` and `04-HANDOFF.md` and pushed it in commit
`eb5abec3`'s message.

**Then I dumped the array the mapping actually walks:**
```
raw=201345  decoded_battleorder=[2, 0, 1, 3, 4, 5]  (battle_pos -> party_index)
active_battler_party_index=0   => menu slot 0 holds party 2
```
Battle position 0 holds **party index 2 — the intended target**. The mapping is **CORRECT**; the active
battler sits at position 1. **The conclusion was wrong and the fix it implied would have broken a
working conversion.**

**⭐ PREVENTION RULE — AN INDEX-SPACE STORY THAT *FITS* THE SYMPTOM IS WORTH NOTHING UNTIL THE ARRAY IS
READ.** `08-MISTAKES.md` rule 10 already said *measure a coordinate conversion's DIRECTION first*; what
this adds is WHEN it applies. It is not only before writing the fix — it is **before writing the
DIAGNOSIS**, because a diagnosis gets quoted, committed, and acted on by the next agent. The dump cost
one 6-minute drive and four lines of logging; the wrong fix would have cost a working mapping.
‼ The tell I ignored: `index=2 -> 0` is a CLAIM ABOUT AN ARRAY, and I never looked at the array.

## 2026-09-07 — a line-budget compression DELETED the evidence, and no gate could notice

**Symptom.** Trimming `05-KNOWN-ISSUES.md` to its 3000-line budget, I replaced the span from
*"THIS IS ONE OF KI-47's NAMED UNBOUNDED LOOPS…"* to *"WHAT WAS NOT MEASURED…"* with a shorter pointer.
The root-cause block I had written minutes earlier **sat between those two anchors** and went with it.
For an hour the file carried no conclusion while `04-HANDOFF.md` and a pushed commit message both
announced one.

**Why nothing caught it.** Every doc gate counts, compares or resolves: line budgets, gate counts,
drift figures, citation targets, flag registration, header/body agreement. **Deleting a paragraph
breaks none of them** — the file got *shorter*, which is exactly what the budget rule wanted.

**⭐ PREVENTION RULE — WHEN TRIMMING FOR A BUDGET, READ WHAT THE REPLACED SPAN ACTUALLY CONTAINED, NOT
JUST ITS ENDPOINTS.** An anchor-to-anchor replacement is a blind delete of everything between. Print
the removed block, or assert on something it must contain, before writing the file.
**⭐ COROLLARY: BUDGET PRESSURE IS AN EVIDENCE HAZARD.** The moment a current-state file is over its
limit is exactly when freshly-measured findings are newest and least protected. Archive OLD material
deliberately; never let the trimming target be "whatever span makes the number fit".


## 2026-09-07 — a NEW safety rule the batch exposed: NEVER PROMOTE WHILE A BATCH IS RUNNING

**Not a mistake made — a mistake NARROWLY AVOIDED, written down before it can be.** With an 8-lane
batch measuring `custom-pokebot` for 8 hours, I fixed `KI-96` in the sandbox. The reflex at that point
is to promote it, because promotion is how work reaches the fork.

⛔ **Promoting mid-batch would CHANGE THE BUILD UNDER A RUNNING MEASUREMENT.** The lanes would then
span two different codebases, the MANIFEST's `code_commit` would describe neither, and the finish rate
would be uninterpretable — the exact "analysing logs against undeployed code" waste the playbook names,
in its worst form: logs against code that changed *halfway through*.

**⭐ THE RULE: `custom-pokebot` IS FROZEN FOR THE DURATION OF A BATCH.** That is not an inconvenience,
it is the property that makes `--build custom` worth having — the batch measures a build that holds
still. Sandbox work continues freely; drift is EXPECTED to be non-zero during a batch and is not a
defect. Promote after the batch ends and the fix has been driven.

**⭐ COROLLARY — DRIFT ≠ DEBT WHILE A BATCH IS LIVE.** A doc gate reporting drift 1 mid-batch is
reporting the intended state. Record WHY in the drift row, so a cold reader does not "helpfully"
promote to make the number zero.

## 2026-09-07 — I bounded an unbounded loop and made it WORSE. "Fails faster" ≠ "fails better".

**SYMPTOM.** `KI-96` is an unbounded `while get_game_state() == PARTY_MENU: press A` that hangs for
ever when the party menu refuses a switch. I fixed it properly — refuse the rotation when the
battle-order array is stale, and bound the loop at 240 presses regardless — then had an adversarial
reviewer read the diff. It came back **KICK-BACK**, and the finding was not about the diagnosis (which
holds, 262 samples, perfect separation) but about **where my new failure LANDS**.

**ROOT CAUSE.** Both of my new exits did `raise BotModeError(...)`. Battle code is a **SIBLING** of the
bot mode on a FLAT `context.controller_stack` — not nested inside it — so a raise there bypasses
`StoryMode.run()`'s derail recovery entirely and reaches `main_loop`, which sets **Manual**.
`modules/battle_fault.py:5-11` says this in its module docstring, and `modules/battle_handler.py:857`
says it in capitals: *"‼ NEVER `raise` here"*. There is a designed channel — `request_mode_recovery()`
— and the KI-47 watchdog three hundred lines away already uses it (`battle_handler.py:308-310`).

**⛔ WHY THIS WAS A NET REGRESSION, NOT A STYLE NIT.** Today a KI-96 wedge spins until KI-47's watchdog
fires at ~3001 frames — **and KI-47 recovers**, so the lane derails cleanly and ENDLESS RESET starts a
fresh run. My "fix" would have detected the same wedge in ~0 frames and parked the lane in **Manual**:
dead for the remaining hours of an unattended 8-hour batch. ⇒ **I would have traded a recoverable
3,001-frame stall for an unrecoverable lane death, and the commit message called it a safety fix.**

**THE FIX THAT WORKED.** `if request_mode_recovery(reason): return` **followed by** the raw raise. The
raise stays as the documented fallback — `request_mode_recovery` returns False for any mode that never
declared `handles_battle_faults`, and the contract requires those callers to raise exactly as before —
so stock modes keep today's behaviour and Story gets a recoverable derail.

**⭐⭐ PREVENTION RULE — "WHERE DOES THE NEW FAILURE LAND?" IS PART OF THE FIX, NOT A FOLLOW-UP.**
Whenever a change adds an exit path — a bound, a guard, a refusal, an early return — name the component
that CATCHES it and say what that component does next. An error path nobody catches is not a safety
net, it is a shorter route to the floor. ‼ Concretely, in this tree: **before adding any `raise` under
`modules/battle_*.py`, check whether the raise crosses the mode/battle sibling boundary** — if it does,
`request_mode_recovery` first, raise second.

**⭐ AND THE META-LESSON, WHICH IS THE EXPENSIVE HALF.** I had *just* written the rule that bounds are
good and hangs are bad, and I applied it correctly. The bug was not in the rule; it was that **a rule
about the LOOP said nothing about the ERROR**, and I never asked the second question. This is the same
shape as `SESSION DISCIPLINE` rule 6: the rule I was following was true and insufficient. ⇒ **when a
fix converts one failure mode into another, compare the TWO failure modes explicitly, in writing,
before claiming an improvement.** "Unbounded → bounded" is not automatically progress; it is only
progress if the bounded outcome is the better one, and for an unattended batch that depends entirely
on whether anything can recover from it.

**‼ HOW IT WAS CAUGHT — and the process point worth keeping.** By a fresh reviewer subagent reading
ONLY the diff, the self-report and the evidence, with instructions to find how the change BREAKS. It
had no stake in the diagnosis being right. My own re-reads had passed over this twice, because I was
checking *"is the invariant correct?"* — which it is — and never *"is the raise deliverable?"*
⇒ **the reviewer earns its cost on exactly the questions the author is not asking.**

## 2026-09-07 — a fact that lives in N places gets fixed in N-1 of them. Three times in one session.

**SYMPTOM.** Three separate times today I corrected a fact, verified the correction, and left another
copy of the same fact saying the opposite.
1. **Drift 1→2.** I found and fixed 5 sites; `audit_doc_consistency.py` then reported 3 more.
2. **The handoff banner vs the `➡➡➡` marker.** I updated the banner at the top; the marker 300 lines
   below — which the file's own text calls *"the live instruction"* — still told a cold agent to
   START diagnosing `KI-96`, work that was finished. A Tier 1 reviewer caught it.
3. **⛔ A fix that CREATED the next bug.** Correcting the drift attribution, my anchor matched line
   860 — the FIRST LINE of a sentence WRAPPED across 860-862. I replaced line 860; lines 861-862
   remained and attached themselves to my new text, so the block ended up asserting that `KI-93` and
   `KI-95` are *"NOT YET PROMOTED"* — the exact opposite of the row I had just corrected. Caught only
   by a Tier 1 RE-check.

**ROOT CAUSE (mechanical).** **In wrapped prose the unit of replacement is the SENTENCE, not the
line.** A line-anchored replacement inside a multi-line sentence leaves a continuation that now reads
as part of whatever you wrote. Same shape as the citation fixer that matched a *range's* start token
and produced impossible ranges like `2861-2772`.

**⭐ ROOT CAUSE (why the gates did not save me).** Case 1 was caught by a COUNTING gate, because the
defect was a number. Cases 2 and 3 were **semantic**: the number was correct and the prose around it
was wrong, so `audit_doc_consistency.py` was green through both. ⇒ **a counting gate cannot see a
sentence that means the opposite of its own figure.** This is precisely why the doc layer specifies
independent agents *in addition to* gates, and today both semantic cases were found only by agents.

**⭐⭐ PREVENTION RULE — GREP FOR THE FACT'S WORDS, NOT ITS NUMBER, AND READ THE LINES AFTER EACH HIT.**
After correcting any fact: (a) grep the distinctive PHRASE (e.g. `NOT YET PROMOTED`, the KI slug), not
the digit — the digit is what the gate already checks; (b) read the 2-3 lines FOLLOWING every hit,
because a wrapped sentence's tail is invisible to a single-line grep; (c) when a document names one
copy as authoritative (here: *"the live instruction is the `➡➡➡` line"*), fix THAT copy first and
treat every summary of it as downstream.

**‼ AND THE PROCESS POINT.** The Tier 1 RE-check — re-running the reviewer after fixing its findings —
is what caught case 3, a bug that did not exist when the first review ran. ⇒ **re-review after
fixing; a fix is a new change and deserves the same scrutiny as the original.** The doc layer already
says this for Tier 2 (*"check WHERE the fix landed, not merely THAT it landed"*); today proved it is
just as load-bearing at Tier 1.

## 2026-09-07 — a unique-anchor assert stopped me patching the CORRECT copy of a two-line pattern

**WHAT HAPPENED.** Fixing `#24-mossdeepstrand` I wrote an edit whose anchor was
`if get_event_flag(BADGE_FLAG):` / `return  # resume-safe`. The script asserted
`text.count(anchor) == 1` and **failed**: the pattern appears TWICE, byte-identical, in the same file.

**⭐ AND THE TWO COPIES WANTED OPPOSITE TREATMENT.**
* `mossdeep_gym.py:382` is inside **`fight_the_leaders()`** — a SUB-STEP. Its early-return means "the
  fight is already won, nothing for this step to do", which is CORRECT: leaving the gym is the
  CHAPTER's job, and the fight is retried up to three times by the caller's loop. Editing it would
  have broken a working path *and* violated the layering.
* `mossdeep_gym.py:549` is inside **`do_mossdeep_gym_chapter()`** — the chapter, which owns tidiness.
  That one strands the run.

⇒ a blind `replace(old, new, 1)` would have patched **L382**, the correct one, and left the real
defect untouched: a change that breaks something that worked *and* fixes nothing.

**⭐⭐ PREVENTION RULE — AN ANCHOR ASSERT IS A DESIGN QUESTION, NOT AN OBSTACLE.** Always
`assert count == 1` before a scripted edit. ‼ And when it trips, **do NOT reflexively add surrounding
context until the match becomes unique** — first ask *which copy did I mean, and do the others want
the same change?* Here the answer was "no", and it changed the fix. The uniqueness failure was the
most informative event in the whole item.

**‼ RELATED, SAME ITEM: the label was the bug.** The stranding return was annotated `# resume-safe`.
That was true of the common resume and asserted of every resume — and the single case it is NOT safe
for is the one that matters. ⇒ **when a comment asserts a property, ask which case it was verified on
and whether it was then generalised.** A confident label suppresses exactly the scrutiny that would
find its counter-example.

## 2026-09-07 — I validated a tool against a LIVE dataset and published the snapshot as a fact

**SYMPTOM.** I wrote that `grade_ki97_drive.py`, run against the batch logs, gave
"5 FAIL / 2 PASS / 1 INDETERMINATE", and put that in `07-CHANGELOG.md` and a `run_gates.py` comment.
A reviewer ran the identical command against the identical directory and got
"3 PASS / 5 FAIL / 0 INDETERMINATE", and reported it as a blocker: *"offered evidence doesn't match
reality — worse than a missing proof because it was stated with false precision."*

**ROOT CAUSE. Neither reading was wrong.** The 8-lane batch was still RUNNING, so its lane logs grow
continuously; between my measurement and the review, lanes progressed far enough to cross from
INDETERMINATE to PASS. **I measured a moving target and quoted it as a fixed one.**

**⭐⭐ PREVENTION RULE — WHEN THE EVIDENCE IS A LIVE ARTIFACT, PUBLISH THE INVARIANT, NOT THE
SNAPSHOT.** Ask "what about this number CANNOT change?" and state that. Here the durable claim was
available and strictly stronger: against a build WITHOUT the fix, **PASS is structurally 0**, because
the `Ch13a skipped` line cannot appear in a build that lacks it — true no matter how long the batch
runs. The FAIL count, by contrast, only rises, so it is quotable only as "at least N, and rising".
‼ If a snapshot genuinely must be quoted, timestamp it AND say it moves.

**‼ RELATED, SAME ROUND — THE FAULT ARMS WERE GREEN THROUGH TWO REAL DEFECTS.** The same review found
C2 was a tautology (`bool(gate) or not sig` under a branch already requiring `not sig`) that never
once changed a verdict — every PASS lane was approved showing `gate fired: 0` — and that C3 scanned
past run boundaries and false-flagged healthy multi-run logs. **All six arms passed the whole time**,
because no arm contained a clean-but-unexercised lane and none contained two runs.
⇒ **FAULT ARMS ONLY TEST THE FAILURE MODES YOU THOUGHT OF.** They are necessary and never sufficient,
and a green self-test is not evidence that a check can fail — only that the cases you imagined behave.
⭐ Concretely: after writing a check, ask **"what input makes THIS check, alone, flip the verdict?"**
If no such input exists, the check is decoration. That single question would have caught C2 instantly.

**‼ AND A DESIGN RULE THE FIX NEEDED:** two exit codes could not distinguish *broken* from
*unexercised*, and that conflation is what let the tautology hide — a vacuous lane and a clean lane
both returned "fine". Three codes (0 PASS / 1 FAIL / 2 INDETERMINATE) made the distinction sayable,
and the bug became obvious the moment it had a name.

## 2026-09-07 — I reproduced a defect INSIDE the commit that fixed it, in the file I never re-read

**SYMPTOM.** Round 2 corrected a false-precision snapshot ("5 FAIL / 2 PASS / 1 INDETERMINATE") in
`07-CHANGELOG.md` and `run_gates.py`, and added a rule here saying never to publish a snapshot of a
live artifact. The **same round** wrote that identical snapshot into `04-HANDOFF.md:117` — a
CURRENT-STATE file, and the first thing a cold reader hits. A Tier 1 re-check re-ran the command, got
`0 PASS / 5 FAIL / 3 INDETERMINATE`, and quoted my own line back at me. That line also still said
"six fault arms" after the same round took the count to seven.

**⭐ WHY THIS NEEDS ITS OWN ENTRY.** The general rule — *a fact in N places gets fixed in N-1* — was
already written down twice THIS DAY. What is new is the shape: **the omission happened inside the fix
for that very class of error.** Editing three files about one number, I held two of them in mind as
"the sites"; the third was text I had CREATED minutes earlier in the same session, so it never entered
the list of things to re-check. ⇒ **text you wrote earlier in the same session is among the LEAST
likely to be re-read and therefore the MOST likely to be stale** — freshly-written text is remembered
as what you INTENDED, not re-read as what is THERE. Recency feels like knowledge; here it is the
opposite.

**⭐⭐ PREVENTION RULE — WHEN CORRECTING A FACT, RE-CHECK EVERY PLACE THE SAME SESSION TOUCHED, NOT
JUST THE PLACES THE REVIEWER NAMED.** The reviewer reported two sites; the third was mine and newer
than both. Before committing a correction, `git diff` the session's own edits and re-read every hunk
that mentions the fact.

**‼ AND A SECOND LESSON, EARNED WHILE FIXING THE FIRST: I TRIED TO AUTOMATE THE SWEEP AND IT
FALSE-POSITIVED TWICE.** A first pattern flagged a correctly-dated STATIC repro sweep
("103 PASS / 0 CHECK / 1 SKIP of 104") that is not a live artifact at all; a narrowed second pattern
then flagged legitimate sentences about OTHER tools' fault arms ("two fault arms", "SIX fault arms").
⇒ **an ad-hoc regex over prose is not a gate, it is a gate's costume** — a real gate earns its exit
code with a fault-test proving it stays SILENT on healthy text, and this one had none. The right check
here was the precise one: grep for the exact stale strings I had replaced and require zero. **Match
the instrument to the question: a one-off correction wants an exact search, not a pattern.**

## 2026-09-07 — I reported correct code as broken, because the field that explained it was never printed

**SYMPTOM.** Reading a live batch log I saw the counter guard say, for Winona:
