## 2026-09-10 — I shipped a crash to BOTH forks, and the A/B I ran to measure something else caught it

**Symptom, measured.** Batch `20260910-203458` (8 lanes, 180.1 min, VERDICT OK, `code_commit
b0841b7e`): **11 runs crashed** with
`UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'PokemonCenter' where it is not associated with a
value`, at ~1.6M frames each — i.e. hours into the game, at badge 7. `[DEXCATCH]`/`[DEXFENCE]` lines:
**0**. The fence never fired once, so the A/B measured **nothing** about the thing it was run for.

**Root cause, and it is placement, not the import.** `PokemonCenter` is bound at **twelve** places
inside `_play`, every one of them inside an `if not _done("BADGEnn_GET")` branch. I built
`tate_liza_fight` / `juan_fight` at **indent 8 — OUTSIDE the guard** — so the dicts construct on
EVERY pass through `_play`, including resumed runs where no badge branch ran and `PokemonCenter` is
therefore unbound. `winona_fight`, the precedent I copied from, is at **indent 12 — INSIDE its
guard**.
⇒ ⭐ **I COPIED THE DICT'S CONTENT AND NOT ITS PLACEMENT.** That is the *"copy a pattern WHOLE"* rule
from earlier the same day, failing a second time in a form the rule as written did not cover: I was
watching which LINES accompany the call, not which BLOCK they live in.

**Why every safety net missed it.**
* My own review caught the conditional-import trap and I added a local import — for
  `_lead_best_matchup` and `heal_in_pokemon_center`. **`PokemonCenter` was in the line I had written
  FIRST and was not in the set I was thinking about.** A name-by-name fix protects exactly the names
  you enumerate.
* Gate #53's C7 asserted `import _lead_best_matchup` was present. It was. C7 passed.
* A Tier 1 reviewer read the diff and did not catch it either.
* ⇒ **Nothing that reads SOURCE caught it, because the code is valid Python.** It only fails on a
  path — a RESUMED run — that no probe drives and no fixture starts from.

**What actually caught it: the batch.** This is the clearest case this project has for the
distinction it already records — *drivers answer CORRECTNESS questions; batches answer FREQUENCY
questions*. Add a third: **only a real run answers "does this path ever execute?"**

**The fixes.**
1. Both dicts moved INSIDE their guards (indent 8 → 12), matching `winona_fight`.
2. Every function-local name the block touches is imported in that same block.
3. C7 rewritten to check **every** name the block uses (derived from the block, not from a list I
   remember), and to use the **AST** rather than a character window — a window cannot express "the
   same `if` block", which is precisely what an `UnboundLocalError` is about.
4. A new `POKEBOT_LATEBOSS_FAULT=unbound` arm reproduces the shipped defect exactly, so this
   regression now has a permanent test.

‼ **AND THE FIRST VERSION OF THAT ARM WAS ITSELF WRONG** — `src.replace("from modules.map_data
import PokemonCenter", "", 2)` stripped two of the **fourteen** occurrences elsewhere in the file and
left my blocks untouched. The arm exited 1 while printing *"FAULT ARM DID NOT REACH THE CODE"* — the
self-check catching a bad arm. ⇒ **an arm that mutates the wrong thing is not an arm**, and a fault
arm needs its own anchor check.

⭐ **Prevention rule (one line):** *When you copy a code pattern, copy its PLACEMENT as well as its
content — check the indent level against the precedent, because scope is invisible in a diff.*

⛔ **AND THE PROCESS LESSON, which is the expensive one:** I PROMOTED this to `custom-pokebot`
before the A/B ran. The promotion was verified by a DRIVE — `ACCEPTANCE: PASS` — but that drive
started from `post_vr_exit.ss1`, a fixture whose badges are already earned, and it never re-entered
`_play` from the top. A green drive proved the promoted code LOADS, not that it SURVIVES a resume.
⇒ **Do not promote code whose first real exercise is still ahead of it.** Promote after the batch,
not before — the rollback tag existed for exactly this and it is why the cost was recoverable.

## 2026-09-11 — I "overturned" my own correct conclusion by reading a warp table, and an agent refuted me

**What I claimed.** Earlier the same day I wrote that Meteor Falls' L33-40 rooms are "the deep ones
behind Waterfall", so unavailable before badge 8. Hours later I read
`data/maps/MeteorFalls_1F_1R/map.json`, found **`(5,4) → B1F_1R` and `(26,28) → B1F_1R`**, and
announced a "major finding": a warp needs no HM, so B1F is reachable early and my earlier claim was
wrong. I even flagged it as correcting myself — which made it sound MORE reliable, not less.

**What is actually true.** The warps are real; the warp TILES are not reachable. A flood fill from the
real §Ch11 anchor (27,18), using the game's own elevation rules, reaches **262 tiles on foot and 299
with Surf, and contains NEITHER warp tile**. Flooding outward FROM them shows why: **(5,4) sits in a
closed 32-tile pocket and (26,28) in a closed 29-tile pocket** — they are where you come UP from B1F.
Only Waterfall (badge 8) opens a route at all.

**So the original conclusion was RIGHT and my reason for overturning it was WRONG.** That is the
mirror image of the mistake I recorded that same morning ("a conclusion can be right while its
mechanism is wrong") — here a *correct* conclusion was nearly discarded because the *obvious* mechanism
for it did not hold and I mistook that for a refutation.

⭐ **Prevention rule (one line):** *A warp table proves an edge EXISTS, never that the player can STAND
on its tile — reachability is a flood fill, not an adjacency list.*

‼ **AND THE DURABLE PART: I wrote the counter-evidence into `training_areas.py` itself**, beside the
entries, because the agent flagged the obvious risk — *"anyone re-checking only the warp table will
overturn this again"*. A conclusion whose supporting evidence lives somewhere else gets re-litigated
by the next reader who finds the same seductive half-fact. ⇒ **put the refutation where the tempting
evidence is.**

⚠ Credit where due: the finding came from an agent whose decoder was CONTROLLED first — it re-derived
this project's own documented Granite Cave region (126 tiles, zero cracked floors, muddy slope at
(9,9)/(9,10), promoted tile (3,18)) before it was allowed to answer anything about Meteor Falls. That
control is why I believed a coordinate I could not cheaply re-derive myself.

## 2026-09-11 — I filed a behavioural defect off a LOG LINE; the code was correct (rule 7, again)

**Symptom.** I read `"Nearest reachable counters: Bagon (Dragon) on Meteor Falls (B1F) 2R (tile
unmapped, NOT HUNTABLE, …) — UNREACHABLE"` in a batch log and filed `#24-counterhmgate`: *"the
counter recommender offers grounds it cannot reach."*

**Root cause.** I graded the CANDIDATE LIST instead of the ACTION. `best_huntable`
(`counter_plan.py:435`) is the only function an executor may use and requires
`huntable AND hunt_tile is not None`; Meteor Falls carries `tile=None`, so it could never be chosen.
The log had already printed **both** disqualifying markers on that very line.

**Why it is worth an entry even though nothing shipped.** This is **SESSION DISCIPLINE rule 7** —
*"INSTRUMENT THE ACTION, NOT THE INPUT TO THE ACTION. ⛔ A CANDIDATE IS NOT AN ATTEMPT"* — and I
violated it while holding the rule in context. Worse, `counter_plan.py:477` carries a comment
recording the **same misreading of the same log line** on 2026-09-07 (*"reported the recommender as
broken. It was correct… The line, not the logic, was the defect"*). ‼ Two people, same log, same
wrong conclusion ⇒ the log line is a defect surface, not a coincidence.

⭐ **Prevention rule (one line):** *Before filing a defect from a log, open the function that CONSUMES
the logged value and check whether anything acts on it — a list the executor filters is a diagnosis,
not a recommendation.*
⇒ Filed as `#24-countermsg2` (fix the misleading LABEL at `story_mode.py:1094`), with the retraction
kept in the item so the phantom is not re-filed a third time.

## 2026-09-11 — "It hangs" was never measured. It was slow, and that cost 16 days of a red suite.

**Symptom.** `repro_gym_whiteout_guard.py` produced an EMPTY log and got killed at the suite's 900s
bound, repeatedly, from 2026-08-26. Everyone (me included) called it a HANG.

**Root cause.** It was PACED. The gate never set `context.emulation_speed = 0`, so the emulator
throttled itself to 60fps by BLOCKING on an audio write every frame — and 900s at 1× is only
~54,000 frames, which a long gym route exceeds. Unthrottled: **107s, 5/5 pass.**

⛔ **THE DIAGNOSTIC ERROR, AND IT IS THE REUSABLE PART: nobody asked whether the process was STUCK or
merely SLOW.** An empty log is consistent with BOTH, and the two have opposite fixes. Three
successive diagnoses (gate parallelism, machine load, an unbounded `sounddevice.write`) all assumed
"stuck" and went looking for what was blocking. The first two were correctly refuted by measurement;
the third found something genuinely wrong — the audio errors ARE real — and stopped there.
⭐ **A TRUE SYMPTOM IS THE MOST EXPENSIVE PLACE TO STOP**, because it feels like an answer.

**Prevention rule (one line):** *Before calling anything a hang, measure its RATE — frames/sec,
lines/sec, bytes/sec. "Stuck" and "slow" produce the same empty log and have opposite fixes.*

‼ **And I made the same class of error inside the fix itself**, twice, both caught by checking:
1. I wrote in the punch list that `_reset_audio`'s fallback "is only reached when `_audio_stream` is
   falsy, and the error path never permanently clears it". Reading it properly: `_reset_audio`
   **succeeds** in re-opening a stream each time, so there is no failure counter. Same conclusion,
   wrong mechanism — the thing this project already has a rule about.
2. I asserted `context.audio = False` was decorative because libmgba never reads `context.audio`.
   It is a **property whose setter calls `set_audio_enabled`** (`context.py:153-156`). One grep is
   not a reading. ⇒ the line is not decorative, it is merely INSUFFICIENT — which is a different
   and more interesting fact.
3. I assumed `story_harness.py` shared the bug because it appeared in the same "no `set_throttle`"
   list. **MEASURED instead: 491 fps over 1,200 frames — already unthrottled** (it sets
   `emulation_speed = 0` at `:126`). A list of files matching a grep is a list of CANDIDATES.

⇒ Closed as `#26-gatestartupcontention`, gated as #54 `probe_gate_unthrottled.py`.

## 2026-09-11 — My vacuity check "rejected" four stubs with an AttributeError and I nearly believed it

**Symptom.** To answer *"could a stub that ignores its inputs pass gate #55?"* I ran four stubs
through the probe and got:
```
  always None        -> rc=raised AttributeError  failing cases=0  ✅ rejected
  always slot 1      -> rc=raised AttributeError  failing cases=0  ✅ rejected
```
Four ✅s. The conclusion I wanted — *"no stub survives"* — was right there, and every line was green.

**Root cause.** My harness redirected stdout into a `StringIO`, but the probe calls
`sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8")` (which this project added everywhere after three gates
falsely failed on a cp1252 console). `StringIO` has no `.reconfigure`, so the probe blew up during
IMPORT — before a single case ran. `failing cases=0` was not "it passed nothing"; it was
**"nothing executed"**. ⇒ my harness was broken, and the stubs were never tested at all.

⭐ **Prevention rule (one line):** *A rejection for the WRONG REASON is not a rejection — when a
check reports failure, read WHY it failed before recording the verdict it happens to agree with.*

‼ This is the same shape as `#26-gatestartupcontention` earlier the same day (an empty log read as
"stuck" when it meant "slow") and as the project's standing rule *"when a probe FAILS, read the
failing line before touching the thing under test"*. **The dangerous version is the one here: the
broken instrument AGREED WITH ME.** A disagreeing instrument gets investigated; an agreeing one gets
quoted.

**The fix, and the real answer.** Gave the capture object a no-op `reconfigure`, then re-ran FIVE
stubs including the strongest one (right predicate, but skipping the cost and heal checks):
```
  always None                                rc=1  fails= 6  ✅ rejected
  always slot 1                              rc=1  fails=13  ✅ rejected
  always weakest                             rc=1  fails= 9  ✅ rejected
  weakest below target                       rc=1  fails= 9  ✅ rejected
  weakest below floor (no cost/heal check)   rc=1  fails= 6  ✅ rejected
```
⇒ the conclusion survived — **fewest failures by any stub: 6** — but it is now EARNED. Had the
harness stayed broken it would have certified a vacuous gate as discriminating, which is precisely
the failure gate #55's own C13 exists to prevent, one level up.

## 2026-09-11 — `yield` inside `finally`: the obvious cleanup shape is a latent crash in a generator

**Symptom (never observed in the wild — found by audit, which is the point).** A generator that
yields from a `finally` raises `RuntimeError: generator ignored GeneratorExit` when closed while
suspended inside the matching `try`. CPython closes abandoned generators at GC time, so a mode
switch or a discarded story run is enough.

**Root cause.** `try/finally` is the *obvious* way to guarantee "restore the lead whatever happens",
and in ordinary code it is correct. In a generator it is not. I wrote it in `#24-maintain`'s new
step, and `victory_road.py:2099` had already shipped it to production with the comment
*"⛔ IN A `finally` ON PURPOSE"*.

⭐ **Prevention rule (one line):** *In a generator, never `yield` from a `finally` — use
`except GeneratorExit: raise` / `except BaseException: <cleanup>; raise` / `else: <cleanup>`.*
✅ ENFORCED, not requested: gate #56 `probe_yield_in_finally.py`, which reproduces the RuntimeError
at runtime on every run rather than trusting the rule.

‼ **The second lesson is about the comment.** `victory_road.py`'s read *"IN A `finally` ON PURPOSE"*
— emphatic, dated, reasoned. It is why nobody looked again. ⇒ **a deliberate-looking comment is not
evidence of safety; it is evidence that someone THOUGHT about it once, with whatever they knew then.**

---

## 2026-09-11 — I nearly shipped a gate BYPASS while fixing a gate, and equal totals hid it

**Symptom.** The correct generator-cleanup shape uses `except BaseException`, so gate #27's ratchet
counted it as new abort-swallowing debt (24 vs baseline 23). I taught the detector that a handler
ending in a bare `raise` cannot swallow — correct in itself — and the gate went back to **exactly
23, PASS**.

⛔ **23 = 23 WAS A COINCIDENCE.** My exemption returned True if ANY handler in the `try` re-raised.
The shape it wrongly exempted is real — `story_mode.py` has `except BotModeError: raise` beside
`except Exception: yield`, one handler re-raising while its SIBLING swallows.
‼ **PRECISION, ADDED AFTER A TIER 1 REVIEWER CHECKED MY CLAIM AND NARROWED IT:** that file is NOT in
`probe_abort_swallowing.py`'s `SCAN` (the gate covers `modules/story/` plus one helper), so within
the gate's OWN corpus the ANY-vs-ALL distinction currently changes **nothing** — both detectors
return the same 23 sites. My whole-tree control arm is what surfaced it. ⇒ the bug in my exemption
was real and the shape it admits is real, but I over-stated the blast radius by not checking the
gate's scope before describing the finding. **A defect found by a tool run OUTSIDE a gate's scope
is a defect in the code, not evidence about what the gate was counting.**

**How it was caught.** Not by the total — by diffing the SITE LISTS under the old and new detectors
and requiring that the exempted set contain *only my own two handlers*. It contained a third.

⭐ **Prevention rule (one line):** *When you change what a ratchet COUNTS, diff the SET, never the
TOTAL — equal counts routinely hide an equal-sized swap.*
‼ This is the same shape as the project's standing rule that a count netting to zero reads TRUE when
nothing happened (one deposited, one caught). Here it was one exempted, one added. ⇒ the exemption is
now ALL-quantified over the broad handlers, with a self-test carrying that exact sibling shape.

## 2026-09-11 — I published an affordability table computed against boss bands I never read

**Symptom.** I documented "5,732 – 146,166 frames" as the cost of early-game maintenance, in four
files, and used it to argue that a settled 2026-09-10 ruling did not cover this case.

**Root cause.** The targets in that table (15/20/26/31/34/38) were my ASSUMPTIONS about the gym
bands. The code's actual bands are `(13,17) (14,16) (20,24) (24,29) (27,31) (29,33)`. I read them
only when a recon agent quoted them back with line numbers.

**Direction of the error.** Favourable — real targets are LOWER, so the real range is **4,299 –
63,052** and the conclusion strengthens. ⛔ That is not a defence. A number published without being
read out of the code is wrong whichever way it later moves, and this one was load-bearing in an
argument against a DO-NOT-REOPEN ruling.

⭐ **Prevention rule (one line):** *A constant used in an argument must be READ from the code and
cited `file:line` in the same edit that uses it — never recalled.*
⭐ **And the recompute paid for itself immediately:** with the real bands, a laggard facing Tate &
Liza or Juan needs `catchup` 35-40, i.e. exactly the late grind the ruling killed. Measuring that
showed **all 4 late cases are REFUSED on cost (581k-882k vs a 150k budget)** — the single most
important property of the design, and the guessed table could not have shown it.

## 2026-09-11 — The yield-in-`finally` rule was written on 2026-07-26. It did not stop the bug in September.

**Found by an adversarial agent, not by me.** While I was congratulating myself on catching a latent
crash, it pointed at `08-MISTAKES.md` (2026-07-26), which already said:
> *"Call `_lead_strongest_battler()` at the end of `train_team`, after the loop and before the
> `finally` (a `yield` inside `finally` raises if the generator is being closed…)"*
— with the prevention rule *"when you write a helper whose docstring names a hazard, grep for every
path that hazard can reach, not just the one you were looking at."*

And `early_game.py:2108-2111` obeys it: `train_team` deliberately places its cleanup AFTER the loop,
citing exactly this reasoning.

⛔⛔ **SIX WEEKS LATER `victory_road.py:2099` SHIPPED THE BUG ANYWAY** — to production — under the
comment *"⛔ IN A `finally` ON PURPOSE"*. The rule existed, was correct, was written down, was obeyed
in one file, and the very next author to reach for a cleanup guard reached for `finally`.

⭐⭐ **THE LESSON IS NOT "read the mistakes file harder."** It is the project's own rule 6, confirmed
with a six-week natural experiment: **a rule that can be expressed as a gate MUST be, because prose
does not fire when you are thinking about something else.** The 2026-07-26 entry even anticipated the
failure mode ("grep for every path that hazard can reach") and still did not prevent it, because
grepping is something you have to REMEMBER to do.
⇒ Gate #56 `probe_yield_in_finally.py` now does the grep on every commit, and re-derives the
RuntimeError at runtime so it cannot quietly guard nothing.

‼ **AND THE HAZARD WAS REACHABLE, not theoretical** — the same review found two live `.close()` call
sites that would have triggered it: `story_mode.py:3052` (`_play_gen.close()`, fired on any
recoverable battle fault — entirely plausible mid-training, since maintenance trains via real wild
battles) and `story_mode.py:4999` (`inner.close()` when a per-run frame budget is exceeded).
⇒ I had called the exposure "large but unobserved". It was large AND reachable by two named paths.

## 2026-09-11 — A "budget" that nothing checks at runtime is a wish, not a budget

**Symptom.** `MAINTAIN_MAX_FRAMES = 150_000` read like a safety ceiling. An adversarial review showed
it gated only the PRE-FLIGHT `estimate_frames_to_level(...)`. Once a case was admitted, the only live
bound was `train_team`'s `guard > 500`, which counts **rounds, not frames**.

**Why that matters here specifically.** The estimator is `battles * FRAMES_PER_WILD_BATTLE` and has
**no term for heal round-trips** — a cost this same file measures elsewhere as dominant (*"78 heal
round trips in one run … every HP dip is a full Poké Center walk"*). So the estimate is
systematically optimistic in exactly the direction that matters, and the headroom was 2.6%
(150,000 vs a 146,166 worst case) before the figures were even corrected.

**Fix.** Drive the training through `_yield_bounded(gen, budget)` — a HARD frame cap that closes the
sub-generator on timeout — and REPORT which outcome occurred. "SHORT" alone cannot distinguish *"the
ground was wrong"* from *"it ran out of frames"*; those have different fixes, and the second means the
estimate was too optimistic.

⭐ **Prevention rule (one line):** *If a constant is called a budget, find the line that STOPS work
when it is exceeded — if there isn't one, it is an estimate with a reassuring name.*
‼ Note the two fixes are load-bearing for each other: `_yield_bounded` closes the sub-generator on
timeout, which is a `GeneratorExit` into `train_team` — safe only because gate #56 now guarantees no
story-surface generator yields from a `finally`. Adding this bound BEFORE that fix would have
converted a timeout into a `RuntimeError`.

---

## 2026-09-11 — The gate I wrote to catch a real bug had a false positive, found by attacking it

**Symptom.** Gate #56 (`probe_yield_in_finally.py`) flagged this as an offender:
```python
try:
    yield 1
finally:
    def inner():
        yield 2          # <- belongs to `inner`, not to the enclosing generator
    register(inner)
```
Defining a nested generator during cleanup yields nothing from the outer one. **Not the hazard.**

**Root cause.** `ast.walk` descends into nested function bodies, so any `yield` lexically under the
`finally` matched — including ones in a different function's scope.

**How it was found — and this is the reusable part.** Not by running the gate (it was green: no
story-surface file happens to contain that shape). I went looking for ways to **DEFEAT** it: nested
functions, a `try` inside the `finally`, a `with` inside the `finally`, a lambda, an async generator.
Four were correctly handled; the nested `def` was not.
⭐ **Prevention rule (one line):** *After writing a gate, spend five minutes trying to DEFEAT it — in
both directions. A gate you only ever tried to satisfy has been tested on one side.*

‼ And a Tier 1 reviewer then found a SECOND hole the same way: `try/except*` (PEP 654) parses to
`ast.TryStar`, which is **not** an `ast.Try`, so an exception-group `try` with a yielding `finally`
was invisible. Inert today — there is no `except*` anywhere in the tree — and fixed anyway, because
*"nothing uses it yet"* is a statement about today. ⇒ self-tests now run **13** cases pinning both
directions (S9 the false positive, S10 that the fix did not over-correct, S13 `except*`).

⛔ **The meta-lesson: a gate is CODE, and new code is where defects live.** I wrote #56 to stop a
class of bug and shipped a bug inside it on the first try. The gate had already been proven against
the real defect it was written for — which is necessary and, on its own, not sufficient.

## 2026-09-11 — A solved problem is only solved WHERE it was solved

**Symptom.** `_maintain_lagging_battler` called `_rotate_lead_safely(slot)` and never checked it
landed. That function gives up after 3 attempts by setting `context.message` and returning NORMALLY
(`early_game.py:1660`). On a give-up, `train_team(scope="lead")` finds a high-level mon in slot 0,
computes an EMPTY `need`, returns instantly — and the code logged
`done ... L13->L13 (wanted L14, SHORT)`, which is **byte-identical to a real training failure**.

**Root cause.** Not ignorance of the hazard — this tree already carries the defence.
`victory_road.py:2062-2081` asserts by PID that the rotation landed, under a comment spelling out
this exact failure. I wrote a new caller of the same helper and did not carry the guard across.

⭐ **Prevention rule (one line):** *Before calling a helper that "gives up gracefully", grep for an
EXISTING caller of it — if one asserts something afterwards, that assertion is part of the calling
convention, not that caller's private business.*

‼ Note what this is NOT: it is not "read the mistakes file". The hazard was documented in a CODE
COMMENT at the only other call site, which is the best possible place for it, and it still did not
travel. => the durable version of this lesson is that **a helper whose failure is silent should carry
its guard INSIDE itself, or return a value the caller cannot ignore.** Logged as a candidate
improvement to `_rotate_lead_safely` rather than done here, because changing a helper used across the
story surface deserves its own item and its own drive.

⛔ **And the discovery route matters more than the bug.** It was found by an ADVERSARIAL agent asked
to refute a plan, before the experiment existed — not by running anything. The experiment as planned
would have printed a plausible number and hidden it.

## 2026-09-12 — I diagnosed the loudest log line, then the wrong route, before reading the verbatim log

**Symptom.** An overnight A/B showed 1,745 occurrences of `Cannot reach PETALBURG_CITY: it is not
walkable from ROUTE104` in ARM-ON and 0 in ARM-OFF. I reported that as the feature's root cause,
and separately reported "all 27 manual derails are ROUTE111 `(25,55)`" as *the* defect to fix.

**Both were wrong, for two DIFFERENT reasons — and that is the useful part.**
1. **The PETALBURG line is `derail #2`.** It is what the run hits *after* the auto-restart, having
   already been knocked off course by `derail #1`. Counting it measured a **consequence**. The
   project already had a rule for instrumenting the ACTION rather than its inputs; this is the same
   error pointed at *outputs* — a downstream symptom is no more the cause than an upstream candidate.
   ⇒ **Rule: when a system retries after failure, count PRIMARY failures. Every post-restart error
   is downstream of the first one and will out-number it.**
2. **ROUTE111 appears in BOTH arms** (145 ON / 79 OFF). A cause that is present in the control
   cannot be what the treatment broke. I had read a large ARM-ON number without checking the same
   number in ARM-OFF — the one comparison the whole experiment existed to make.
   ⇒ **Rule: in a two-arm experiment, no single-arm count is a finding. Quote both arms or say nothing.**

**Root cause of my error:** I ran `sort | uniq -c | sort -rn` and reported the top row. The ranking
was correct and the *question* was wrong. Reading three verbatim log excerpts — which took one tool
call — produced the real chain immediately, including the `stage:` and `map (0,19)` fields that name
Route 104 north.

**The actual defect** (now fixed, gate #57): `best_training_grass` chose a training ground on level
fit alone with no notion of the player's position, and the errand re-raised the resulting
`UnreachableDestinationError` into the run instead of abandoning a best-effort side quest.

**⭐ The most valuable thing in the whole round:** the fix's justification was *already written in
the file*, twelve lines above the bug, applied to a different failure path in the same function.
⇒ **Prevention rule: when you write "we abandon rather than raise, because this is best-effort",
grep that same function for every other `raise` and make them agree — a policy that holds on one
path and not its neighbour is a bug with a comment defending it.**

**Second prevention rule, from the metric:** `probe_maintain_window.py` made the harmful arm look
BETTER (fewer laggard episodes, lower median gap) because its runs died before they could
accumulate gap. ⇒ **Any per-batch count is uninterpretable across arms whose runs have different
lifetimes. Normalise per run, or compare only lifetime-independent quantities.**

## 2026-09-12 — I reported a metric with n=14 while a metric with n=945 sat in the same log files

**Symptom.** Grading the maintenance A/B, I counted `BADGE07_GET` and reported *“badge 7 reached:
5 (0.9%%) vs 9 (3.7%%) — 4x worse”*, and wrote that figure into the changelog, the handoff banner,
the punch list, the decisions log, the flag registry AND the new gate's docstring.

**What was wrong with it.** `BADGE07_GET` is a **Ch18-only STEP line**, not a badge-progress
marker — which is why badges 1-6 all counted **ZERO** in both arms. I saw those zeros, noted they
were “suspicious”, and *still published the derived percentage first*. A run cannot reach badge 7
without earning 1-6, so the zeros were proof the metric did not mean what I called it.
⇒ **Rule: an impossible zero beside your metric is a REFUTATION of the metric, not a curiosity to
mention. Stop and re-derive before any number built on it is written down.**

**What was actually available**, in the same files, found one tool call later: `BADGE: <name>
(<leader>, <city>)` — the real per-badge line. **945 events** instead of 14:
ARM-ON **398 badges over 552 runs = 0.72/run**; ARM-OFF **547 over 243 = 2.25/run** (3.1x better),
with every single tier lower in ARM-ON in ABSOLUTE terms despite 2.3x the runs.

**Why it matters even though the conclusion held.** The verdict (net-harmful) was unchanged and in
fact strengthened — which is exactly the trap. **A correct conclusion reached on weak evidence is
indistinguishable, to the next reader, from a correct conclusion reached on strong evidence**, and
this project's own playbook already warns against quoting an underpowered rate from one batch
(`14-AGENT-PLAYBOOK.md`). I had the rule and did not apply it to a metric I had just invented.

**Prevention rule:** *before publishing a derived rate, count the EVENTS behind it and say the n out
loud.* If n is small, grep the logs for a denser signal first — and if a sibling value in the same
table is impossible, treat the whole metric as unproven until re-derived.

## 2026-09-12 — I quoted rates from a batch whose own manifest says "do not quote a rate from this"

**Symptom.** I reported the confirmatory A/B to the user as decisive — median run duration, badges
per run, 77 abandonments — and wrote those numbers into the changelog, the decisions log, the
handoff and the punch list. An adversarial agent then read
`x4-runs/20260912-050244/MANIFEST.txt:5-11` and found it begins:

> ⛔⛔ **MIXED BUILD — THIS BATCH SPANS MORE THAN ONE COMMIT.** A finish rate whose build is ambiguous
> is NOT a measurement. Do not compare this batch against another, and do not quote a rate from it.

Lanes H1-H8 ran `2dc1ba24`, H9-H19 ran `2dc1ba24-dirty`, H20-H32 ran `26dc25d4`.

**ROOT CAUSE — I DID IT.** I committed a docs note (`26dc25d4`) **while the batch was running**, and
the tree was dirty mid-edit when lanes respawned. The batch tooling detected exactly that and said
so, in a file I never opened.

**Why I missed it.** I *did* check the builds — I ran a grep for `commit` against `ARM-*.txt` and
`summary.json`, got **empty output**, and moved on. ⇒ **An empty result from a check you invented is
not a PASS; it is a check that did not run.** The authoritative file was `MANIFEST.txt` and I never
looked at it.

**Does the conclusion survive? Yes — and that is the trap.** `git diff --name-only 2dc1ba24
26dc25d4` = **1 file, 0 `.py`** (`04-HANDOFF.md`), and ARM-OFF was a clean SINGLE BUILD. An
independent build-matched subset test agrees: lanes on the later commit gave 0.800/run vs 0.826/run
on the earlier, against 0.813 for the whole arm — no confound. **But I did not know any of that when
I published the numbers.** A correct conclusion reached without checking is indistinguishable, to
the next reader, from one that was checked.

**PREVENTION RULES (two, both new):**
1. ⛔ **NEVER COMMIT, STAGE, OR EDIT THE TREE WHILE A BATCH IS RUNNING.** The project already had
   "do not PROMOTE while a batch is running" (2026-09-07); this is the same hazard one step milder
   and it bit within a week. Park doc edits until the batch ends — the batch is the only thing that
   cannot be redone cheaply.
2. ⛔ **READ `MANIFEST.txt` BEFORE QUOTING ANY NUMBER FROM A BATCH.** It is the batch's own verdict
   on its own admissibility. Quoting a rate without reading it is the measurement equivalent of
   citing a paper by its title.

## 2026-09-12 — A fault arm passed because my fix gave its target a second home

**Symptom.** Gate #57's `healbare` arm reverts `raise HealWalkFailedError(` to `raise BotModeError(`
and should red case F7. After I added a SECOND `HealWalkFailedError` raise site (the fast-fail for
non-scripted errors), the arm ran and the gate printed **"⛔⛔ A FAULT ARM WAS ACTIVE AND NOTHING
FAILED — this gate proves nothing."**

**Root cause, two compounding halves.** The arm used `str.replace(..., 1)` — first occurrence only —
so it reverted one site and left the other. AND F7 was written as *"is `HealWalkFailedError` raised
**anywhere** in this function?"*, which the surviving site still satisfied.

**Fix.** The arm replaces ALL occurrences; F7 now asserts **`"BotModeError" not in raised`** as well
as the good type being present.

**Prevention rule:** ⇒ **presence of the good thing is not absence of the bad thing.** When a gate
asks "does X appear?", adding a second X silently disarms it. Assert the NEGATIVE too. And the only
reason this was caught is that the arm was RUN and its verdict READ — the "A FAULT ARM WAS ACTIVE AND
NOTHING FAILED" line exists for exactly this, so never skip running the arms after editing the thing
they point at.

## 2026-09-12 — A two-anchor slice deleted 58 punch-list cells, and only a SANITY NUMBER caught it

**Symptom.** To free space under a line budget I replaced a span of `03-PUNCH-LIST.md` between two
string anchors:
```python
start = s.index("### ‼ `#26-healmap-lavaridge`")
end   = s.index("### 🔶 `#24-maintain`")     # ← the trap
s = s[:start] + NEW + s[end:]
```
The script printed **“saved 1995 lines”** when I expected ~45. `git diff --stat` confirmed **1977
deletions, 106 → 48 cells** — 58 punch-list items destroyed, including `#24-abortswallow`,
`#24-ballstarve`, `#24-canary` and 55 more.

**Root cause.** `str.index` returns the FIRST match. My `end` anchor appeared EARLIER in the file
than I assumed relative to `start`— so the slice spanned almost everything between them. A
two-anchor slice silently deletes whatever sits between the anchors, and *nothing in the operation
itself knows how much that is*.

**What saved it.** The script PRINTED the line delta. ⇒ the number looked absurd, I checked
`git diff --stat` instead of moving on, and restored with `git checkout HEAD -- <file>` (the only
uncommitted content in that file was the corruption itself, so nothing of value was lost).
⛔ Had the script printed nothing, Tier 0 would have passed — **`lint_docs` measures the budget and
would have been HAPPIER with the file 1995 lines shorter.** The gate that exists to protect this
file would have actively rewarded the destruction.

**PREVENTION RULES:**
1. ⛔ **NEVER slice between two independently-located anchors.** Locate the start, then find the end
   **relative to it** (`s.index(end_anchor, start)`) — or match the whole block and `replace(old,
   new, 1)` so a wrong anchor fails LOUDLY with 0 matches instead of quietly eating the middle.
2. ⛔ **EVERY bulk doc edit must PRINT its line delta and ASSERT a bound on it.** `assert
   after >= before - 60`. An edit that cannot say how much it changed cannot be reviewed.
3. ⭐ **ASSERT A STRUCTURAL INVARIANT, not just the size** — here, the `### ` cell count. Size alone
   would have accepted 1995 lines of deletions spread thinly; the cell count would not.
4. ‼ **A GREEN GATE IS NOT A SAFE EDIT.** A budget check rewards shrinkage. When the thing you are
   editing is protected by a size rule, the size rule is the LAST thing that will notice you broke it.

## 2026-09-12 — Flipping a default silently turned the A/B script into a VACUOUS experiment

**Symptom (caught BEFORE running, by the post-status-change staleness sweep, not by a gate).**
`Run-Maintain-AB-Batch.bat` built its control arm as `set "POKEBOT_MAINTAIN="` — *remove the
variable and you get the shipped default*, which was `0` (OFF). Two hours after the user ruled the
feature ON, the shipped default became `1`. ⇒ **ARM-OFF would have been ON.** Both arms identical.

**Why this was nearly invisible.** The script would have run its full duration, exited **0**, written
`ARM-ON.txt` and `ARM-OFF.txt`, and produced two result folders with a plausible small difference
between them. Every integrity check it has — same lanes, same minutes, forced `--build sandbox`,
SETLOCAL so the variable cannot leak, explicit arm labels — would have PASSED. **The script's own
header even warns about this exact failure** (*“if ARM OFF inherits it, BOTH arms are really ARM ON
… a FALSE result, which is worse than no result at all”*) — it guarded against LEAKAGE and never
imagined the default moving underneath it.

**Root cause.** The control arm was defined RELATIVE to a default owned by other code. A control
must be an absolute statement of the condition it holds, not a reference to someone else's choice.

**FIX:** ARM-OFF is now `set "POKEBOT_MAINTAIN=0"` — explicit, in both arms.

**PREVENTION RULES:**
1. ⛔ **AN EXPERIMENTAL ARM MUST NEVER LEAN ON A DEFAULT.** “Unset”, “empty”, “whatever ships” are
   not conditions — they are pointers to a condition someone else can change. State the value.
2. ⛔ **WHEN YOU FLIP A DEFAULT, GREP FOR EVERY PLACE THAT CONSUMES IT BY ABSENCE** — not just the
   places that name it. `grep POKEBOT_MAINTAIN` finds the arm that SETS it; only reading the arm
   that UNSETS it reveals the break. The dangerous consumers are the ones that mention the flag
   without mentioning its value.
3. ⭐ **The sweep found this, and no gate could have.** Gate #57 G2 checks that the code default and
   the registry agree — both were correct. The broken thing was a `.bat` file outside every scan,
   whose failure mode is a WRONG NUMBER rather than a red check. ⇒ after any status flip, sweep the
   TOOLING that measures the thing, not only the docs that describe it.

## 2026-09-12 — Backticks in a `python -c "..."` shell string silently DELETED content, and Tier 0 passed over it

**Symptom.** A changelog entry was written via `py -3.12 -c "...">` inside a **double-quoted** shell
string. Bash treats a backtick as COMMAND SUBSTITUTION, so several `` `term` `` spans were executed
and replaced by their empty output:

    written:  ### THE PROOF — `--driver rotzero`, two arms, MEASURED
    landed:   ### THE PROOF — , two arms, MEASURED

    written:  | | `unguarded` | `guarded` |
    landed:   | |  |  |

    written:  | `change_lead_party_pokemon` calls | **`[0]`** | **`[]`** |
    landed:   |  calls | **** | **** |

**What caught it.** Only the shell's own noise — `--driver: command not found` and six siblings —
printed *beside* a line that otherwise said the write succeeded. Had the mangled terms happened to
be valid commands, there would have been no error at all.

**⛔ WHAT DID NOT CATCH IT: TIER 0.** `lint_docs.py` PASSED. `audit_doc_citations.py` PASSED.
`audit_doc_consistency.py` failed — **for an unrelated reason** (a drift count), which is the only
thing that sent me back to look. Why the doc gates are blind here:
* a Markdown table with EMPTY cells is perfectly valid Markdown;
* a citation check can only verify citations that are PRESENT — one that has been deleted cannot
  fail anything;
* nothing in the suite asserts that a sentence still contains words.
⇒ **A green Tier 0 means the document is well-FORMED, never that it still SAYS anything.**

**PREVENTION RULES:**
1. ⛔ **Never pass prose containing backticks through `python -c` in a double-quoted shell string.**
   Write it to a scratchpad `.py` file and run that file. This project already writes its doc edits
   that way — this entry was the exception, which is why the rule is now explicit. *(Single-quoting
   the shell string also works, but the file is the habit worth having: it is re-runnable, diffable,
   and survives a retry.)*
2. ⛔ **After ANY scripted write to a doc, READ BACK the region you wrote** — not the file's tail,
   the specific region. ‼ My first read-back landed on a *quotation* of the mangled text inside the
   very note describing it, and briefly looked like the repair had failed; the second, anchored on
   the repaired string itself, confirmed it. **Anchor a read-back on the text you expect to find,
   and assert the text you expect to be GONE is gone.**
3. ⭐ Generalisation worth keeping: **the gates in this repo check STRUCTURE and REFERENCES, not
   MEANING.** Any corruption that leaves valid syntax behind — an emptied table cell, a deleted
   clause, a truncated sentence — passes every one of them.

## 2026-09-12 — I shipped a test arm that could not fail, and called it a proof

**Symptom.** `--driver rotzero`'s `guarded` arm was written as:
```python
if arm == "guarded":
    slot = 0
    if slot != 0:
        yield from _yield_bounded(_counted(slot), 3000)
```
It PASSED, I wrote *"SLOT-0 GUARD: PROVEN BY DRIVING"* in the handoff, and a Tier 1 reviewer killed it
in one sentence: **`slot` is hardcoded inside the test, so `slot != 0` is False BY CONSTRUCTION.** The
arm never reads `story_mode.py`. Delete the real guard tomorrow and it would print PASS forever.

**What it actually proved:** that Python's `if` works. Nothing about the shipped code.

**Why I did not see it.** I had just built the `unguarded` arm, which is genuinely strong — it calls
the real `change_lead_party_pokemon` and watches PIDs swap on a live emulator. The two arms sat
side by side and *looked* symmetric, so the rigour of one masked the vacuity of the other.
⇒ **An A/B is only as strong as its WEAKER arm, and a strong arm actively camouflages a weak one.**

**FIX.** The `guarded` arm now reads the PRODUCTION source of the build under test
(`inspect.getsource(StoryMode._maintain_lagging_battler)` — so `--build custom` checks custom, and a
hardcoded path cannot silently check the wrong fork), asserts by AST that the `if slot != 0` guard
wraps the `_rotate_lead_safely` call, and makes `guard_ok` a **conjunct of the verdict**.

**FAULT-TESTED, which is the only reason I now believe it** (backup → break → run → restore, restore
verified by MD5):
    guard removed (`if True:`)  →  `PRODUCTION GUARD PRESENT: False`  →  **ACCEPTANCE: FAIL**
    guard present               →  `PRODUCTION GUARD PRESENT: True`   →  **ACCEPTANCE: PASS**

**PREVENTION RULES:**
1. ⛔ **A test arm that supplies its own input to the condition under test is a TAUTOLOGY.** If the
   value that drives the branch is written in the test, the test measures the test. Bind to the
   artefact: read the production source, import the real predicate, or call the real function.
2. ⛔ **Ask of every arm: "what edit to PRODUCTION would make this fail?"** If the answer is "none",
   it is decoration. This is the same question `probe_*` gates answer with fault arms — a DRIVEN arm
   needs it just as much, and I had not been applying it to drivers.
3. ⭐ **Check the weak arm first.** The convincing one is where attention goes; the vacuous one is
   where the error hides.

## 2026-09-13 — I built text anchors from PRETTIFIED output, and separately re-ran a script by importing it

Two tooling mistakes in one edit, both cheap to make and both silent.

**(a) The anchors were copied out of a display, not the file.** I read the handler sites with
`sed -n '...p' file | sed 's/^/   /'` — the second `sed` adds three spaces so the output lines up in
a terminal. I then hand-copied those lines into a replacement script. Every multi-line anchor was
therefore indented by **3 extra spaces** and matched nothing: the script reported
`SKIP (0 matches)` three times and applied **0 of 3** edits while exiting successfully.
‼ I then mis-diagnosed it as a CRLF problem, "fixed" that, and it still failed — the file is `\n`.
The actual proof took one command: `sed -n '3449,3453p' file | cat -A`, which shows the true bytes.
⇒ **Prevention rule: never build a match anchor from output you reformatted for reading.** Read the
raw line, or better — **derive indentation from the file at edit time** (`raw[:len(raw)-len(raw.lstrip())]`)
and never type it. The rewritten script does exactly that, and also verifies each target line's
CONTENT before inserting, so a stale line number cannot write into the wrong place.

**(b) `import`ing a script RE-RAN it.** Trying to reuse the edit definitions, I imported the module —
which executed it top to bottom a second time and applied the one edit that HAD matched **twice**.
`grep -c` showed the comment block present 2x. Caught only because I checked.
⇒ **Prevention rule: a script that performs edits at module scope must never be imported to reuse
its data.** Either guard it with `if __name__ == "__main__":` or parse the source as text. And after
any re-run of an edit script, **count the marker** — an idempotent-looking edit usually is not.

⭐ **The general shape behind both:** a scripted edit that matches nothing exits 0 and looks like
success, and one that matches twice also exits 0. **Neither failure is visible without counting.**
⇒ every bulk edit should print how many sites it changed AND assert the expected number.

## 2026-09-13 — A denominator, an instrument that could not reach its own bug, and an assert written after the write

**(a) I quoted a rate without its denominator, and picked the flattering one.** I reported
*"87% of run deaths"* from 124/143 **ENDED** runs. 207 runs STARTED; 64 were censored at the batch's
wall-clock bound. The true figure is **60% of started runs**, and the censoring is not neutral —
watchdog deaths average 454k frames against 1.31M for boss-losses, so a fixed-time batch
**structurally over-samples short deaths into the "ended" bucket**. Length-corrected ≈ 67%.
⇒ **Prevention rule: state the denominator in the same sentence as the rate, and when runs are cut
off by a time bound, say so — a survival statistic taken over completed runs only is biased toward
whatever kills fastest.**

**(b) I built an experiment knob that was structurally incapable of reaching the bug — and it
returned GREEN, which is the dangerous direction.** `POKEBOT_WALLY_PHASE` shifts the mash phase.
It cannot work: identical consecutive presses cancel (`libmgba.press_button:476`), so a cycle emits
`A, B, nothing`, and shifting the phase also shifts how fast the dialogue advances — the choice
box's open frame **co-moves with the offset**, which therefore partly cancels itself. Both swept
phases came back `beat=True`.
‼ Worse, the same property had ALREADY produced a false negative an hour earlier: **the very first
repro, run against UNFIXED code, printed `ACCEPTANCE: PASS`.** Two green results, zero information.
⇒ **Prevention rule: a fault arm must fire DETERMINISTICALLY, by construction. If whether it fires
depends on timing, luck, or a fixture's incidental state, it is not an arm — replace it with one
that forces the faulty ACTION directly** (here: `=decline`, which presses B at the box and asks the
causal question outright). And the gate that says so belongs in the probe: `probe_wally_phase_sweep`
grades G1 = *"did the fault arm decline at ANY phase?"* and prints
*"this sweep does not demonstrate the fix repairs anything"* when it did not.

**(c) I wrote the file, THEN asserted the invariant.** `reg_wally.py` did
`write(...)` and then `assert after - before == 3`. The assert failed — **after** the bad content
was already on disk (a stray blank line had split a markdown table in two). The earlier session
rule *"every bulk edit must print how many sites it changed AND assert the expected number"* is
satisfied by a script that asserts after writing, and is still useless.
⇒ **Prevention rule: compute the new content, ASSERT every invariant on it, and only then write.
An assertion after the write is a report, not a guard.** Every edit script in this round now
follows that order — three of them refused to write and cost nothing but a re-run.

---

## 2026-09-13 (batch close-out) — four wrong assumptions: a counter I never defined, an impossible zero, an overclaim, and a marker I did not move

**(a) I called `finished = 0` a DEFECT, and treated "12 finishes → 0" as a REGRESSION. Both wrong.**
Symptom: I reported *"no run has ever completed the game"* as evidence something had broken, and
hung part of the Wally narrative on a finish count dropping from 12 to 0.
Root cause: **I quoted a counter without reading its definition.** Two facts, both in our own tree:
`story_mode.py:4865` says *"END OF BUILT CONTENT. Next build: THE POKÉMON LEAGUE — Chapter 24"* —
**the endgame is not implemented, so no run CAN finish** — and
`repro_endless_per_run_state.py` already documents the old number as a bug: *"`outcome` defaulted to
'finished' … All 16 P1 'finished' runs were dead runs … the batch summary read ~80% success against
a true ~20%."* A 120-minute lane cannot reach the end of the built ladder either.
‼ This is the **THIRD** counter in one session that measured something *adjacent to* the event:
`global_watchdog` reported 1398 for 637 real firings (one string matching three log lines), and
STUCK dumps re-fire every **3,000** frames rather than 300, so **zero** are emitted during the
fatal wedge the dumps were being used to explain.
⇒ **Prevention rule: before quoting ANY counter, read its DEFINITION and its CADENCE, and say what
it counts in the same sentence you quote it. A counter named for an event is not a count of that
event.** And here specifically: **the progress metric for this bot is LADDER DEPTH, never
`finished`,** until Chapter 24 exists.

**(b) My own depth table contained an impossible zero, and my own rule is what caught it.**
Symptom: the first table reported **Norman 0%** beside **Fortree 60%** — Fortree is the NEXT gym, so
reaching it without Norman is impossible. A badge histogram built the same way returned `0 badges`
for 100% of runs in BOTH batches.
Root cause: hand-written `grep` keys that never existed in the logs (the real step is *"entering
Petalburg Gym to challenge Norman"*; the badge field is not `badges=` in the debug log).
Fix: re-measured with keys verified to OCCUR in the logs first; Norman is **71%**. The badge
histogram was discarded, not repaired.
⇒ **Prevention rule (already written on 2026-09-11, and it fired exactly as intended): an impossible
zero beside your metric refutes the METRIC, not the subject. Before reporting a distribution, prove
every key MATCHES SOMETHING — a key that matches nothing is indistinguishable from a true zero.**

**(c) I wrote "every number below is re-derivable from the repo alone" — and it was not.**
Symptom: the changelog entry claimed full re-derivability after I copied the batch MANIFEST and both
`summary.json`s into the tracked `evidence/` dir.
Root cause: the summaries carry `runs_ended`, `whiteouts` and `end_reasons` — but the **beat rate and
the whole depth table come from per-run debug logs, and `x4-runs/` is gitignored.** Half the claims
had no committed backing.
Fix: derived `evidence/2026-09-13-wallyfix-ladder-depth.txt` as the committed record, and rewrote the
sentence to say exactly which numbers are re-derivable and which are merely recorded — keeping the
original wording in a parenthetical.
⇒ **Prevention rule: "re-derivable from the repo" is a claim about EVERY number in the entry. Check
it per number, not per file, and remember that copying a summary does not cover figures computed
from artifacts the summary does not contain.**

**(d) ⛔ I updated the queue PROSE and left the file's own LIVE-ACTION MARKER pointing at finished work.**
Symptom: a Tier 1 reviewer failed P1. `04-HANDOFF.md` documents its own ritual — *"EXACTLY ONE LINE
IN THIS FILE BEGINS WITH THE `➡➡➡` MARKER, AND IT IS THE LIVE NEXT ACTION"* — and that one line still
read *"THE NEXT STEP NEEDS THE USER … the feature is ON in SANDBOX only … PROMOTED to
`custom-pokebot`"*. The user had already been asked, had answered, and the promotion had shipped.
⇒ a cold agent following the file's OWN documented ritual would have re-asked a settled question
instead of starting `#24-rival110`, while the prose 60 lines below correctly said otherwise.
Root cause: I treated "QUEUE ITEM 0" prose as the next-action pointer. **It is not — the file names
its own pointer, and I did not grep for it.**
⇒ **Prevention rule: when a document defines its OWN pointer convention, updating the narrative is
not updating the pointer. On finishing an item, run the file's own documented query
(`grep -n "^>    ➡➡➡"`) and re-read what it returns.** ‼ P1 says "banner ↔ queue item 0" — this
failure sat in NEITHER half, which is why the reviewer had to catch it: **a pair check protects
exactly the two things it names.**

## 2026-09-13 (evening) — I ranked the next work item against a build I had personally superseded, while holding the new batch

**Symptom.** Within an hour of closing `#24-wallydecline` — a fix I had just proven at scale — I filed
`#24-rival110` as *"the largest measured defect, 52.3% of every whiteout"*, made it queue item 0, set
the handoff's single `➡➡➡` live-action marker to it, and briefed the user on it. Re-derived on the
build that fix produced, Route 110 is **6.3% of losses and the 6th site**; the real #1 is Norman's gym
at **24.0%**.

**Root cause — three compounding errors, and the first is the one that matters.**
1. ⛔ **I ranked on PRE-FIX data while holding the POST-FIX batch.** I had already parsed
   `20260913-092254` to prove the fix worked. The same batch answers "what is biggest now", and I did
   not ask it. **I had even recorded, in that same session, that the fix's whole effect was to
   RELOCATE deaths** — so the one thing I knew for certain was that the old ranking was stale.
2. ⛔ **I pooled the treatment and control arms of an A/B.** The two source batches are
   `POKEBOT_MAINTAIN=1` and `=0`; they disagree on the very statistic I pooled (44.1% vs 57.9%).
3. ⚠ **I relayed two figures I had not derived** ("55.6% of compute is grinding", "ROUTE116 is 28.2%
   of every frame"), which could not be sourced. Both withdrawn.

⇒ **Prevention rule: A PRIORITY RANKING IS A MEASUREMENT, AND IT EXPIRES WHEN THE BUILD CHANGES.
After shipping any fix, re-derive the ranking on the FIRST batch that contains it, before choosing
what to do next — and name the commit the ranking came from in the same sentence as the ranking.**
‼ Corollary, because this is what made it embarrassing rather than merely wrong: **"this fix relocates
deaths" is a statement that the ranking is about to change. If you write that sentence, you owe the
next ranking a re-derivation.**
⇒ **Second prevention rule: never pool two batches without checking their arm/flag declarations.**
`MANIFEST.txt` / `ARM-*.txt` state them; two batches run back-to-back on the same commit can still be
two different regimes.

**What caught it.** An adversarial agent, told to refute the claim rather than check it. The three
non-adversarial agents on the same subject all worked *within* the superseded frame. ‼ That is the
standing case for the adversarial angle: the other agents answered the question I asked, and the
question was wrong.

## 2026-09-13 (late) — I opened a second item for a defect that was already open, already diagnosed, and already RULED ON — and my instinct was the option the user had rejected

**Symptom.** Having correctly re-derived that Norman's gym is the #1 loss site (24.0%), I filed
`#24-norman-lead` as a fresh *"Hypothesis (UNVERIFIED)"* that `_lead_best_matchup` fronts a weak mon,
made it queue item 0, moved the handoff's live-action marker to it, and briefed the user.

**It was a duplicate three times over.**
* **KI-25** (opened **2026-07-27**, severity HIGH) names the same function, quotes the same line, and
  measures it **at the same boss**: *"P4 led Shedinja L20 vs Norman … lost to Slaking's Faint Attack"*.
* **`#24-leadpolicy`** is OPEN in the live punch list with that diagnosis already written out.
* **The user RULED on it on 2026-07-29**: *"`#24-leadpolicy` → OPTIONS A + C … **Level-gap weighting
  (B) NOT adopted.**"*

⛔ **And that last clause is the part that matters.** My stated signal was *"the median LEAD is L29
while the median TOP mon is L35 — six levels below our own best."* **That is level-gap weighting. That
is option B.** I was one step from building the thing the user had explicitly turned down fourteen
sessions earlier.

**Root cause.** I *did* run the Standing-Directive-#11 grep — for `route110|rival110`, the item I was
leaving. I did not re-run it for the item I was ARRIVING at. The check was treated as a per-session
ritual instead of a per-item one.
⇒ **Prevention rule: RUN THE DECISIONS-LOG GREP FOR THE ITEM YOU ARE ABOUT TO OPEN, NOT THE ONE YOU
ARE CLOSING — and grep `05-KNOWN-ISSUES.md` and the punch list for the FUNCTION NAME too, not just
the slug.** A defect that has been known for seven weeks will not be filed under the slug you just
invented for it; it will be filed under the function it lives in (`_lead_best_matchup`).
‼ **Second prevention rule, from the same failure: when you catch yourself reasoning from a
DIFFERENCE (a level gap, a count gap, a time gap), check whether that exact framing is a rejected
option.** Rulings reject *approaches*, and an approach re-derived from data looks new even when it
is not.

**What caught it.** A Tier 1 reviewer, given the pair list — the same way `#24-dexcatch` was caught
on 2026-09-05, which is itself recorded in `03-PUNCH-LIST.md` as *"⛔⛔ DO NOT OPEN A SECOND ONE."*
‼ **That warning was already in the file I was editing.** ⇒ a prevention rule filed under one item
does not fire when you are working on another; only a mechanical check does.

## 2026-09-13 (night) — I hunted a defect the docs described, in code that no longer works that way; and I twice measured the wrong population

**(a) ⛔ I TRUSTED A DOCSTRING AND A KNOWN-ISSUE OVER THE CODE, AND SPENT A ROUND ON IT.**
`_lead_best_matchup`'s docstring says *"Picks the battler minimizing the foe's WORST-CASE STAB
multiplier … breaking ties by higher level"* — purely defensive, exactly what KI-25 diagnoses. Both
are **STALE**: the body delegates to `team_policy.lead_rank_key`, which has carried the ruled (a) and
(c) terms since commit `9252e238` (2026-08-01). KI-25 still quotes the replaced expression and its
old line number. I read the docstring and the top of the function, saw the defensive `_incoming`
helper, and stopped.
⇒ **Prevention rule: when a docstring and the body can disagree, the BODY is the fact. Read to the
`return`/the ranking expression before concluding what a selector optimises** — a helper defined
inside a function is not evidence that it is the only term. ‼ And: **a KNOWN-ISSUE entry that quotes
code is a claim with an expiry date**; treat a quoted line number older than the last refactor as
unverified until re-read.

**(b) ⛔ I MEASURED "NORMAN" AND ACTUALLY MEASURED A WHOLE GYM.** I reported 119 W / 180 L = 40% for
Norman from battles whose MAP was `PETALBURG CITY`. That map contains **three gym trainers** fought
before the boss. Isolating by the opponent named in the `[TURN]` lines: Norman is **59 W / 172 L =
26%**, and the trainers are won **88%**. The direction of the error flattered the bot by 14 points.
⇒ **Prevention rule: a MAP is not an OPPONENT.** When the question is about one fight, filter by the
foe, not by where the foe stands — the logs name it on every turn line.

**(c) ⚠ AND I READ AN EMPTY SHELL PIPE AS A ZERO.** `grep -hc Slaking … | paste -sd+ | bc` produced
nothing, and I reported *"Slaking is never named"*. It is named **165 times**. A pipeline that fails
prints nothing, which is indistinguishable from a true zero unless you check.
⇒ **Prevention rule: a zero from a multi-stage shell pipe must be confirmed by a positive control** —
run the same pipe against something you KNOW is present. (This is the same shape as the earlier rule
*"an impossible zero refutes the metric"*, but its cause is the shell, not the key.)

⭐ **WHAT WENT RIGHT, AND IS WORTH KEEPING.** Before building anything I ran the win-vs-loss
comparison **in the same population**, and it refuted my own hypothesis: the lead/top level gap is
**6.0 in wins and 6.0 in losses**. That is the check I failed to run on the "fainted lead" claim
earlier in the day, applied in time. ⇒ **a signal measured only on failures is not a signal;
measure it on successes too, or do not report it.**

**Symptom.** With the queue correctly pointed at story content (`#24-e4healing` steps 2-4), I
commissioned a workflow — 4 recon angles, 4 adversarial verifiers, 1 synthesis, ~1.5M subagent
tokens — to research the problem and produce a build spec. `PROJECT KNOWLEDGE/ai-research-notes/`
already contained **EIGHT** Ch24 notes, including **`2026-09-07-ch24-elite-four-BUILD-SPEC.md`** (a
12-leg chapter shape whose legs 5b-8b are literally *"heal between fights"*, i.e. step 2) and
`2026-09-08-ch24-league-RECON.md`, which already states *"`heal_party_from_bag` IS BUILT, DRIVEN, AND
HAS ZERO CALLERS … This is `#24-e4healing` steps 2-4"*.

**What the workflow actually bought.** Three things, of which one is genuinely valuable and I
verified it myself against the ROM (halls 1/2/3/5 have three adjacent warp tiles at the arrival end,
so a sidestep while healing warps backward; HALL4 is the only safe hall). The rest was re-derivation,
and its own adversarial layer said so — one verifier wrote that the recon *"re-derived a nine-day-old
note and came back LESS accurate than it"*.

**Root cause.** My recon design DID include "check `ai-research-notes/`" — as **point 4 of one of the
four angles**. So the check ran *inside* the expensive thing it was supposed to make unnecessary.
⇒ **Prevention rule: READ `ai-research-notes/00-READ-THIS-FIRST.md`'s INDEX BEFORE COMMISSIONING
RESEARCH, NOT AS AN ANGLE INSIDE IT.** The index is one file and lists every note by headline. A
prior-art check is a PRECONDITION of the spawn, not a task for the spawned.

(`#24-norman-lead` vs the open `#24-leadpolicy`) had the same shape — a "have we done this already?"
check placed after the work instead of before it. **Both times the adversarial reviewer caught it,
and both times that was too late to save the cost.**

⭐ **WHAT THE DESIGN GOT RIGHT, AND IS WORTH KEEPING.** Pairing every recon agent with an adversarial
verifier is what surfaced the duplication at all, and it also caught: a stale coordinate ((6,12) not
(6,13)), an omitted fifth warp, an "unknown" that was in the first 30 lines of the handoff, and a
headline ("WORSE THAN RECORDED") that the project's own decisions log had already recorded nine days
earlier. ⇒ **keep the adversarial pairing; move the prior-art check in front of it.**

## 2026-09-13 — I sent a diff for review and then kept editing it, so the reviewer audited a snapshot that no longer existed

**Symptom.** I captured `git diff` for a code change, spawned a Tier 1 reviewer on it, and then — while
it ran — hardened the same two files (status normalisation + four gate checks + a module comment).
The reviewer BLOCKED, correctly, with: *"The diff under review is stale relative to the working tree
— a material amount of unreviewed logic already exists on disk … 127 lines, roughly double the 62
lines these two files account for in the diff."* It also caught that my self-report said "48 checks"
while the tree actually had 52.

**Why this is worse than it looks.** A review is only worth the snapshot it audited. Had it returned
RECOMMEND-COMMIT, I would have committed a code path — the enum-normalisation branch — that **no
reviewer ever saw**, under a self-report describing a narrower, older version of the same function.
The reviewer would have been cited as the safety check that never examined the risky part.

⇒ **Prevention rule: THE TREE IS FROZEN FROM `git diff` UNTIL THE REVIEW RETURNS.** If something must
change, cancel the review or re-submit — never let both run at once. And **re-capture the diff AND
the raw evidence together, at the moment of submission**, so the check counts in the report and in
the evidence file provably describe the same bytes. ‼ Quote an MD5 of each reviewed file in the
submission so the reviewer can detect drift itself — which is what the re-submission did, and it is
the only reason the second review could trust its inputs.

⭐ **AND THE RULE FIRED THE SAME HOUR.** While the RE-review was running I found two more edge cases
worth fixing (a lowercase status silently declines; an object whose `.name` property raises
propagates the exception). I did **not** apply them — applying them would have re-created the exact
defect I had just been blocked for. They are deferred to the next pass. ⇒ *the test of a prevention
rule is whether it stops you when it is inconvenient.*

**A second, smaller thing the same review caught, worth keeping:** my self-report paraphrased the
gate result instead of attaching raw output. *"Per the fixed rule this is an automatic fail."* The
reviewer then ran the gate itself and got a DIFFERENT count than I had claimed — which is how the
staleness was detected in the first place. ⇒ **attach raw stdout, never a paraphrase; a number you
retype is a number you can retype wrongly.**

## 2026-09-13 — I nearly shipped a feature that could never fire, hidden behind a safe `getattr`

**Symptom.** Wiring `#24-e4healing` step 3, I wrote
`getattr(mon, "status_condition", None)` to read the active Pokémon's status. `mon` here is a
**`BattlePokemon`**, which has **no `status_condition` property** — that one belongs to `Pokemon`.
The battle object exposes `status_permanent` and `status_temporary`.

**What would have happened.** `getattr` with a default does not raise. The policy would have been
handed `None` every single turn, declined every single time, and the feature would have been
**inert forever** — while all 66 policy checks passed, the commit said "the bot can now cure status
in battle", and nothing anywhere contradicted it. The same draft also used `get_party` without
importing it in that scope (it is imported inside a *different* function as `_gp`), which would have
raised `NameError` — and `decide_turn` wraps `_maybe_use_item` in `try/except Exception`, so that
too would have been swallowed into a silent None.
⇒ **Two independent silent-failure paths in ten lines, both invisible to a green test suite.**

**What caught it.** Not a test — a habit: before trusting an attribute name, I listed the class's
actual `@property` names. Then I verified end-to-end with the REAL enum
(`StatusCondition.Sleep → Full Heal`, `Poison → None`) rather than with a stand-in.

⇒ **Prevention rule: A SAFE DEFAULT ON AN ATTRIBUTE YOU HAVE NOT VERIFIED IS A SILENT OFF-SWITCH.**
`getattr(x, "name", None)` and `try/except` around a caller are both fine — but they convert a
*typo* into *permanent silence*, which is strictly worse than a crash. Before reading an attribute
off an object you did not construct, ENUMERATE its properties; and prefer the direct access
(`mon.status_permanent`) once verified, so a future rename FAILS LOUDLY instead of going quiet.
‼ **And gate the wiring, not just the policy.** The 66 checks tested a pure function that was
perfect; the bug was entirely in how it was CALLED. Six static source checks now pin the call site —
including that the caller passes the UNFILTERED item list, because passing the filtered one would
silently re-create the very `parameter > 0` bug this item exists to remove.

## 2026-09-13 — my 72 checks tested a perfect policy while its INTEGRATION was broken

**Symptom.** I wired `choose_status_or_revive_item` into `_maybe_use_item`, with 72 gate checks
green: the pure policy verified exhaustively, the call site verified statically, the item names
verified against `items.json`, five fault arms proven. A Tier 1 reviewer then traced the wiring
against code the diff *did not touch* — the no-op detector — and found that a **SUCCESSFUL status
cure reads as a FAILED item**, because the detector judges by HP delta and a cure never raises HP.
Two cures in one battle would have set `_items_ineffective = True` and **disabled all item use,
including HP-emergency healing, for the rest of that fight** — in the Elite Four, which is the one
place the feature was built for.

**Root cause.** Every check I wrote pointed at the thing I ADDED. None pointed at the thing I was
adding it INTO. The policy was pure and provable, so I proved it; the integration was a stateful
interaction with three-iteration-old code, and I checked it only by reading.
⇒ **Prevention rule: WHEN WIRING A NEW ANSWER INTO AN EXISTING DECISION PATH, THE THING TO TEST IS
THE PATH, NOT THE ANSWER.** Ask specifically: what does the surrounding code MEASURE to decide
whether my action worked — and is that measurement meaningful for the new kind of action? Here the
answer was "it measures HP, and my action does not change HP", which is the whole bug in one line.
‼ **And the shape generalises:** a no-op/effectiveness detector built for action A will silently
misjudge action B unless it knows the kinds apart. Gate #60 exists to keep it knowing.

**What made the fix safe.** The kind check runs FIRST and returns early, so the HP branch — three
measured iterations deep (KI-34, the 2026-08-10 same-subject fix, the index-space flip) — is not
modified at all. ⇒ *when extending safety-critical code, prefer a branch in front of it to an edit
inside it.*

‼ **A ratchet also caught the fix's own cost.** The new telemetry handler took
`repro_no_silent_except` to 80/79 OVER. The honest response was not a budget bump but an explicit
justification of WHY that swallow is correct (telemetry must never break a battle; the branch above
has already cleared the marker, so a swallow cannot change behaviour) — 79/79 without funding debt.

## 2026-09-13 — a `is None` check on a value that is never `None`, and a grade that scored the wrong quantity

**Three near-misses in one work item, all of the same family: a check that cannot fail, or fails for
the wrong reason.**

**1. `get_battle_state() is None` is NEVER TRUE.** `ch24probe`'s post-battle wait loop tested it.
The function is annotated `-> BattleState` and unconditionally constructs one from raw symbols
(`battle_state.py:808-824`); there is no `return None` in it. ⇒ the loop could never break and the
`raise` guarding it could never not-fire. **The probe beat Sidney and was killed by the watchdog
every single time, having printed no verdict.** It looked like a bot hang; at the moment of the
"hang" the game was `OVERWORLD`, `DialogueNotActive`, player controllable at (6,6) — *nothing was
stuck except the condition.* Fixed to `get_game_state() != GameState.BATTLE`.
⇒ **Prevention: before writing `x is None`, CHECK THAT THE CALLEE CAN RETURN None** — read its
return annotation and grep its body for `return None`. A sentinel check against a value that never
takes the sentinel is a silent infinite loop, and it reads as perfectly defensive code.
‼ What actually caught it: **an unstaged BASELINE arm**. It reproduced the identical hang with zero
env vars set, which is what proved the defect was pre-existing rather than mine — and *that* is what
sent me to read the predicate instead of my own new code.

**2. `import os as _os` was NOT in scope, and `py_compile` says nothing about that.** The fault-arm
check I added to `_maybe_use_item` used `_os.environ`; `os` is **not** imported at module scope in
`story_mode.py` (local-import convention). `decide_turn` wraps the whole method in
`try/except Exception: action = None`, so the `NameError` would have been swallowed into a silent
decline — **the cure never firing, the fault arm looking permanently ON, every gate still green.**
Identical in shape to the `status_condition` dead path in the same file, and to the out-of-scope
`get_party` in the same draft.
⇒ **Prevention: `py_compile` / a clean import proves SYNTAX, never NAME RESOLUTION.** In a file that
imports locally by convention, verify the name is bound in *your* scope. ⭐ The A/B on gate #60 is
what proved the fix: arm OFF `ALL PASS (11 checks)`, arm ON `FAIL CONTROL … None` — and because that
gate calls `_maybe_use_item` DIRECTLY, a surviving `NameError` would have crashed the passing arm.

**3. The grade scored "any item while frozen" instead of the cure.** Caught by an ADVERSARIAL
subagent before the drive. `_maybe_use_item` returns HP items too, and the live run used three Full
Restores. That grade gives a **false PASS** in the live arm and a **false FAIL** in the control —
*from the same line.*
⇒ **Prevention: when a grade counts events, ask what ELSE produces that event.** Prefer a
STRUCTURAL discriminator over a plausible one: `parameter == 0` works because the HP policy is
handed a list pre-filtered to `> 0` (`story_mode.py:723`), so it *cannot* produce one — that is a
proof, not a heuristic.

**4. And the tree told me something false about the game.** Three production comments said *"Gen-3
freeze never thaws on its own"*; Emerald self-thaws **20% per attempted move**
(`battle_util.c`, `CANCELER_FROZEN`, `if (Random() % 5)`). A gate in
`repro_overworld_items.py` **asserted the false wording**, so correcting the comment turned the
suite red — *the gate was defending the error.*
⇒ **Prevention: A GREEN GATE IS NOT EVIDENCE A FACT IS TRUE — it only pins what someone once wrote.**
When a gate fails after a factual correction, suspect the EXPECTATION before the change.
‼ And the live control arm demonstrated the real behaviour in passing: `DECISION#9 status=Healthy`
after 8 frozen turns with **no item used**. Had the grade scored "the freeze cleared" rather than
the ACTION, that control would have published a refutation of a feature that works.

## 2026-09-13 — I corrected one clause of a 41,789-character line and shipped the contradiction three more times

**Symptom.** `#24-e4healing` step 3 went from "not wired" to "done and driven live". I updated the
punch-list summary cell and three handoff queue lines. Tier 1 returned **KICK-BACK**: the handoff's
own `➡➡➡` NEXT ACTION line still said *"step 1 of 4 done"* — **in the tail of the very line whose
head I had just edited.** I fixed that, re-ran, and Tier 1 returned **ESCALATE**: a SECOND
`STEPS 2-4` claim survived ~28,000 characters further into the same 41,789-char line, plus a
verbatim copy on another line. A post-condition I added then caught a FOURTH.

**Root cause — two separate mistakes, and the second is the reusable one.**

**(1) A LINE IS NOT A CLAIM; IT IS A PARAGRAPH.** `04-HANDOFF.md:145` is 41,789 characters,
`:533` is 45,203, `03-PUNCH-LIST.md:391` is 3,004. "I updated that line" does **not** mean the line
is now true. ⇒ **After editing a mega-line, RE-READ IT END TO END and grep it for the OLD claim
before moving on.** The edit tool confirms a replacement happened; it says nothing about the other
forty kilobytes.

**(2) ⛔⛔ MY OWN STALENESS SWEEP VOUCHED FOR THE STALE CLAIMS — a proximity filter masked them.**
I swept with "cue word near topic word, unless a retraction marker is within ±300 characters". Both
survivors sat ~170 characters after an **unrelated** clause reading *"— superseded: too vague, and
`08-MISTAKES.md` records it as published in error."* ⇒ **A NEIGHBOUR'S RETRACTION TAG SILENTLY
CERTIFIED A DIFFERENT SENTENCE.** In a 40KB line, ±300 characters is a different subject entirely.
⇒ **Prevention rule: ANCHOR AN "ALREADY MARKED HISTORICAL" TEST TO THE HIT'S OWN CLAUSE, NEVER TO A
CHARACTER WINDOW.** Split on sentence/parenthetical boundaries and require the marker inside the
same clause. Re-running that way took 2 survivors → 0. ‼ And the `staleness-sweep` skill already
says *"judge every hit by hand — do NOT auto-fix"*; I auto-**filtered**, which is the same error
wearing the opposite coat: the skill's warning is about trusting a machine to decide relevance, and
a suppression rule is exactly that decision.

**(3) A HISTORICAL WRAPPER AROUND A PRESENT-TENSE VERB IS STILL A LIVE CLAIM.** The fourth survivor
sat inside `*(historical ordering, now partly DONE: …)*` and read *"Items (3) §Ch24 and (4)
`#24-e4healing` steps 2-4 **remain**"*. A reviewer had judged that occurrence acceptable because of
the wrapper. ⇒ **Judge the VERB, not the parenthetical.** "Remain" asserts the present tense no
matter what it is nested inside.

**What finally worked, and is now the habit.** The fix script carries its own **POST-CONDITION**:
after editing, it re-scans the whole file for any unretracted survivor of the old claim and
**refuses to write** if one is found. It fired immediately and caught the fourth occurrence — before
any file was touched, because the assert runs before the write.
⇒ **Prevention rule: A DOC FIX THAT REPLACES A CLAIM MUST END BY PROVING THE CLAIM IS GONE
FILE-WIDE.** Round 1 "passed" without that check and shipped two survivors; round 2 could not.
