## 2026-09-13 — five review rounds on one status change: a grep finds spellings, a reviewer finds claims

**Symptom.** After `#24-e4healing` step 3 shipped, it took **five** independent review rounds to make
the docs true. Rounds 1-2 are written up above (an under-corrected mega-line). Rounds 3-5 failed for
three NEW reasons, each worth its own rule.

**(1) ⛔⛔ A KEYWORD SWEEP PROVES THE ABSENCE OF A SPELLING, NOT OF A CLAIM.** My round-2 sweep
returned **0 survivors**. A fresh reviewer then found four, none of which contained any word I had
searched for:
    *"Status is completely unhandled."* · *"The 8 Full Heals cannot be used."*
    *"the bot cannot use Full Heal or Revive at all"* · and an **unchecked checkbox**,
    `- [ ] 3. Decide whether the in-battle policy should get status/revive awareness`
⇒ **Prevention: SWEEP BY CAPABILITY, NOT BY PHRASE.** State the question the change answers — here
*"can the bot cure a status condition during a battle?"* — and find every sentence, table cell,
checkbox and status marker that answers it. ‼ **AN UNCHECKED CHECKBOX IS A CLAIM**, and so is a
bare table cell reading `⛔ NO`. This is failure #1 in the `staleness-sweep` skill, stated verbatim
there; I had the skill open and swept for spellings anyway.

**(2) ⛔ THE CONSISTENCY TIERS ARE SCOPED TO `PROJECT KNOWLEDGE/`, SO A CLAIM RESTATED ANYWHERE ELSE
IS INVISIBLE TO EVERY REVIEWER.** `tools/story-dev/saves/FIXTURES.md5` pinned `post_league_shop.ss1`
with *"no code path we currently have can use them, in or out of battle"* — false since step 1
(2026-09-04) and false again since step 3. No tier looks there; `audit_doc_consistency.py` does not
either. I found it only by cross-checking bag arithmetic against the pin for an unrelated reason.
⇒ **Prevention: when a CAPABILITY changes, grep the WHOLE REPO — fixture pins, gate docstrings, code
comments — not just the docs directory.**

**(3) ⛔⛔ A RETRACTION CAN OVER-CORRECT, AND IT INHERITS THE SUBJECT OF THE SENTENCE IT FOLLOWS.**
My own fix to `03-PUNCH-LIST.md:437` appended *"(As of 2026-09-13 they ARE used …)"* directly after
a sentence reading *"a sleep/**paralysis** from any of the five would simply persist."* ⇒ it read as
*"paralysis is cured now"* — **which is false.** The policy cures Sleep and Freeze ONLY; those are
the only members of `TURN_COSTING_STATUSES`, and Poison/Burn/Paralysis are excluded deliberately
because they do not cost a turn. The reviewer caught it; nothing mechanical would have.
⇒ **Prevention: after appending a correction, READ THE SENTENCE BEFORE IT** and confirm the
correction does not appear to answer that sentence too. **Carry the SCOPE into the retraction**, not
just the verdict. ‼ Under-claiming leaves work undone; **over-claiming makes someone build on a
capability that is not there**, which is strictly worse — and these files are skimmed, not read.

**(4) And the numbers had to be DERIVED, not carried.** "33 of 44 usable" appeared in four places.
The honest update was not a search-and-replace: from the pinned basket (Hyper Potion 30 + Full
Restore 3 + Full Heal 8 + Revive 3 = 44) step 3 moves the 8 Full Heals ⇒ **41 usable, 3 unusable**
(the Revives). I asked the reviewer to CHECK the arithmetic rather than assert it, and where a
figure could not be re-derived (`"33 of the 44"` inside another item) I marked it STALE and
**refused to restate it** rather than guess.

⇒ **The meta-rule: a status change is not "update the status line". It is a CLAIM RETRACTION across
every place the old claim was ever restated, in whatever words — and the only reliable finder of
those is a reader who is asked the CAPABILITY QUESTION, not a grep.**

## 2026-09-14 — the prevention rule fired on its second day, and an A/B measured the opposite of its theory

**1. ⛔ `UnboundLocalError`, caught BEFORE shipping, by the rule written 24 hours earlier.**
Step 4's knob read `_os.environ` at the top of `_maybe_use_item`. `os` is not imported at module
scope in `story_mode.py` (local-import convention), and the local `import os as _os` sat **40 lines
later**, inside a conditional branch. ‼ In Python a local `import` anywhere in a function makes that
name **local for the entire function**, so the earlier read is an `UnboundLocalError` — *which even a
module-level `os` would not have rescued.* And `decide_turn` wraps the whole method in
`try/except Exception: action = None`, so the failure would have been SILENT: **no item used in any
battle, every gate still green.**
⇒ **Prevention (reinforced, not new): bind such a name ONCE, at the TOP of the function, and never
re-scatter it into branches.** The 2026-09-13 rule ("verify the name is bound in YOUR scope") is what
caught it. ⭐ Gate #60 would also have caught it, because it calls `_maybe_use_item` DIRECTLY rather
than through `decide_turn`'s swallow — a gate that bypasses the production try/except is worth more
than one that goes through it.

**2. ⛔⛔ THE A/B MEASURED THE OPPOSITE OF THE THEORY, AND THE FIRST READING OF IT WAS STILL WRONG.**
Raising `HEAL_AT_FRACTION` 0.35 → 0.50 turned a WIN into a LOSS. The tempting conclusion —
*"healing earlier is bad, keep 0.35"* — is **wrong**. Both arms spent the same 2 items, which is not
what a bound threshold should look like, and that oddity was the thread worth pulling: the raised arm
requested items earlier, the bag **failed to open**, the strategy re-decided the same turn, and the
no-op detector read two misses and disabled ALL healing for the remaining 30 decisions.
⇒ **Prevention: WHEN AN A/B INVERTS ITS THEORY, FIND THE MECHANISM BEFORE ACCEPTING THE RESULT.** An
outcome flip is a pointer, not an explanation, and the honest answer here was neither "0.35 is right"
nor "0.50 is right" but **"the threshold cannot be tuned until item execution is reliable."**
‼ And I nearly filed that execution bug as NEW. **Rule 11 (grep `06-DECISIONS-LOG.md` first) stopped
it**: the 2026-08-10 promotion ruling accepts the guard in writing. What was new was only the
INTERACTION, and that is what got written down.

**3. ⛔ I COULD NOT TELL "THE ARM RAN THE OVERRIDE AND LOST" FROM "THE ARM SILENTLY RAN THE DEFAULT".**
The first 0.50 run recorded no evidence of which threshold the policy was actually called with — only
which env var I had set. Both arms then showing 2 items made the result uninterpretable.
⇒ **Prevention: AN A/B ARM MUST LOG THE VALUE THE CODE ACTED ON, NOT THE VALUE YOU SET.** The knob now
records `self._effective_heal_fraction` at the call site and the driver prints `heal_frac=` on every
decision, so an arm that silently ran the default is visible AS THAT. (Session-discipline rule 7,
"instrument the ACTION", applied to a *parameter* rather than to a choice.)

**4. Citation drift stopped being a lesson and became a tool.** It fired FIVE times in two days,
always the same mechanical repair, always hand-typed — and hand-typing a line number is how a wrong
one gets introduced while fixing a stale one. `tools/story-dev/fix_doc_citations.py` now applies the
corrections `audit_doc_citations.py` already computes.
⇒ **Prevention: A RULE BROKEN FIVE TIMES IS NOT A RULE, IT IS A MISSING TOOL.** (CLAUDE.md already
says "anything enforceable belongs in a GATE, not in prose"; the same applies to anything REPAIRABLE.)

## 2026-09-14 — the same doc defect twice in 24 hours, so it stopped being a rule and became gate #61

**Symptom.** `#24-e4healing` states each step's status in THREE places: a numbered checklist, the
item's cell header, and a STATUS line. On 2026-09-13 step 3 shipped — checklist ticked, STATUS line
stale, caught by Tier 1. On 2026-09-14 step 4 was answered — checklist ticked, **and BOTH the cell
header and the STATUS line left stale**, caught by Tier 1 again. Same item, same shape, one day
apart, with the P5 rule already written and already applied to that exact line.

**Root cause.** P5 is prose, and prose does not fire while you are thinking about something else.
⇒ **`tools/story-dev/probe_punchlist_step_status.py` is now gate #61 (enforcing).** It encodes one
mechanical property: *if an item's checklist ticks step N `[x]`, no other line in that same item may
say step N "remains".* Fault-tested — restoring the old wording reds it naming both line numbers,
and it does NOT fire on a dated retraction that QUOTES the old wording (the live tree contains
exactly such a quote and the gate passes). ‼ CLAUDE.md already said this: *"a rule already broken
twice is evidence that prose failed — write the gate instead."* It took a third breach to act on it.

**And three sharper lessons, each of which cost a cycle today:**

**1. ⛔⛔ A RETRACTION THAT ASSERTS A NEW PRESENT-TENSE STATUS ROTS EXACTLY LIKE THE TEXT IT
REPLACED.** Yesterday I repaired a stale clause by writing *"…step 3 is DONE AND DRIVEN LIVE, and
step 4 … **is the CURRENT target**"*. Today step 4 was answered and **my own retraction became the
stale claim** — in three copies. The clause it sat beside even carries the warning *"THIS SENTENCE
IS A CLAIM ABOUT ANOTHER LINE, SO IT GOES STALE WHEN THAT LINE MOVES — AND IT HAS, FOUR TIMES."*
It went stale a fifth time, and the fifth time was mine.
⇒ **Prevention: a retraction should say what the old text SAID and that it is superseded. The moment
it makes a fresh live claim it becomes another half of the pair that must be maintained.** Point at
the queue marker; do not restate the queue.

**2. ⛔ NEVER INLINE A PROGRAM CONTAINING NON-ASCII THROUGH THE SHELL.** A `py -3.12 -c "…"` whose
source contained `➡➡➡` was mangled by bash (`$'\236\236\236': command not found`) and the glyphs
were **silently deleted** from the written text, leaving *"see the  marker"*. No mojibake, no error
in the file — just missing characters, in a document nobody would re-read.
⇒ **Prevention: write the program to a FILE and run the file** (every other repair this session did;
this one broke the pattern and paid). ‼ And note what caught it: **not the five "FIXED" lines the
script printed, but reading back what was actually written.** An edit's success message describes
the SUBSTITUTION IT ATTEMPTED, never the RESULT.

**3. ⛔ A VERIFICATION PATTERN THAT ENCODES INCIDENTAL FORMATTING VERIFIES THE FORMATTING, NOT THE
FACT.** My read-back check for *"total = enforcing + advisory"* required the literal `(**` bold
markers, so a line writing the same fact unadorned — `61 gates (57 ENFORCING + 3 ADVISORY` — sailed
through it and was caught one run later by the real gate. The check reported **"0 inconsistent"**
about a file that was inconsistent.
⇒ **Prevention: match the FACT (a number, a keyword, a number), never its decoration. And ASSERT THE
PATTERN MATCHED SOMETHING** — a post-condition that finds zero instances "passes" for the wrong
reason, which is precisely how that one lied. The corrected version requires `found >= 2`.

⇒ **The thread running through all three: every one was a CHECK that was wrong, not a subject that
was wrong** — session-discipline rule 4, which now has more instances in this file than any other.

## 2026-09-14 — a blocker that stood for a week was a WRONG ARGUMENT, not a missing capability

**Symptom.** `KI-94` blocked the entire §Ch24 chapter from 2026-09-07 to 2026-09-14 on the finding
that the prepared party could not reach the League door. The measurement behind it was real: Fly to
Ever Grande deposited the party at the Poké Center (27,49) and `calculate_path` raised
`PathFindingError` to (18,5).

**Root cause.** The drive flew to the destination named `EverGrandeCity`. Emerald has **two** fly
destinations for that map section, and our own `modules/region_map.py:53-54` has always modelled
both — `PokemonLeague = (28,10)` distinct from `EverGrandeCity = (28,11)`, gated by
`LANDMARK_POKEMON_LEAGUE`. Flying to the other one lands at **(18,6)**, the door apron. One
environment variable separated "blocked for a week" from "solved".

⇒ **Prevention 1: WHEN A CAPABILITY LOOKS MISSING, ENUMERATE ITS OPTIONS BEFORE CONCLUDING IT IS
ABSENT.** "Fly doesn't reach the League" was really "the destination I picked doesn't reach the
League". The enumeration lived in our own source file the whole time.

⇒ **Prevention 2: ⛔⛔ WHEN TWO FILES IN OUR OWN TREE DISAGREE, *THAT IS THE FINDING* — go resolve
it before building on either.** `region_map.py` (data, generated from the game) said the League was
a separate fly target; `victory_road.py:362` (prose, written by a person) said the two halves were
"connected only THROUGH Victory Road". The prose won for a week because it was the one written in
the place people were reading. **Grade GENERATED DATA above HAND-WRITTEN COMMENTARY** when they
conflict, and correct the commentary the moment you notice.

⇒ **Prevention 3: KI-94 DID EVERYTHING RIGHT AND STILL COST A WEEK.** It stated its own limit
precisely — *"`calculate_path` is not able to use warps or fly… a warp route has NOT been ruled out
by measurement… it must be checked, not assumed"* — and nothing checked it for seven days. **A
correctly-hedged unknown is still an unknown, and hedging it does not schedule the check.** ‼ When a
KI names an unresolved question that BLOCKS a chapter, the question belongs in NEXT ACTIONS, not
only in the KI body. That is precisely what a cold-start audit surfaced this session, and answering
it took one adversarial agent and one 40,000-frame drive.

---

## 2026-09-14 — four ways a POST-CONDITION lied to me in one afternoon

Every doc repair I ran today ended with a read-back post-condition. They caught real defects — and
**four of them were themselves wrong**, in four different ways. Collected here because the pattern
is more useful than any one instance, and because session-discipline rule 4 ("read the failing line
before touching the subject") now has more entries in this file than any other rule.

**1. TOO NARROW — it encoded INCIDENTAL FORMATTING.** A check for *"total = enforcing + advisory"*
required the literal `(**` bold markers, so a line writing the same fact unadorned —
`61 gates (57 ENFORCING + 3 ADVISORY` — sailed through and reported **"0 inconsistent"** about an
inconsistent file. The real gate caught it one run later.
⇒ **Match the FACT (a number, a keyword, a number), never its decoration.**

**2. TOO BROAD — it matched a FRAGMENT that lives elsewhere.** A check that the pending-promotion
note was gone asserted on `"not this one"`, which occurs three times in an unrelated sentence about
the OWNER filter. It failed on an already-correct file.
⇒ **Match the CLAIM, not a fragment that could appear anywhere.** 1 and 2 are the same error in
opposite directions, and I made both within hours.

**3. IT PASSED FOR THE WRONG REASON — it matched NOTHING.** A post-condition that finds zero
instances "passes". ⇒ **assert the pattern matched something**: the corrected version requires
`found >= 2` before trusting a clean result. A check that cannot fail is not a check.

**4. IT RAN BEFORE THE WORK FINISHED.** A script did its edits, asserted, then would have appended a
changelog entry. The assert fired, so the append never ran — and the script still printed its
"FIXED" lines and looked like a partial success. The missing entry was found only by reading
`git status`.
⇒ **Put ALL edits before ALL post-conditions, or make each step independently re-runnable. And
trust `git status`, never a script's self-report.**

‼ **AND THE ONE THAT WAS NOT A CHECK AT ALL:** a correction that SPANS LINES opened
`*(The superseded clause read: "…` and never closed the quote or the parenthetical, because the
close belonged on the CONTINUATION line. Python does not complain about a comment and no gate can
see it. **A malformed marked-up retraction is worse than none — it makes the OLD wording look like
live text again.** It was caught by `diff`-before-promoting, which is now two-for-two at finding
defects that every other check missed.
⇒ **When a correction spans lines, check the continuation, not only the line you edited.**

## 2026-09-15 — a KNOWN-WRONG instrument was compensated with prose, in triplicate, instead of being fixed

**Symptom.** `promote.py --check` — called *the authority* on fork drift in four documents — printed
a permanent `drift: 1 file(s)` for a file git stores as ONE blob. To stop readers acting on it,
`04-HANDOFF.md` carried a hand-copied caveat (*"the residual 1 differing file is ENCODING-ONLY …
⛔ Do NOT 'fix' it by flipping endings"*) in **three separate places**, and `DIVERGENCE-LOG.md`
carried a fourth.

**Root cause.** `core.autocrlf=true` plus three instruments that all hashed RAW BYTES. A copy git
checked out carried CRLF; a copy a Python tool wrote carried LF.

**‼ THE ACTUAL MISTAKE IS NOT THE MIS-MEASUREMENT — IT IS WHAT WAS DONE ABOUT IT.** The 2026-09-14
session diagnosed this exactly, wrote the correct prevention rule (*"NORMALISE LINE ENDINGS BEFORE
JUDGING A DIFF"*), made the RIGHT call on the file itself (preserve CRLF so the diff shows 91 real
lines, not a 1,173-line flip) — and then left the instrument lying and paid for it in prose. By the
next morning that prose had to be edited in 4 places across 2 files just to change a digit.

**The fix that worked.** Normalise newlines inside the comparison; report line-ending-only files as
their own category rather than swallowing them; do it in ALL THREE instruments so no two authorities
disagree; and put it behind gate #62, fault-tested in both directions (blind meter → arms A+E red;
normalisation removed → arm B red; `promote.py` restored byte-identically afterwards).

⇒ **Prevention: WHEN YOU CATCH AN INSTRUMENT LYING, FIX THE INSTRUMENT IN THAT COMMIT. A caveat you
have to write TWICE is a gate you have not written yet** — and the second copy is the signal, not
the thoroughness. ⛔ Corollary, because the tempting shortcut here was the wrong one: **fix the
MEASUREMENT, not the thing being measured.** Flipping the file's endings would have turned the
number green while destroying the reviewable diff that a deliberate earlier decision had bought.


---

## 2026-09-16 — I read a TRUNCATED GREP as an ABSENCE, and published it as `[VERIFIED-BY-ME]`

**Symptom.** A committed research note and the `04-HANDOFF.md` banner both stated that
`gBackupMapLayout` *"appears nowhere in module code"*, and built a §Ch24 build-order decision on it:
that our pathfinder is structurally blind to the runtime-opened Elite Four door and that a live-grid
reader would have to be written.

**Root cause.** My own command:

    grep -rn "gBackupMapLayout" sandbox-pokebot/modules/ 2>/dev/null | head -5

`modules/data/symbols/*.sym` sorts first, so the five symbol-table hits consumed the entire output.
The real module-code hits — `sootopolis.py` (10), `early_game.py` (4), `sootopolis_gym.py` (1) —
were below the cut. **`head` answers "show me some". It never answers "is there any".**

**What it cost, and what it nearly cost.** Nothing shipped: a Tier 2 cold-start audit re-ran the
grep and caught it. Had it stood, the next session would have been told to build from scratch a
live-grid reader **that already exists** — `sootopolis.py:871` `_live_collision_grid` and `:939`,
written 2026-09-02 for the §Ch21 Sky Pillar crack floors, which is *the identical defect shape*
(a `setmetatile` write invisible to our ROM-cached grid). The error made the good news invisible.

⇒ **Prevention: NEVER CONCLUDE ABSENCE FROM A TRUNCATED COMMAND.** If the claim is "there are none",
the command must be able to say so: use `grep -c`, `| wc -l`, or exclude the noisy path — and a
`| head -N` in the evidence line of an absence claim is itself the defect. ⛔ Corollary: the
`[VERIFIED-BY-ME]` tag is a promise about the METHOD, not merely about having run something; a tag
applied to a truncated command is worse than no tag, because it transfers unearned confidence.

‼ **AND THE SECOND-ORDER LESSON, which is the one worth keeping.** This is the *third* time in two
sessions that the instrument, not the subject, was the thing that was wrong — a phantom `drift: 1`
from raw-byte hashing, a `distinct_pos=0` stuck-check whose regex could not match map names
containing spaces, and now this. Every one was caught by looking at the failing command rather than
at the thing under test. **The project rule already said it** (*"when a probe FAILS, read the
failing line before touching the thing under test"*) — the extension earned today is that it applies
to probes that SUCCEED too: a command that returns a clean, plausible, wrong answer is the more
dangerous case, because nothing prompts you to look.

## 2026-09-16 (second) — I announced a "new prerequisite defect" that was an OPEN, INSTRUMENTED, FILED ISSUE

**Symptom.** I wrote a §Ch24 section headed *"THE PREREQUISITE DEFECT — OUR PATHFINDER CANNOT SEE
THE DOOR IT MUST WALK THROUGH"*, changed the build order on the strength of it, and put it in the
handoff banner as a discovery.

**What was actually true.** It is **`KI-74`**, filed 2026-08-13, still open, which had already cost a
drive on 2026-09-01. Better still, the project had already built everything I was about to propose:
`sootopolis._live_collision_grid()` as the production oracle (whose docstring explains the ROM-vs-RAM
divergence more precisely than my section did) and `tools/story-dev/probe_live_mapgrid.py` as the
offline instrument, with a calibrated border offset.

**Root cause — and it is NOT "I failed to grep".** I did grep, and the grep that mattered
(`gBackupMapLayout`) I truncated with `| head -5`, which is its own entry above. The deeper cause is
that **I searched the CODE for a mechanism and never searched `05-KNOWN-ISSUES.md` for the
SYMPTOM.** The KI is titled almost exactly what I "found": *"`setmetatile` tiles are INVISIBLE to the
shared map model"*.

⇒ **Prevention: BEFORE WRITING THE WORDS "NEW DEFECT" OR CHANGING A BUILD ORDER, GREP
`05-KNOWN-ISSUES.md` AND `08-MISTAKES.md` FOR THE SYMPTOM IN THE PROJECT'S OWN VOCABULARY** — the
mechanism's name (`setmetatile`, `gBackupMapLayout`), not just the file you found it in.
`precheck_prior_art.py` exists for this and I did not run it. ‼ The cost of the omission is not the
duplicated analysis — it is that a reader of my version would have believed the fix had to be built,
when it was sitting in `sootopolis.py` with a docstring explaining itself.

⭐ **WHAT THE ROUND GOT RIGHT, AND IT IS THE PART WORTH KEEPING.** The adversarial angle asked *"what
if the ROM already marks those tiles walkable?"* — the one question that would have collapsed the
whole plan — and that turned into `probe_e4_door_rom_view.py`, which answered it OFFLINE, for all
five rooms, with controls, and **without the drive everyone assumed was needed**. The premise
survived. ⇒ **A refutation attempt that FAILS is still the cheapest thing you can buy**, and
checking the premise before the build is what a day of drives would otherwise have cost.
