## 2026-09-16 (third, small but corrupting) — BACKTICKS IN A DOUBLE-QUOTED `git commit -m` ARE EXECUTED

**Symptom.** Commit `2c5973c5`'s body reads *"measure offline with , which is an existing…"* — a
tool name vanished mid-sentence. The shell printed `probe_live_mapgrid.py: command not found` and I
nearly read that as a failed command rather than as a corrupted commit message.

**Root cause.** `git commit -m "… `tool.py` …"` inside DOUBLE quotes: bash command-substitutes the
backticks, runs the contents, and splices the (empty) output into the message. Every other commit
this session used `git commit -F -` with a **quoted** heredoc (`<<'MSG'`), which passes text through
literally; this one slipped to `-m`.

**Not fixed, deliberately.** The commit is already pushed and `CLAUDE.md` forbids rewriting
published history. The message remains readable — the same tool is named un-backticked earlier in
it — so the honest cost is one mangled clause, recorded here rather than papered over.

⇒ **Prevention: NEVER put a commit message in a double-quoted `-m`. Use `git commit -F -` with a
quoted heredoc (`<<'MSG'`).** This project's commit messages are dense with backticked identifiers,
so the failure is not an edge case here — it is the default outcome. ‼ And the tell is subtle: the
commit SUCCEEDS, exit 0, with a stray `command not found` on stderr that looks like it belongs to
something else entirely.


---

## 2026-09-16 (fourth) — I REUSED A *MEASUREMENT* CLASSIFIER TO *SELECT WHAT TO DELETE*

**Symptom.** Retiring closed issues from `05-KNOWN-ISSUES.md`, I generated the candidate list with
R7's own closed/open classifier (`lint_docs.py`). It returned **24 sections**. Reading them:
`KI-88` — *"upstream helper; NOT fixed, ROUTED AROUND"* — matched because the substring "FIXED"
appears inside "NOT fixed". `KI-66` — *"PARTLY FIXED"* — matched because the hedge list had "MIXED"
and "STILL OPEN" but not "PARTLY". Several were already-archived 2-line stubs whose correct end state
is to stay exactly where they are.

**Root cause — and it is NOT "the classifier is buggy".** R7's classifier is CORRECT FOR ITS JOB. It
computes a FRACTION over ~3,000 lines, where a handful of misfiled sections moves the number by under
a percent and changes no decision. I borrowed it for a job with a completely different error budget:
**deciding which blocks to REMOVE from a document, where ONE false positive deletes a live issue.**

⇒ **Prevention: A CLASSIFIER'S ACCURACY REQUIREMENT COMES FROM THE DECISION IT FEEDS, NOT FROM THE
CLASSIFIER.** Before reusing one, ask what a single false positive COSTS in the new job. Same code,
same inputs, same output — and a tolerance that is fine for a statistic is reckless for a deletion.
‼ The practical rule that saved it: **for any irreversible selection, print the FULL candidate list
and READ IT.** 24 -> 7 after a stricter filter, 7 -> 5 after reading. The two rejected at the last
step were a 2-line stub whose whole purpose is to stay, and a block containing a LIVE caveat.

⭐ **AND THE SECOND HALF, WHICH THE TOOL COULD NOT CATCH FOR ME.** Two pointers I wrote claimed *"FULL
ENTRY ARCHIVED VERBATIM"* while 105 and 41 lines of body remained beneath them.
`archive_doc_block.py` verified its invariants honestly — a `###` IS a real block boundary, so
INVARIANT B (no orphan) passed correctly. **The tool guaranteed the MOVE; I wrote the CLAIM, and the
claim was false.** ⇒ **a tool's invariants protect what the TOOL does, never what YOU SAY it did.**
After any archiving, measure what actually remains under each pointer before believing your own
summary line.

---

## 2026-09-16 (fifth) — MY FIX JUDGED ITSELF BY A PROXY, AND THE PROXY WAS NOISE WITH A LUCKY SIGN

**Symptom.** The `KI-101` fix made in-battle items land (5 faints → 2, causally proven). Its verdict
asked *"did the target's HP rise?"*. An adversarial review of my own diff pointed at my own evidence:
`use 2: 2/147 -> 6/147`. A Full Restore maxes HP, so **6 is not the heal's result**.

**Root cause, and it is worse than the review supposed.** It was NOT a counter-hit eating the heal —
`worst hit` never rises above 81, so no 141-damage blow ever landed. The post-turn HP read is a
**transient**. My verdict keyed on the SIGN of a noisy value and survived twice by margins of +4 and
+74. A different timing flips a working heal to "no effect", and two of those disable every item for
the rest of the battle — in the five-fight one-way gauntlet the feature exists for.

**What I should have done first.** The decomp had already told me while I was reading it for
something else: `RemoveBagItem(item, 1)` sits ONLY in the success branch of `ItemUseCB_Medicine`, and
a non-Revive HP item on a 0-HP mon is refused *without* consuming it. **"Did the count drop" is the
action itself.** I had that fact in hand and still reached for HP — because HP was what the existing
code already measured.

⇒ **Prevention: WHEN YOU INHERIT A VERDICT, RE-ASK WHAT IT OBSERVES — do not merely make the existing
signal FRESHER.** I spent the whole first fix making a stale HP read fresh and never asked whether HP
was the right quantity at all. ‼ The standing rule *"instrument the ACTION, not the input"* already
covers it; what is new is the failure mode — **inheriting a proxy from the code you are repairing and
improving it instead of replacing it. A fix that makes a bad oracle more accurate is still built on a
bad oracle.**
⭐ And the tell was sitting in my own SUCCESS evidence: a Full Restore reporting **+4** should have
stopped me cold. **A result that succeeds by an implausible margin is a measurement to distrust, not
a win to bank.**


---

## 2026-09-16 (sixth) — I READ A COUNTER THRESHOLD AS A DURATION, AND CALLED A HANG A "FRAME COST"

**Symptom.** `#24-e4postbattlestall` was filed as *"the post-win dialogue stalls ~1,200 frames … It
RECOVERED … a FRAME COST and not yet a hang."* An adversarial cold-start audit checked the cited
evidence: **all four** drives end `HANG CONFIRMED (20000 frames no progress)` with
`final mode=Manual`. **4 for 4. None recovered.**

**Two independent errors, and both are general.**
1. **`NO-PROGRESS x1200` IS NOT A DURATION.** It is the first rung of an escalating counter ladder —
   x1200, x3000, x8000, x15000 all appear in the same log. I quoted the threshold at which an
   instrument first speaks as though it were the size of the thing it measured.
   ⇒ **Prevention: before quoting a number out of a log line, find the OTHER values that field
   takes.** One sample of a ladder looks exactly like a measurement.
2. **`ACCEPTANCE: PASS` HID A TOTAL LOSS OF CONTROL.** The probe's acceptance says *"must REACH
   Sidney and MEASURE an outcome; winning is not required"* — it asserts nothing about the bot being
   able to CONTINUE. I read PASS as "the run was fine".
   ⇒ **Prevention: an acceptance line is a claim about EXACTLY what it enumerates.** Ask what it does
   NOT assert before treating it as a health check. ‼ And the handoff's own advice — *"read the
   `ACCEPTANCE:` line, not the last line"* — is sound in general and is what produced this error
   here; it does not license ignoring `HANG CONFIRMED` on the last line.

⭐ **CONSEQUENCE, and it is why this matters more than the label:** §G' told the next session *"only
the walk is unbuilt"*. In fact **regaining control after a victory is also unbuilt, and it is what
actually stops every run today** — the first thing Leg 1 would hit, inside six minutes, while the
docs called it a footnote.

---

## 2026-09-16 (seventh) — I EXTRAPOLATED FROM ONE INSTRUMENT TO ANOTHER TOOL'S BEHAVIOUR, UNDER A HEADING THAT SAID "MEASURED"

**Symptom.** §G' ruled out `calculate_path` for the §Ch24 door: *"The planner will refuse, correctly,
for ever"*, under a heading reading **"each ruled out by measurement, not opinion"**. The audit found
`map_path.py:841` skips the collision refusal when `tile == destination_tile and tile.warps_to`, and
`calculate_path`'s own docstring says *"setting a door as the destination will lead to the path
leading to the map that door connects to."* `(6,2)` is a warp tile.

**Root cause.** `probe_e4_door_rom_view.py` measured a **tile-collision value**. I concluded a
**planner behaviour**. Those are different instruments answering different questions, and **no
`calculate_path` call has ever been made against that tile.**

⇒ **Prevention: A MEASUREMENT LICENSES A CLAIM ABOUT THE THING MEASURED, AND NOTHING DOWNSTREAM OF
IT.** If the claim names a tool ("the planner will refuse"), the measurement must have RUN that tool.
‼ This is the same shape as the earlier retraction where I compared *attempts* to *failures* — and as
the KI-101 verdict built on a proxy. Three times in one session I measured X and concluded about Y.
⭐ The cheap discipline that would have caught all three: **write the claim, then ask which command
produced it.** If no command produced it, it is an inference and must be labelled one.


## 2026-09-16 (eighth) — I COPIED THREE NUMBERS FORWARD WITHOUT CHECKING ANY OF THEM, AND ALL THREE WERE WRONG

**SYMPTOM.** I had diagnosed the §Ch24 post-victory stall correctly and was about to build on it. A
6-angle recon then corrected **four** things I had written down — three of which were numbers I had
copied out of our own docs, and one of which was a warning our own harness carried.

* *"~40 call sites"* for `wait_until_truly_controllable` → **262**. (40 is the count of call sites
  lexically inside a LOOP — a real number, measuring a different thing.)
* *"f28976 = f27174 + 1800 EXACTLY"* → the delta is **1802**. Two frames of Manual teardown.
* *"4 drives out of 4"* → **at most TWO trajectories**; three of the four logs are frame-identical.
* *"the researched (6,7) is WRONG, the landing is (6,11)"* → **neither is wrong.** Both are correct
  readings at different instants of one six-step scripted walk.

**ROOT CAUSE.** Not one of them came from a measurement I made. Each arrived inside a sentence that
already read as established — the punch list said 1800, so I wrote 1800; the changelog said ~40, so
I wrote ~40. **A number inherits the authority of the sentence around it, and re-typing it feels
like citing it.** The (6,7) case is the sharpest: the discriminator (`elite4_state_in_room = 0`,
which can only be 0 before `WalkInCloseDoor` returns) **was already printed in our own log**, in the
same run, three lines from the coordinate it settles. Nobody had subtracted.

**THE FIX THAT WORKED.** An adversarial recon whose brief listed the "measured facts" as things to
CHECK rather than to build on. Its first three findings were arithmetic.

**PREVENTION RULE.** ⛔ **BEFORE A NUMBER CROSSES FROM ONE DOCUMENT INTO ANOTHER, RE-DERIVE IT — RUN
THE GREP, DO THE SUBTRACTION.** A figure you re-typed is a figure you asserted. And when two sources
give different values for a coordinate, **look for the discriminator in the run you already have**
before declaring either one wrong.


## 2026-09-16 (ninth) — I INSTRUMENTED THE INPUT TO THE ACTION TWICE IN ONE PROBE, WHILE WRITING ABOUT THAT EXACT RULE

**SYMPTOM.** Building `--driver e4dismiss`, I filed a prediction that it would issue 1–12 presses.
It issued **50**, tripping my own falsifier. Later, the continuation check reported *"OK 6
waypoint(s)"* — a number equally consistent with the route AROUND the defeated trainer and a straight
run THROUGH him, which have opposite consequences for the leg.

**ROOT CAUSE, IDENTICAL BOTH TIMES.** `presses_issued` counts duty-cycle ticks on which the press
GATE was true; most land during `PrintingCharacter`, where there is nothing to dismiss. A waypoint
COUNT is the size of the answer, not the answer. **Both are the INPUT to the thing I cared about, or
its shape — neither is the thing.** CLAUDE.md rule 7 says exactly this, and I was writing a document
about rule 7 at the time.

**THE FIX THAT WORKED.** `prompts_cleared` — `WaitForButton` → anything-else transitions, i.e.
prompts the game actually consumed (**2**, consistent with the decomp's 3 for a mid-sequence
fixture). And dumping the waypoint TILES **with their map**, which is what revealed the real result:
the path goes around the trainer and then **follows the warp onto `HALL1 (5,12)`**.

**PREVENTION RULE.** ⛔ **A COUNT IS NOT AN OBSERVATION. Before reporting a number, ask which
DIFFERENT outcomes would produce the same number** — if two answers with opposite consequences share
it, the number is not the measurement. Dump the items, not the length.


## 2026-09-16 (tenth) — A GREEN GATE WAS CITED AS PROOF OVER FILES THE GATE CANNOT SEE

**SYMPTOM.** A changelog entry recorded two post-victory saves as *"Now PINNED … `verify_fixtures`
green"*. The md5s it quoted were correct. **No manifest row was ever written**, so neither file was
pinned, and both sat on auto-rotating `stalls/` names that any later drive could overwrite.

**ROOT CAUSE.** `verify_fixtures.py` prints, in its own output, *"74 of 118 .ss1 files on disk have
NO manifest row, so they are neither PINNED nor declared VOLATILE — **this gate cannot see them
drift**."* The gate was green **because** it was blind to those files. Green was read as
corroboration of the sentence next to it rather than as a statement about the gate's own scope.

**THE FIX THAT WORKED.** Adding the two rows (unlisted 74 → 72) and then asserting the bytes
explicitly: `verify_fixtures.py --assert post_sidney_door_open.ss1=62313696` → OK. An assertion
names the file; a suite-level PASS does not.

**PREVENTION RULE.** ⛔ **A PASS IS ONLY EVIDENCE ABOUT WHAT THE GATE ENUMERATES.** Before citing a
green gate for a specific artifact, check that the artifact is IN its enumeration — and prefer an
assertion that names the artifact over a suite result that does not. (Same family as "a checklist
protects exactly what it enumerates", and as the `--quick` suite that prints *"THIS IS NOT A GREEN
SUITE"* about its own 8 unrun gates.)


## 2026-09-16 (eleventh) — I BROKE PAIR P3 IN THE COMMIT THAT DOCUMENTED PAIR BREAKS, AND I HANDED THE REVIEWER A SHORT PACKET

**SYMPTOM.** Two findings from the same Tier 1 review:
1. My new `#26-victoryroadgap` refuted the claim *"30.3% reach Ever Grande ⇒ the approach to the
   League is not the bottleneck"*. I recorded the refutation in the punch list and the changelog —
   and left the **handoff banner**, the half a cold reader meets FIRST, still asserting the
   superseded inference. **Sixth instance of this shape, committed by the session documenting it.**
2. The primary note carrying the refuted headline (`2026-09-16-endless-batch-REVIEW.md`) got **no
   stub marker at all**, so anyone opening it directly still read a refuted claim as measured fact.

**ROOT CAUSE.** I updated the documents I was already typing in. The banner and that note were not
among them. ‼ **Also mine:** the review packet I handed the agent contained only the
`PROJECT KNOWLEDGE` diff — the two tool diffs and a second untracked file were missing, and the
reviewer had to fetch them itself to answer at all. It said so, which is the only reason I know.

**THE FIX THAT WORKED.** An **independent** reviewer given the pair list explicitly — and then the
slug grep the advisory hook prescribes, which turned up a **seventh** stale copy ("the post-victory
dialogue stalls ~1,200 frames (it recovers)") sitting in the routing note's KNOWN HAZARDS, where a
leg builder would have read it.

**PREVENTION RULE.** ⛔ **WHEN YOU REFUTE A CLAIM, `grep` FOR THE CLAIM — NOT FOR THE ITEM SLUG.**
The slug finds the places that already cite the item; the *claim* finds the places that repeat it
without naming it, which is where it does damage. And ⛔ **hand a reviewer `git status` in full, not
the diff you think is relevant** — a review is only as good as its inputs, and choosing the inputs is
choosing the findings.


## 2026-09-16 (twelfth) — I HANDED OFF A SPEC THAT WAS VACUOUS ON THE FIXTURE IT PUSHED HARDEST

**SYMPTOM.** My handoff told the next session to build §Ch24 leg 1 and to grade it on
`DEFEATED_ELITE_4_SIDNEY`. It named two fixtures and never said which one the LEG runs from. A Tier 2
cold-start auditor read the flag out of both, offline:

    post_ch24_atdoor.ss1        ELITE_4_STATE=0   DEFEATED_ELITE_4_SIDNEY=False
    post_sidney_door_open.ss1   ELITE_4_STATE=1   DEFEATED_ELITE_4_SIDNEY=True   <- before a frame runs

⇒ **a leg graded on that flag from the post-victory fixture passes without doing anything.**

**ROOT CAUSE, AND IT IS THE PART WORTH KEEPING.** The vacuous fixture is the one my own documents
recommend most enthusiastically, for a reason that is *correct in its own context*: it IS the stall
state, and it makes the dismiss and door questions cost ~4,000 frames instead of ~29,000. I wrote
"this fixture is the cheap way to measure X" five times without noticing that the property making it
cheap for X — **the victory has already happened** — is exactly the property that destroys a grade
for Y. ‼ **A fixture is not fast or slow in the abstract; it is fast or slow FOR A QUESTION, and the
shortcut that makes one question cheap can make the next one meaningless.**

**WHY NOTHING CAUGHT IT EARLIER.** Tier 0 can't see it. Tier 1 reviews a doc DIFF and the pairs all
agreed. The probes themselves are fine — they grade on control and position, never on the flag. It
took an agent that tried to *begin the next item* and computed the discriminator on the named
fixture, which is precisely why CLAUDE.md's Tier 2 clause (4) exists. It has now paid for itself
twice.

**THE FIX THAT WORKED.** One sentence in the live `➡➡➡` marker and in the punch-list item naming the
start fixture and saying, with the measurement, why the other one is vacuous.

**PREVENTION RULE.** ⛔ **WHEN A HANDOFF NAMES A GRADING SIGNAL, IT MUST NAME THE START FIXTURE IN
THE SAME BREATH — AND STATE WHICH AVAILABLE FIXTURES MAKE THAT GRADE VACUOUS.** "Grade on X" and
"start from Y" are one instruction, not two. If several fixtures are in play, read the signal out of
each and write the table down; the one that is cheapest to reach is the one most likely to be
vacuous, because cheapness usually means the work is already done.


## 2026-09-16 (thirteenth) — I CITED A "STANDING RULING" THE PROJECT HAD ALREADY RETRACTED AS NON-EXISTENT

**SYMPTOM.** I planned a change to shipped bot code and justified it as *"following KI-83's standing
ruling to bound tasks_scripts helpers at the call site."* An adversarial agent replied that no such
ruling exists, and `05-KNOWN-ISSUES.md:2490` says so in terms: **"NOT FIXED UPSTREAM — A CASE-BY-CASE
CALL, NOT A RULING. ⛔ *(This read 'same ruling as KI-88' until 2026-09-05. There is no such ruling…)*"**

**ROOT CAUSE, AND IT IS A NEW VARIANT OF A RECORDED ONE.** `08-MISTAKES.md` already carries *"A
KI-TO-KI CITATION CHAIN IS NOT A RULING"* — an agent following KI-89 → KI-88 → KI-83 and finding
nothing decided at the bottom. **I did not follow a chain.** I read `KI-83`'s **HEADER**, which is
phrased as an imperative — *"⛔ NOT OURS AND DELIBERATELY NOT FIXED — bound it AT THE CALL SITE"* —
and an imperative in a header **reads like a decision**. The retraction lives 80 lines below, in the
body. ⇒ the existing rule pointed at chains; the same error arrived through a headline.

**WHY IT MATTERED.** The false authority was doing real work: it was my whole justification for
touching shipped code, and it steered me at unboundedness while a MEASURED, silent, higher-severity
defect (`KI-89`, wrong-cursor) sat on one of the same three lines.

**PREVENTION RULE.** ⛔ **A RULING IS SOMETHING IN `06-DECISIONS-LOG.md`. NOWHERE ELSE.** Before
citing any "standing ruling", `grep -i` that file for it — the project's own rule 11 already says to
grep the decisions log before escalating; this extends it to *before invoking*. ‼ And specifically:
**an imperative in a KI HEADER is a recommendation, not a decision** — the header is the half that
gets skimmed, and this tree's headers are written in the imperative voice as a matter of style.
If the decisions log does not have it, say "no ruling found" and make the case on evidence instead.


## 2026-09-16 (fourteenth) — I TRANSPLANTED A LOOP WITHOUT ITS CONTRACT, AND IT BROKE THE ONLY THING IT TOUCHED

**SYMPTOM.** `use_item_on_party_member` waits on a SINGULAR context-menu task while the same file
defines all four and documents that naming one *"cost four drives"*. I replaced the single-name wait
with the accept-any-task loop the TEACH path already ships. The heal driver went **PASS → FAIL, 7
actions → 0**: nothing healed.

**ROOT CAUSE.** The two are not interchangeable and the difference is invisible at the call site.
`wait_for_task_to_start_and_finish(TASK, "A")` presses A **through** the context menu — start AND
finish — which is what SELECTS "Use". The teach path's loop is **start-only**: it stops pressing the
moment the menu opens, because on that path the *next* block does the selecting. I matched the
task-name semantics and silently dropped the press semantics.

**THE FIX THAT WORKED.** Revert, and record the A/B in the code at the line, so the next reader sees
why an obviously-correct-looking change is not.

**PREVENTION RULE.** ⛔ **WHEN COPYING A LOOP FROM ANOTHER PATH, COPY ITS CONTRACT — ASK WHAT THE
CALLER DOES *NEXT*.** A wait that ends when a state ARRIVES and a wait that ends when a state is
DISMISSED look identical at the call site and differ completely in effect. ‼ And: **the A/B is what
made this a five-minute finding instead of a shipped regression** — baseline the driver BEFORE
touching shipped code, every time, even for a change that looks like a strict improvement.


## 2026-09-16 (fifteenth) — I QUOTED A LEVEL-SPECIFIC NUMBER AS A PROPERTY OF THE MATCHUP, INSIDE A RULING

**SYMPTOM.** I wrote, in `06-DECISIONS-LOG.md` and twice in `04-HANDOFF.md`: *"Wallace is
arithmetically out of reach — Milotic L58 has Recover (~98 HP/turn) vs our best measured hit of
66-78."* An adversarial agent challenged it, and the source I was quoting refutes the framing in the
very same sentence: *"Sceptile **L53** Leaf Blade does 66-78 ⇒ a net −20/turn losing race.
**Break-even is L62.**"* — followed by a conversion curve ending **"L75 88% CLEAR THE GAUNTLET"**.

**ROOT CAUSE.** The 66-78 figure is the damage **one Pokémon at one level** deals. I lifted it into a
sentence about the *matchup*, where it reads as "our party cannot beat Wallace" rather than "our
party at L53 cannot beat Wallace". The qualifier was two words away in the source and I dropped it.
‼ This is the same shape as every "measured X, concluded about Y" already in this file — attempts vs
failures, a proxy HP delta vs item consumption, a tile collision vs a planner's behaviour — and I did
it **while writing a ruling**, which is the document type most likely to be quoted back as settled.

**WHY IT MATTERED.** It was load-bearing for build ORDER. "It cannot be won" argues for abandoning
legs 2-5; "it cannot be won *at L53*, and break-even is L62" argues for **grinding**, using
`--driver ch24grind`, which already exists and took the party to L60 in ~30 minutes. Two opposite
plans from the same numbers.

**THE FIX THAT WORKED.** An adversarial angle whose brief told it to attack the PREMISES rather than
the conclusions, and a dated correction in all three places (the decisions log gets an append, since
it is append-only; both handoff halves were edited together).

**PREVENTION RULE.** ⛔ **A DAMAGE/HP/TIMING NUMBER CARRIES ITS LEVEL, ITS FIXTURE AND ITS PARTY.
Quote it with them or do not quote it.** If a figure came from a simulation, say so in the same
breath — the source here explicitly says *"THESE ARE SIMULATION RESULTS, NOT DRIVES — say so when
citing them"*, and I cited them without it. ‼ And when a conclusion would change the BUILD ORDER,
re-read the source paragraph to its end before writing it into a ruling: the sentence that qualifies
a number is usually the next one.


## 2026-09-16 (sixteenth) — I SCALED FROM "EXP PER BATTLE" WHEN ONLY "EXP PER WIN" TRANSFERS

**SYMPTOM.** I sized a L60→L75 grind by scaling the previous grind's measured throughput: *"449,328
EXP in 623 battles, ~30 min"* ⇒ 721 EXP/battle ⇒ 912k EXP needs ~1,264 battles ≈ **61 minutes**. I
wrote that ETA into the handoff, in both halves. The run itself refuted it within 150,000 frames:
**99 `RanAway` vs 15 `Won` — an 87% flee rate** ⇒ ~1,032 EXP per **win**, 13.2% win rate,
**~6,700 battles ≈ 2.4 hours**. Out by ~2.4×.

**ROOT CAUSE.** "EXP per battle" is not a property of the grass or the party — it is a property of
*that run's flee rate*, which was silently baked into the figure I borrowed. **EXP per WIN is the
transferable quantity** (it depends on the defeated Pokémon), and the win RATE has to be measured
separately for each run. I even reasoned correctly that "EXP per battle is constant in Gen 3 because
it depends on the defeated mon" — which is true of a WIN and false of a battle that ends in a flee.
‼ The sentence that made it sound rigorous is the one that hid the error.

**WHAT MADE IT CHEAP.** The run was started in the background and checked early. The refutation cost
~4 minutes of wall clock, not the 61 I had promised.

**PREVENTION RULE.** ⛔ **BEFORE SCALING ANY THROUGHPUT FIGURE, ASK WHAT ELSE IS BAKED INTO IT.** A
rate quoted per-attempt carries the success rate of the run it came from; a rate quoted per-SUCCESS
does not. Convert to the per-success quantity, then measure the success rate for the new run — and
⭐ **check a long run EARLY against its own prediction**, because the first few minutes are usually
enough to refute an estimate that is wrong by more than 2×.

‼ **AND A CONSTRAINT THIS SURFACED, WORTH MORE THAN THE ETA:** `victory_road.py:1988` records
`WILD_MAX = 40` — VICTORY_ROAD_1F's strongest wild is **L40**. Grinding a L60 party toward L75 on L40
encounters is the real throughput ceiling here. No tuning of the flee rate beats finding better
ground, and that question has never been asked for the post-L60 range.


## 2026-09-16 (seventeenth) — I STARTED A 2-HOUR RUN ON A FIXTURE I HAD NOT CHECKED THE MOVESET OF

**SYMPTOM.** Acting on the corrected "grind first" build order, I started a L60→L75 grind from
`post_grind_L60.ss1`. Nine minutes in, two problems: it had stalled (15 wins, then 338 straight
flees, zero EXP), and — far worse — **that fixture has no Ice Beam and no Fly.** Grinding it to L75
would have produced, after ~2.4 hours, a party that cannot reach the League and has no answer to
Drake's Flygon.

**ROOT CAUSE.** I verified the fixture's LEVELS (the property the grind cares about) and inherited
everything else from `FIXTURES.md5`, whose row says *"Verified by RELOADING the file
(`probe_anchor_inventory.py`)"*. That probe **does not print movesets** — a caveat this project had
already written down for the *other* §Ch24 fixture and did not apply to this one. ‼ The row read as
strongly verified precisely because it named a verification method; naming a method is not the same
as the method covering the claim.

**WHAT SAVED IT.** Checking the run EARLY against its own prediction. The stall was visible in four
minutes, and looking into *why* is what surfaced the moveset. Had I trusted the 61-minute ETA and
walked away, the first sign of trouble would have been a finished grind with a useless party.

**PREVENTION RULE.** ⛔ **BEFORE COMMITTING A LONG RUN TO A FIXTURE, CHECK THE PROPERTIES THE
*DESTINATION* NEEDS, NOT THE ONES THE *TOOL* NEEDS.** The grind needs levels and a tile; §Ch24 needs
Ice Beam, Fly, HP and a position. A fixture that satisfies the tool can still be useless to the goal.
‼ And: **when a manifest says "verified", read WHAT the named instrument actually prints** — a probe
that is blind to a property does not become sighted by being run carefully. ⭐ Corollary, cheap and
general: **a long unattended run should be checked against its own prediction within the first few
minutes**, because that is when an estimate wrong by >2× is still cheap to abandon.


## 2026-09-17 — I WROTE "REFUTED" FROM A STATE THAT WAS NOT THE STATE UNDER TEST

**SYMPTOM.** The `ch24grind` stall (15 wins, then hundreds of consecutive flees with zero EXP) had two
obvious candidate causes: no PP, and low HP. I checked both, found them healthy, and recorded in the
changelog and in BOTH halves of the handoff that they were **REFUTED** and the mechanism was
**UNKNOWN**. ⛔ **PP was the cause.** The stall state reads `Surf:0/15  Water Spout:0/5
Waterfall:0/15` with only a BANNED move (`Dive`) left.

**ROOT CAUSE.** I had killed the run, so no shutdown save existed and the capture only fires on a
completed level step. I therefore read the **START** save — the one the run began from — and reported
its healthy PP as evidence about the STALL. Those are different states separated by 29,000 frames and
15 battles, which is exactly the interval in which the PP was spent. ‼ I even wrote the caveat
("those readings are from the START save") into the agent brief — and then let the word "REFUTED"
stand in the documents anyway.

**WHAT IT COST, AND WHAT IT NEARLY COST.** It sent a four-angle agent fan-out out with two correct
hypotheses explicitly marked "do NOT re-propose without new evidence". The diagnosis was ~30 seconds
of emulator time away the whole time.

**THE FIX THAT WORKED.** Re-run the SAME driver with a bounded `--frames 90000` so it exhausts its
budget and shuts down cleanly, writing the save. The stall is early (f28,779) and deterministic, so
the repro is trivial once you ask for it.

**PREVENTION RULE.** ⛔ **A READING FROM A STATE THAT IS NOT THE STATE UNDER TEST REFUTES NOTHING.**
Before writing "REFUTED", name the state the reading came from and check it IS the state in question;
if it is not, the honest word is **"not yet observed"**. ⭐ And when a run has to be killed, the first
question is *"what bounded run would have captured this cleanly?"* — a frame budget that ends the run
on its own is the difference between a save and an inference. ‼ Corollary: **do not hand agents a
hypothesis marked "already refuted" unless the refutation came from the right state** — a wrong
exclusion is more expensive than no exclusion, because it is not re-examined.


## 2026-09-17 (second) — A FINDING RECORDED AS PROSE NEXT TO ONE DRIVER DID NOT STOP THE SECOND DRIVER REPEATING IT

**SYMPTOM.** `Ch24GrindMode` stalled for ever because it never installed `SwapTrainBattleStrategy`.
The project had **already diagnosed and written up that exact defect** for `Ch23TrainMode`, in a
detailed comment at `victory_road.py:3400-3410` ending *"the DRIVER NEVER INSTALLED SWAP-TRAINING"*.
The second driver was written anyway, with the same one-line `return StoryItemBattleStrategy()`.

**ROOT CAUSE.** The fix for driver #1 was recorded as **prose, attached to driver #1**. Nothing made
it reachable from driver #2: no shared helper every harness driver calls, no gate that fails when a
training-shaped driver installs a non-rotating strategy, no entry in a checklist a new driver is
written against. CLAUDE.md rule 6 already says this — *"a rule already broken twice is evidence that
prose failed — write the gate instead"* — and here prose failed on its FIRST re-use.

**WHY IT WAS EXPENSIVE OUT OF PROPORTION.** The symptom (flees everything, gains nothing, never
hangs, never errors) looks like a bot/strategy/PP problem, so it pulled a four-angle agent fan-out
and a fixture investigation before anyone looked at the six lines of the driver that CHOOSE the
strategy. The already-written answer was one grep away the whole time.

**THE FIX THAT WORKED.** Mirror production's gate in the driver, and A/B it on the same fixture and
frame budget: 15 Won/50 RanAway → **38 Won/0 RanAway**, with the bench fighting and a heal firing.

**PREVENTION RULE.** ⛔ **WHEN A HARNESS DRIVER MISBEHAVES IN A WAY PRODUCTION DOES NOT, SUSPECT THE
DRIVER'S OWN `on_battle_started` / setup BEFORE SUSPECTING THE BOT.** A harness driver is not a
`StoryMode`, so every strategy, listener and guard that `StoryMode` installs is ABSENT unless the
driver re-installs it — and that absence is silent. ⭐ And the general form: **a fix written as a
comment protects exactly one call site.** If the same mistake is possible at a second site, the fix
belongs in shared code or a gate; if neither is practical, the comment must at least live where the
NEXT author will read it, not only where the last bug was.

‼ **SECOND, SMALLER RULE FROM THE SAME ROUND:** a recovery trigger scoped to the PARTY
(`_team_is_out_of_pp()`) cannot rescue a failure scoped to the LEAD
(`LevelUpLeadBattleStrategy.decide_turn`). **When you add a "can I continue?" check, check that its
RECOVERY has the same scope** — five healthy bench mons kept the party-scoped trigger False while the
lead was unable to act, for 457 consecutive battles.

## 2026-09-17 (third) — I OVER-APPLIED A TRUE RULING AND IT KEPT THE GRIND ON THE WRONG PARTY FOR A DAY

**Symptom.** `Ch24GrindMode`'s docstring said, correctly: *"The League fixtures cannot be used: from
the League door `calculate_path` reaches neither grass nor a Poké Center."* I read that as *"the
§Ch24 lineage cannot be grinded"*, and therefore planned to repair a **different** party
(`post_grind_L60.ss1`) by re-running the entire prep chain — including a ~700,000-frame Abandoned
Ship trip — to give it the moves the §Ch24 lineage already had.

**Root cause.** The ruling is a statement about **one tile, (18,6)**. The §Ch24 lineage does not live
only at (18,6): the prep chain ends with a Fly, and `post_ch24ready.ss1` sits at the **Poké Center,
(27,49)** — the other side of the plateau, a question the ruling never asked. Measured in seconds
once asked: `(27,49) → VR apron (18,42)` is **OK, 22 waypoints**.

**The fix that worked.** `probe_grind_lineage_route.py` — route from the tile each save is ACTUALLY
on, under a two-sided control (the Poké Center door must come back OK; the League door must come
back FAIL, reproducing the pinned reading). Both separated, so the positive was trustworthy.

**‼ WHAT MADE IT EXPENSIVE WAS NOT THE MISREADING, IT WAS THAT NOTHING RE-ASKED.** A recon of four
agents was commissioned against the repair plan and returned genuinely good findings — none of which
questioned the premise, because the premise was not what they were asked about.

⇒ **PREVENTION RULE.** *A ruling is scoped to the state it was measured in. Before inheriting one as
a constraint, name the tile / save / party it was measured on and ask whether YOUR state is that
one.* A ruling that says "from X you cannot reach Y" is not "Y is unreachable" — and when a ruling
is the load-bearing reason for expensive work, re-measure it from the state you are actually in
BEFORE commissioning the work, not after.

## 2026-09-17 (fourth) — ANNOTATING A FIXTURE SILENTLY UNPINNED IT

**Symptom.** I rewrote `post_grind_L60.ss1`'s row in `saves/FIXTURES.md5` to say it is a dead branch,
and in doing so wrote the description straight into the `kind` position. The format is positional —
`<md5>  <name>  <PINNED|VOLATILE>  <description>`, two spaces between fields — so the parser read
`kind = "⛔⛔ **A DEAD BRANCH…"`, `kind == "PINNED"` became False, and the MISSING/CHANGED
enforcement for that fixture switched **off**. Nothing failed; the run stayed green.

**⛔ AND IT HAD ALREADY HAPPENED ONCE, UNNOTICED.** `post_b1f.ss1` had been carrying
`⚠ SUPERSEDED BY …` in the same position for ~13 days. Two occurrences, zero detections.

**Root cause.** The failure mode is perverse: **the more carefully someone annotates a fixture, the
more likely they are to unpin it** — and the result is invisible, because "not PINNED" is exactly
what a VOLATILE row looks like. A silent misparse is indistinguishable from a deliberate choice.

**The fix that worked.** `verify_fixtures.py` now REFUSES a row whose kind is neither `PINNED` nor
`VOLATILE`, with a message naming the format, and exits non-zero. Fault-tested both ways: healthy =
exit 0; one field removed on a scratch copy = exit 1 naming the fixture, manifest restored after.
Both bad rows repaired.

⇒ **PREVENTION RULE.** *A positional format parsed by a script must refuse an unrecognised field
rather than fall through — a parser that cannot classify a row is reporting on a file it is no
longer checking.* Caught by a Tier 1 reviewer reading the diff, not by any check; the check exists
now.

## 2026-09-17 (fifth) — PAIR P3 BROKE A THIRD TIME, SO IT STOPPED BEING PROSE AND BECAME A GATE

**Symptom.** I re-pointed the banner, the queue head, the decisions log, the changelog, the punch
list AND `FIXTURES.md5` off the dead `post_grind_L60.ss1` lineage — and left `04-HANDOFF.md`'s
HOW TO RUN block carrying the literal command that regrinds it. A Tier 1 reviewer quoted both halves.
Its note is the part worth keeping: *"same class of break, recurring in this commit"* — the file
already documents committing this exact break once before, **while documenting P3 breaks**.

**Then the gate found a third instance the reviewer had missed**: a second runnable recipe naming the
same dead save, whose own adjacent comment had said *"⛔⛔ NOT A REPRO ANY MORE"* for nine days while
the command line stayed executable. ⇒ **a comment that says a command is dead does not make it dead.**

**Root cause.** Recipes are the one part of the handoff a reader EXECUTES rather than reads, so a
stale line there does not cost a minute of confusion — it costs hours of emulator time and returns an
unusable party. And updating six places while missing the seventh is precisely the P5 shape the
project already knows about: **a checklist protects exactly what it enumerates.**

**The fix that worked.** `probe_runrecipe_fixtures.py`, gate #61: every `*.ss1` named on a RUNNABLE
line of the recipes block must exist in `FIXTURES.md5` and must not be marked dead there. Fault arm
`POKEBOT_RECIPEGATE_FAULT=1` also scans comments and MUST fail — because the corrected block names
the dead fixture in a warning, and a gate that fired on its own fix would be bypassed. "Named but
never pinned" is REPORTED, not blocking: a different gap, pre-dating the gate, and a gate that
demands unrelated work is one people learn to route around.

⇒ **PREVENTION RULE.** *When you retire a fixture or a repro, disarm the COMMAND, not just the prose
around it — a `#` in front of the line, with the text kept for the record.* And: the third break of
a pair is not a reason to write the rule more emphatically; `CLAUDE.md` already says *"a rule already
broken twice is evidence that prose failed — write the gate instead."*

## 2026-09-17 (sixth) — MY CONTROL ARM FAILED AND THE SUBJECT WAS CORRECT

**Symptom.** `probe_plan_order_guard.py`'s control arm asserted `refusal is None` and reported
**FAIL** against a guard that was working perfectly.

**Root cause.** The probe stubs the actuator (`teach_move_from_bag`) so it can exercise the real
refusal logic without pressing a button. With the teach stubbed, Swellow never actually learns Fly —
so `apply_moveset_plan`'s **own post-teach verification** correctly raised *"taught Fly … and it does
NOT know it"*. The raise was a SECOND guard doing its job. My assertion conflated "the order guard
stayed silent" with "nothing raised at all".

**The fix that worked.** Assert the specific thing: `"OUT OF ORDER" not in refusal`, plus the plan
actually containing Swellow's Fly. Both arms then separated.

⇒ **PREVENTION RULE.** *An assertion must name the specific behaviour under test, never "nothing went
wrong" — a probe that stubs part of the system will trip the parts it stubbed, and scoring that as a
subject failure is how a correct guard gets "fixed".* This is the fourth time in this project that a
failing probe turned out to be a wrong CHECK rather than a wrong subject, which is why the standing
rule is: **read the failing line before touching the thing under test.**


## 2026-09-17 (seventh) — A DEFENSIVE STAT OUTRANKED THE ABILITY TO ACT, AND THE TIE-BREAK ORDER IS WHY

**Symptom.** The faint-replacement ranker sent our worst attacker into the one fight it could not
win: against Phoebe's pure Ghosts it chose Swellow (`incoming 0.00`, outgoing 31) over Mightyena
(`incoming 0.50`, outgoing 68).

**Root cause.** A lexicographic key whose FIRST term was the defensive multiplier. Ghost→Normal is
0×, so a Normal-type scores a *perfect* defensive 0.00 and can never be beaten at term one — no
matter how useless it is offensively. ‼ The deeper point: **"takes 0" and "deals 0" are the same
type relation read from opposite ends.** A key that sorts on incoming damage alone therefore does not
merely tolerate the mon that cannot fight, it *systematically selects* it, and it does so precisely
in the matchups where being unable to fight is fatal.

**The fix that worked.** A leading `cannot_damage` term. Deliberately shaped so it is a no-op unless
some candidate deals literally zero — when all can fight, or none can, the tuple falls through to the
previous ordering unchanged. Fault-tested by reverting it: exactly one case flips.

⇒ **PREVENTION RULE.** *Before a lexicographic key ranks on "how well does this go for us", it must
first rank on "can this act at all" — a sort whose first term is a defensive metric will pick the
thing that is invulnerable BECAUSE it is irrelevant.* And when adding a term to a shared-path
ranking, shape it so it provably cannot change the existing ordering except in the failure case; then
the ordinary-case A/B is a proof rather than a sample.

## 2026-09-17 (eighth) — THE RECON I COMMISSIONED NEVER QUESTIONED THE PREMISE, BECAUSE I DID NOT ASK IT TO

**Symptom.** Four agents were sent to plan the repair of `post_grind_L60.ss1` — how to teach Fly,
how to route the Ice Beam trip, which slot each move should eat. They returned genuinely good
findings, one of which (`#24-planorder`) was a real latent defect worth shipping. **None of them
questioned whether the save should be repaired at all**, and it should not have been: it was on a
dead branch, and a two-minute probe retired the entire plan.

**Root cause.** Every angle was scoped *inside* the plan. "Which slot does Fly eat" presupposes that
Fly is being taught. The adversarial angle in the later leg-2 recon was the one that produced the
most value of any agent this session — and the difference was purely that it was pointed at the
PREMISE ("try to destroy this claim") rather than at the execution.

**What worked.** In the leg-2 recon, one of the four angles was explicitly adversarial and given a
claim to refute. It returned ten objections, two of which invalidate the intended design and one of
which (`#24-gameclearflag`) is an already-wired production defect.

⇒ **PREVENTION RULE.** *Every fan-out gets one agent pointed at the PREMISE, not the plan — and its
brief is to refute, not to review.* A recon where all N angles sit inside the plan can only ever
tell you how to execute it well. This is already the standing rule for Gemini passes ("asking a
second agent the same question produces a second guess; asking it to refute produces information") —
the gap was that it had not been applied to the framing of a whole work item.


## 2026-09-17 (ninth) — I WATCHED CORRECT BEHAVIOUR ON ONE PARTY AND WROTE DOWN A UNIVERSAL LAW

**Symptom.** I asserted, in four documents and a commit, that **"the bot DECLINES level-up moves"**
and that therefore *"a taught move will NOT be undone by grinding — the strongest objection to the
repair plan, refuted by measurement rather than argument."* The objection was correct. Wailord lost
**Ice Beam** to Hydro Pump at **exactly L59** — the very level I had cited as proof it would not.

**Root cause.** I observed one lineage cross L52 and L59 keeping all four moves, and promoted that
observation to a rule. It was not a rule; it was one branch of a conditional. The policy asks "is
this type already covered?", and on that lineage the answer was yes (Water Spout, a TM, sat in the
replaceable slot) so it declined. On the §Ch24 lineage the replaceable slot held Ice Beam, the
census could not see the three Water HMs, and the same code accepted. **Same code, same level,
opposite outcome** — which is exactly what a conditional looks like when you only ever run one arm.

⇒ **PREVENTION RULE.** *An observation over ONE input is evidence about that input. Before writing
"the bot does X", find the code that decides X and read its branches — if it has a conditional you
did not vary, you have measured a case, not a rule.* ‼ And the tell was there in my own sentence: I
was using the claim to DISMISS AN OBJECTION. A generalisation that arrives precisely when it would
let you skip work deserves the opposite of the benefit of the doubt.

⛔ Note what this does NOT overturn: the LINEAGE ruling (`post_grind_L60.ss1` is a dead branch;
`post_ch24ready.ss1` is the right start) still stands on its own measurements. What changed is that
the grind needed a CODE FIX first, not merely a better fixture.

## 2026-09-17 (tenth) — A GATE I WROTE THIS MORNING CAUGHT A REGRESSION I INTRODUCED THIS AFTERNOON

**Symptom.** `verify_fixtures.py` went red with `MANIFEST SCHEMA: 'L57' has kind='Dive, Surf, Ice
Beam,'`. There is no fixture called `L57`.

**Root cause.** Writing the retraction above, I embedded a two-line before/after moveset table inside
a `FIXTURES.md5` description. **That file is LINE-ORIENTED** — every non-`#` line is parsed as a row —
so a multi-line block inside a description does not annotate a row, it MANUFACTURES two bogus ones,
and each bogus row silently unpins nothing while making the real parse ambiguous.

**The fix that worked.** Fold the table inline into the row it belongs to (` / `-separated).

⭐ **THE POINT OF THIS ENTRY IS THE TIMING.** The check that caught it was added *hours earlier, the
same day*, in response to the same class of bug (a description written into the `kind` field). It
paid for itself before the session ended, against its own author, on a different mistake in the same
file. ⇒ evidence for the standing rule that *anything enforceable belongs in a gate, not in prose* —
prose would have told me the format; the gate stopped me shipping a violation of it.

⇒ **PREVENTION RULE.** *Before writing a multi-line block into a data file, ask whether the file is
LINE-ORIENTED. Prose files tolerate structure; manifests parse it.*


## 2026-09-17 (eleventh) — I PARAPHRASED A DECOMP RULE AS A NOTION, AND THE NOTION WAS WRONG

**Symptom.** Asking "can the §Ch24 party Fly from where it is parked?", my check printed
**"✅ yes"** for VICTORY_ROAD_1F. It cannot: Fly is refused in caves.

**Root cause.** I wrote the predicate as `map_type == "Indoor"` — a paraphrase of "is it indoors?" —
when the actual rule is an explicit four-item allow-list (`Overworld_MapTypeAllowsTeleportAndFly`:
ROUTE, TOWN, OCEAN_ROUTE, CITY). A cave is neither "Indoor" nor on the allow-list, so a DENY-LIST
phrased as one type let it through. ‼ The failure direction matters: a paraphrase that is too narrow
produces a **FALSE GREEN**, which is the expensive direction.

**The fix that worked.** Encode the decomp's list verbatim, and treat an unreadable value as NO.

⇒ **PREVENTION RULE.** *When a rule exists as an explicit list in the decomp, COPY THE LIST. Do not
re-express it as a category ("outdoors", "indoors", "a cave"), because the category is your model of
the list and the two diverge exactly at the case you are asking about.* And prefer ALLOW-lists to
DENY-lists for this reason: an allow-list fails closed on anything unanticipated.

‼ This is the third predicate error in one day — a type chart missing a resistance, a collision test
asserting `== 1` where the codebase tests `!= 0`, and now this. All three had the same shape: **the
check tested something narrower than the claim it was standing in for.** The general rule, and the
reason the standing advice is to read the failing line first: *when a probe disagrees with a
carefully-reasoned expectation, suspect the probe's predicate before the subject.*


## 2026-09-17 (twelfth) — I PROVED A FIX WITH A FIXTURE I INVENTED TO PROVE IT

**Symptom.** `#24-ghostreplacement` shipped, gate-green, marked "A/B-PROVEN", and is a **measured
no-op on the real party**: against a pure Ghost the ranker still picks a mon that cannot win — in
fact an **L19 mule**, which is worse than the case the item was filed about.

**Root cause.** The gate arm (C8) was a synthetic mon holding ONLY a Normal move, so its outgoing was
literally zero and the new `cannot_damage` term fired. No mon in the actual party looks like that:
the real Swellow has **Aerial Ace** (Flying, 1× on a Ghost) and the real Zigzagoon has **Surf**. With
a non-zero outgoing the new term is 0 for every candidate and the key falls through to the old
behaviour untouched.

‼ **THE ARM WAS BUILT FROM MY MODEL OF THE DEFECT, NOT FROM THE SITUATION.** I already had the real
party pinned, already had the real measurement that started the item (Swellow 31 vs Mightyena 68),
and still reached for a hand-made mon because it made the demonstration cleaner. A fixture invented
to demonstrate a defect will demonstrate it — that is the one thing it cannot fail to do.

⛔ And the warning was already written, by me, that morning, in another probe's docstring: *"the arms
use the REAL Wailord and the REAL Hydro Pump, not fakes — twice today a hand-built fixture in a probe
was wrong while its subject was right."* Knowing the rule did not make it fire, because I was writing
an arm for a fix rather than a check on a subject.

⇒ **PREVENTION RULE.** *An arm that proves a fix must be the REAL situation the fix was filed for —
the pinned save, the real party, the real move set. A synthetic arm may only ever be an ADDITIONAL
case, never the one the claim rests on.* Concretely: if an item was opened by a measurement, the arm
must be that measurement re-run, not a reconstruction of it.

⇒ **AND A SECOND RULE, ABOUT THE SHAPE OF THE TERM.** `cannot_damage` asks a BOOLEAN question ("is it
zero?") about a CONTINUOUS problem ("how long until this wins?"). A boolean guard on a continuous
quantity only ever fires at the extreme, so it looks correct on a constructed extreme and does
nothing in the middle, which is where real parties live. *When the failure is "too slow", the guard
must measure speed, not presence.*


## 2026-09-17 (thirteenth) — A DRIVER CANNOT WATCH ITS OWN BATTLE, AND THAT ONE FACT FAKED THREE READINGS

**Symptom.** `ch24phoebe` printed `ACCEPTANCE: PASS` with `battle_frames_waited = 0` and
`hp_entering_phoebe` **exactly equal to** `hp_after_phoebe` — which reads as *"the Phoebe fight cost
nothing"*. It also captured an "in-battle" fixture that turned out to hold `Dusclops L51 0/117` and a
Mightyena already levelled to L76, i.e. the END of the fight.

**Root cause — ONE cause, three wrong readings.** When a battle starts, this harness hands the
controller to `BattleListener.fight`; **the driver's own generator is not resumed until the fight
ENDS.** So every statement in the driver body after "battle started" executes POST-battle:
* the capture landed after the last Pokémon fainted,
* `hp_entering_phoebe` was read after the fight, so it equalled `hp_after`,
* and the battle-end wait exited on its first check, because the battle was already over.

‼ I had even written the loop defensively (`if get_game_state() is not BATTLE: break`) and it did not
help — the predicate was fine; the *position in the program* was wrong. `Ch24ProbeMode`'s own comment
records the sibling of this bug (*"THIS PREDICATE WAS `get_battle_state() is None` AND THAT IS NEVER,
EVER TRUE"*), so the class was known and I still walked into a different instance of it.

⇒ **PREVENTION RULE.** *To observe a battle, instrument `on_battle_started` or the battle strategy —
never the driver body. A driver can see the state BEFORE the fight and AFTER it, and nothing in
between.* And the tell is cheap to check: **if a before/after pair comes back IDENTICAL, suspect that
"before" was sampled after.**

⭐ **WHAT SAVED IT WAS GRADING THE CONSEQUENCE ANYWAY.** The run's real verdict rests on
`DEFEATED_ELITE_4_PHOEBE = True` and Mightyena's level going 75 → 76 — facts about the WORLD, not
about my timing. The fight genuinely happened and was genuinely won; only my narration of it was
false. ⇒ a grade built on world-state survives an instrument that mis-times itself, which is the
argument for grading consequences rather than observations.

## 2026-09-17 (fourteenth) — I CHOSE WHICH ITEMS TO WATCH, AND THE HEAL USED A DIFFERENT ONE

**Symptom.** `ch24phoebe`'s bag reading showed **no change** (`Hyper Potion 36 → 36`) across a heal
that demonstrably worked (Mightyena 187/227 → 227/227, `heal_actions=1`). It looked like HP had been
restored for free.

**Root cause.** My `_bag()` helper watched a hand-picked list — Hyper Potion, Full Restore, Full Heal,
Revive — and `plan_healing` chose a **Super Potion**, which was not on it. The heal was correct; the
*instrument* was looking at the wrong shelf.

**What saved it.** `heal_plan` names the item it intends to use
(`[(0, 'Super Potion', 'Mightyena at 187/227')]`), and logging the PLAN beside the bag delta is what
made the discrepancy legible in one line instead of becoming a mystery.

⇒ **PREVENTION RULE.** *Never instrument a hand-picked subset of a resource and report it as the
resource. Either read the whole pocket, or log the decision that names what was spent — ideally
both, because the plan is the intent and the delta is the attempt, and the pair is what catches a
mismatch.* (A candidate is not an attempt; here, a curated view was not the bag.)

## 2026-09-17 (fifteenth) — THE STATE TABLE SAID "NEVER FOUGHT EITHER" AFTER I HAD WON TWO FIGHTS

**Symptom.** A Tier 2 cold-start audit found `04-HANDOFF.md`'s STATE table still reading
*"⛔⛔ §Ch24 IS NOT IMPLEMENTED … ⚠ PREDICTED, NOT OBSERVED; the bot has never fought either"* while
the queue head on the same file said *"TWO OF FIVE ELITE FOUR ROOMS ARE BEATEN AT L75, WITH THEIR
FIGHTS"*. A flat contradiction on the single most important fact in the document.

**Root cause.** I updated the queue head — the place I had been editing all session — and never
touched the STATE table, which is the *structured* summary a resumer is told to trust. **One fact,
two places, one updated.** That is the P5 shape exactly, and P5 exists in `CLAUDE.md` because this
has happened before.

‼ **AND I HAD BEEN WARNED, BY MY OWN PROCESS, TWICE THE SAME DAY.** The diff advisory printed
*"On finishing an item, GREP THE TREE FOR ITS SLUG and re-read every hit"* after each of the
relevant commits. I read it, fixed the handoff↔punch-list pair it names, and did not grep for the
FACT — only for the slug. The STATE table does not mention `#24-sidneyL75` or `#24-phoebeL75`; it
makes the same claim in prose, so a slug grep could never have found it.

⇒ **PREVENTION RULE.** *Grep for the CLAIM, not only for the slug. When a session changes a fact
("§Ch24 is not implemented", "the bot has never fought X"), search for the fact's WORDING across the
current-state files — the place that contradicts you may never name the item.* Concretely: after a
first-of-its-kind result, grep for the negation you have just falsified (`"has never"`,
`"NOT IMPLEMENTED"`, `"no fixture"`, `"never fought"`).

⭐ **WHY TIER 2 CAUGHT IT AND TIER 1 DID NOT:** Tier 1 reads a DIFF and is asked about the pairs the
diff touches. The STATE table was not in the diff — being stale is a *sin of omission*, and a diff
cannot show you the line you failed to edit. Only the cold reader, handed the whole file with no
knowledge of what changed, sees both halves at once. ⇒ that is the argument for Tier 2 surviving two
clean Tier 1s, which `CLAUDE.md` already makes and which this session re-earned.

## 2026-09-17 (sixteenth) — THE FILE PROMISED "WHERE WE ARE RIGHT NOW" AND OPENED WITH HISTORY

**Symptom.** Same audit: `00-README.md` describes `04-HANDOFF.md` as *"Where we are RIGHT NOW + what's
next"*, but after one pointer sentence the file's literal opening content was a stack of banners it
**self-labels as HISTORY**, and the true current state sat ~450 lines further in — inside a single
line that had grown to ~45,000 characters of chronologically APPENDED updates.

**Root cause.** Two habits compounding. Every session appended its update to the end of the queue-head
line (so the newest, most operative text was hardest to reach), and every session prepended its
banner to the top of the file (so the top filled with history). The net effect: **the two places a
cold reader looks first were the two places least likely to be current.**

**The fix that worked.** (1) A one-line CURRENT-STATE answer immediately after `Last updated:` — the
state, the next action, the fixture, and a one-hit grep for the detail. (2) The queue head now LEADS
with current state and is explicitly marked *"PREPEND, DO NOT APPEND"*. (3) The two stale competing
`NEXT ACTION` arrows were retired in place.

⇒ **PREVENTION RULE.** *A document whose reader is told it shows "right now" must answer that in its
first few lines, with no scrolling and no hops. If the newest text is reached by appending, the
document's most current sentence is also its least findable — so prepend current state and append
only history.* ‼ And measure it the way the audit did: **count the HOPS a cold reader needs.** Three
hops through self-declared-stale text is a failure even when every hop is technically correct.

## 2026-09-17 (seventeenth) — I SHIPPED A GUARD KEYED ON A DICT ENTRY THAT ITS OWN COPY-TARGET WOULD RENAME

**SYMPTOM (found before it could fire — by an adversarial reviewer, not by me).** I added a
post-fight capture to `Ch24PhoebeMode` whose guard read `won = R.get("phoebe_flag") is True`, while
the reading itself was written 50 lines earlier as `R["phoebe_flag"] = ...`. The whole point of that
class is to be COPIED per room, and the reading key is exactly the kind of name a copy renames.

**ROOT CAUSE.** A room-N copy that renames `R["phoebe_flag"] → R["glacia_flag"]` at its one obvious
site — the reading — and not at the guard gets `R.get("phoebe_flag") → None`. `None is True` is
False, so `won` is silently False and the capture **REFUSES TO MINT THE NEXT ROOM'S FIXTURE ON A
PERFECT RUN**, logging a refusal that reads exactly like a failed drive. Nothing raises. The run
prints `ACCEPTANCE: PASS` and quietly produces no artifact.

**THE FIX THAT WORKED.** Both drivers now carry a `VICTORY_FLAG` class constant with TWO consumers —
the P-OUTCOME reading and the capture guard — and the guard reads the FLAG, not the reading of it.
One rename, both sites follow.

**PREVENTION RULE.** ⛔ **A guard must read the THING, not a READING of the thing.** If a guard keys
on a dict entry, a local, or a log field that a sibling/copy will rename, it is one careless rename
away from silently inverting. Bind it to a single named constant, or re-derive it at the point of use.

‼ **AND NOTE THE SHAPE, because this project keeps meeting it:** the failure is a *silent False*, not
an exception — the same shape as `get_event_flag("<typo>")` returning **False** for a flag name that
does not exist (measured this session; it does NOT raise). **A predicate that cannot distinguish
"false" from "I could not find it" is not a predicate.**


## 2026-09-17 (eighteenth) — I CITED A PROBE AS "MEASURED" FOR A CLAIM THE PROBE DOES NOT MEASURE

**SYMPTOM.** I wrote, in a committed predictions file, that Hall 2 joins Phoebe's room to Glacia's
was **MEASURED** by `probe_e4_halls.py`, quoting its output row `HALL2  PHOEBE  -> GLACIA   10 (5,12) (5,2)`.

**ROOT CAUSE.** That probe iterates a literal `HALLS` table whose endpoint labels **its own author
typed**. It reads `collision` only — `walkable_column`, `collision_at` — and never touches a warp
destination. So the row genuinely MEASURES the corridor's SHAPE (10 steps, (5,12)→(5,2), with
controls) and merely ASSERTS its connectivity. I read the label as if it were an output. Routing was
precisely what the recon existed to establish, so this was the one claim I most needed to get right.

**THE FIX THAT WORKED.** New `probe_e4_warp_chain.py` reads the ROM warp table via `get_map_data(...).warps`
and follows the chain, with **HALL1 as a control** — HALL1's endpoints are already LIVE-DRIVEN, so a
method that reproduces them works. Result: `HALL2 warp 0 (5,12)→PHOEBES_ROOM, warp 1 (5,2)→GLACIAS_ROOM`.
The whole chain `SIDNEY→HALL1→PHOEBE→HALL2→GLACIA→HALL3→DRAKE` is now endpoint-measured.

**PREVENTION RULE.** ⛔ **Before citing a probe's output as evidence, check that the probe READS the
thing the claim is about.** A string in the tool's own configuration table is not a measurement — it
is the author's belief, printed back at you in the format of a result. ⇒ *This is rule 7
("instrument the ACTION, not the input to the action") wearing a different hat: a LABEL is an input.*

## 2026-09-17 (nineteenth) — I HANDED THE TIER 1 REVIEWER A DIFF THAT UNDERCOUNTED THE ITEM'S OWN DOC FOOTPRINT

**SYMPTOM.** The Tier 1 reviewer reported, as its own finding: *"the `docdiff.txt` I was handed covered
only `03-PUNCH-LIST.md` and `04-HANDOFF.md`, but live `git status` at review time showed
`05-KNOWN-ISSUES.md` and `06-DECISIONS-LOG.md` were also modified (+1 and +39 lines) as part of this
same item."* It checked them anyway and they were consistent — but it had to notice the gap first.

**ROOT CAUSE.** I generated the diff and launched the reviewer, and THEN kept working — appending to
`05-KNOWN-ISSUES.md`, `06-DECISIONS-LOG.md` and `08-MISTAKES.md`. The package was accurate at the
moment it was built and stale by the time it was read. ⛔ **The reviewer is asked "do these halves
agree?", so a pair whose second half is not in the package is a pair it cannot check** — and Tier 1
exists precisely because prose self-checks fail here. A reviewer silently given half an item is a
reviewer returning a PASS narrower than it appears.

**THE FIX THAT WORKED.** None was needed this time — the reviewer caught it and widened its own scope,
which is exactly why the tier requires an INDEPENDENT agent rather than a fork.

**PREVENTION RULE.** ⛔ **Build the Tier 1 package AFTER the last doc edit, never before — and give it
the FILE LIST (`git status`), not only a diff.** A diff is a snapshot; `git status` is a question the
reviewer can re-ask at read time. ⇒ *Same family as "a candidate is not an attempt": a snapshot of
the work is not the work.*

## 2026-09-17 (twentieth) — I WROTE A RESERVED GATE MARKER INTO A FIXTURE ROW AND KILLED MY OWN FIXTURE

**SYMPTOM.** `run_gates.py` went red on `probe_runrecipe_fixtures.py`:
*"⛔ A RECIPE A COLD READER WOULD COPY POINTS AT A FIXTURE THE MANIFEST CALLS DEAD:
`post_hall4_door.ss1` (line(s) [834]) is marked ['DO NOT USE'] in FIXTURES.md5"* — on a fixture I had
pinned minutes earlier and never marked dead.

**ROOT CAUSE.** `probe_runrecipe_fixtures.py:57` defines
`DEAD_MARKERS = ("DEAD BRANCH", "DO NOT GRIND", "DO NOT USE", "WRONG LINEAGE")` and `:125` tests
`m in note.upper()` over the WHOLE manifest row. My row contained the sentence *"AND WHEN GRADING
ROOM 5, DO NOT USE THE `DEFEATED_ELITE_4_*` FLAGS"* — advice about the FLAGS. The gate cannot tell
what the phrase refers to, so it read it as *this fixture is dead* and refused every recipe naming it.

**THE FIX THAT WORKED.** Reword the prose, not the gate: *"AND NEVER GRADE ROOM 5 ON THE
`DEFEATED_ELITE_4_*` FLAGS"*. The row now also says, in place, WHY it is worded that way, so the next
author does not "improve" it back.

⛔ **THE FIX I DID NOT MAKE, AND WHY.** Loosening the matcher (requiring the marker near the fixture
name, say) was tempting and is wrong: this gate is **coarse BY DESIGN** — its own docstring at `:27`
records that it must not fire on its own fix — and a substring test over the row is exactly what makes
it impossible to mark a fixture dead and then quietly keep using it. **The gate was right; my prose
was the defect.**

**PREVENTION RULE.** ⛔ **A manifest row is PARSED, not just read. Never write a reserved marker
phrase into `FIXTURES.md5` prose unless you mean its reserved meaning** — the current set is
`DEAD BRANCH`, `DO NOT GRIND`, `DO NOT USE`, `WRONG LINEAGE` (`probe_runrecipe_fixtures.py:57` is the
authority; re-read it, do not trust this list). If you need to forbid something *else* in a row, say
"never …" or "do not rely on …" instead.
⇒ *Generalised: when a machine reads your prose, your prose has a grammar. This is the same family as
"a candidate is not an attempt" — the gate acts on the TEXT, not on what you meant by it.*


## 2026-09-17 (late) — I SIZED A PIECE OF WORK WITH A NUMBER THE GUARD DOES NOT USE, AND CALLED IT TRACTABLE

**Symptom.** `#24-levelgap` shipped a first draft asserting the fix was *"a new LEG, not a re-plumbing
job"*, sized at *"roughly 500 battles / ~25 min"* on ground *"+22.6% better"*. All three claims were
wrong, and I found them myself an hour later by reading the call site instead of the docstring.

**Root cause — two distinct errors with one shape.**
1. **I quoted the number a RICHER model reports, while the code's decision is made by a CRUDER one.**
   B1F is +22.6% better under the per-species model (950.8 vs 775.6 EXP/battle). The guard that
   decides whether the leg runs uses `CAL × wild_level / 7` ⇒ +5.0% (301.2 vs 286.9). Sizing against
   the first while the second holds the veto is not conservative or optimistic — it is *unrelated*.
2. **I checked that a PARAMETER existed and never checked the CALL SITE.** `target` is genuinely a
   parameter (fixed 2026-09-04). But `grass=TRAIN_SPOT_1F` is hardcoded at `victory_road.py:2088`,
   `WILD_MAX = 40` is a hardcoded local at `:1988`, and **no `TRAIN_SPOT_B1F` exists at all**. The very
   defect the 2026-09-04 fix was written to cure — *"a parameter that only reaches half the function is
   not a parameter"* — was sitting one level out, and I cited that fix as evidence the work was small.

**The fix that worked.** Ran the project's own `estimate_frames_to_level` over four growth curves ×
two grounds × two targets, with land maxima measured from the decomp (1F 40, B1F 42, B2F 44).
**All 16 cells REFUSE** against `MAX_TRAINING_FRAMES = 250_000`; cheapest 513,014 frames (2.05× over).
Corrected the item, and filed the real blocker separately as `#24-trainestimatorcal`.

**⭐ PREVENTION RULE.** *Before calling work tractable, run the CODE'S OWN estimator against the CODE'S
OWN ceiling — quoting a better number from a different model is not sizing, and "the parameter exists"
is not the same as "the call site passes it."*

**‼ Also filed under the same date, same shape, caught the same way:** I labelled a SIMULATED win-rate
curve *"the measured curve"* in two files, and omitted any citation of the standing 2026-09-16 ruling
whose closing clause (*"it is a capability we already shipped"*) my own finding contradicts — so a
future agent reading the decisions log would have concluded the problem was solved. Corrected in place
with retraction markers, plus an appended decisions-log entry as the correction of record.
**Prevention rule:** *when a finding contradicts a standing ruling, cite the ruling and name which half
of it is wrong — in the file the auditor reads, not only in the one you happen to be editing.*


## 2026-09-17 (late) — I FILED A DEFECT THAT WAS A SETTLED QUESTION, BY BREAKING THE EXACT RULE WRITTEN TO PREVENT IT

**Symptom.** Filed `#24-trainestimatorcal`: the training cost estimator is calibrated to Route 102 and
understates Victory Road xp/battle by 2.70×, therefore the `MAX_TRAINING_FRAMES` guard is
over-pessimistic. Reordered the work queue around it and wrote it into three files. **It was wrong, and
the project had already answered it on 2026-09-08.**

**Root cause.** The estimator returns **FRAMES**. I corrected the numerator (xp/battle) and never
looked at the denominator — `FRAMES_PER_WILD_BATTLE = 1433` is *also* a Route 102 measurement and is
*also* wrong for Victory Road in the same direction (~3,192). The errors cancel to ~18%. The 2026-09-08
entry adjudicated this exact disagreement between two agents (2.68× vs 1.18×), concluded *"both are
arithmetically right; they used different denominators"*, and ended with a RULE:
⭐ *"when two analyses of the same quantity disagree by a factor, check the DENOMINATOR before believing
either."* **I had that file open. I had just quoted a line 6,000 lines away from it.**

**Why the existing rule did not fire.** It is filed as the lesson of a 2026-09-08 training analysis. I
was doing §Ch24 wiring recon. ⇒ the recurring shape from SESSION DISCIPLINE: *a rule filed as "the
lesson from bug X" does not fire when you are building Y.*

**The fix that worked.** A Tier 1 reviewer chased my own citation one level further than I did and
found the 2026-09-08 entry. Item withdrawn in place (kept, not deleted — the withdrawal is more useful
than the item), and `#24-levelgap` recomputed on true economics, where **every curve still refuses by
1.46×–2.26×**. ⇒ the conclusion survived; only my explanation of it was wrong.

**⭐ PREVENTION RULE.** *Before filing a NUMBER as a defect, grep the changelog and decisions log for
that number and for the constant's name — a 2.7× discrepancy that is easy to find is one a previous
session has probably already found and ruled on.*
**⭐ SECOND, SHARPER RULE.** *When a formula produces the units you are testing against (here: frames),
check EVERY term for the same calibration flaw. Fixing one term of a ratio and trusting the result is
not a partial fix — it can be worse than the original, because it moves a fail-safe guard toward
PERMISSIVE.*


## 2026-09-17 (late) — “THAT COPY IS JUST HISTORY, LEAVE IT” WAS WRONG **THREE TIMES IN ONE SESSION**

**Symptom.** Having corrected a claim in the place I was editing, I three separate times judged
another copy of the *same* claim to be harmless history and left it. All three were live text a cold
reader would act on, and **none of the three was found by me first**:
1. `03-PUNCH-LIST.md` — a closed `#24-glaciaL75` item still read *“all three prerequisites still
   stand”* after the count became four. *(Tier 1 found it.)*
2. `06-DECISIONS-LOG.md` — my own uncommitted entry still carried *“so this is a new LEG, not a
   re-plumbing job”* after I had retracted that sentence in two other files. *(I found this one, but
   only because a reviewer's warning to “assume there is a sixth error” made me go looking.)*
3. `04-HANDOFF.md` — *“Grind past L62 toward ~L75 BEFORE building more legs”* appears **twice**,
   verbatim. I marked line 6, asserted on the duplicate, told a reviewer I had “judged it historical”,
   and was wrong: the second copy had no supersede marker anywhere near it.

**Root cause.** A retraction is written where the author is *looking*, while the claim lives wherever
it was *copied*. “Is this historical?” is a judgement about the surrounding prose; **“does a marker
sit next to THIS copy?” is a fact about the bytes.** I kept making the judgement instead of checking
the fact — and in a file with a single 64,000-character line, “surrounded by history” is not even
visible without measuring offsets.

**The fix that worked.** Enumerate every occurrence *with its offset*, print the ~300 characters
before and after each, and test each one for an adjacent marker — then **count both**: the clause
appeared 2× and the retraction had to appear 2× before I believed it.

**⭐ PREVENTION RULE.** *After retracting a claim, `grep` its exact sentence and require a marker
ADJACENT TO EVERY OCCURRENCE — then assert `count(claim) == count(marker)`. Never decide a duplicate
is “historical” by reading around it; a supersede marker earlier in the same line does not cover a
copy 20,000 characters later.*


### ✅ UPDATE 2026-09-17 (late) — the "THAT COPY IS JUST HISTORY" rule above is now PARTLY GATED

`tools/story-dev/probe_retraction_coverage.py` (gate #63) mechanises it: every retracted claim must
have a marker within 400/900 chars of **every** occurrence. Four fault arms pass; 34 claims covered.
⚠⚠ **THE PROSE RULE ABOVE IS NOT RETIRED, AND DELIBERATELY SO.** The gate harvests a dead claim only
from the house idiom (a retraction keyword plus a past-reference quotation such as *"THIS clause
READ …"*). **A retraction phrased any other way is never harvested and therefore never checked.**
⛔⛔ **THIS SENTENCE ORIGINALLY CONTINUED "— the gate fails SAFE, which means it misses." THAT IS
WITHDRAWN: SEE THE VERY NEXT ENTRY IN THIS FILE.** The gate does NOT fail safe — it also produces
FALSE POSITIVES on live text, because keyword-adjacency is not claim-relatedness. So the scope limit
described above is real but is only HALF the picture, and the gate is now ADVISORY, not enforcing.
⇒ it is a floor under the rule, not a replacement for it;
treating it as full coverage would be the same over-trust this file warns about elsewhere
(*"a gate is not proven by its own fault arm"*).


## 2026-09-17 (late) — I PROVED FOUR ARMS AND CLAIMED A FIFTH THING THEY NEVER TESTED

**Symptom.** Shipped `probe_retraction_coverage.py` as an ENFORCING gate, justified in three separate
files by the claim that it *"fails safe — an unrecognised idiom is simply not harvested, so the failure
mode is a MISS, never a false alarm."* A Tier 1 reviewer refuted the claim from both directions inside
one review, and I reproduced both failures myself in a single script.

**Root cause — and it is not the regex.** My fault test had four arms and all four passed: real tree
clean, injected defect fires, marked copy stays silent, sub-threshold fragments never harvested. Those
arms exercise the MECHANISM. The sentence I actually shipped on was a claim about a PROPERTY — that no
input can produce a false positive — **and not one arm attacked that property.** Passing arms felt like
evidence for it; they were evidence for something adjacent and weaker.

**What was actually wrong.** (1) The harvester assumes keyword-adjacency implies claim-relatedness, so
a keyword sitting near an unrelated quotation marks a LIVE sentence as dead. (2) It only recognises the
*re-quotation* retraction idiom, and this project's more common style is an **in-place marker** — so it
was blind to its own motivating defect #3 (measured: 2 occurrences, 0 harvested).

**The fix that worked.** Downgraded to ADVISORY, retracted the safety claim in every file that carried
it, and filed both defects with the reviewer's exact repros as the test cases they must pass before it
may be ENFORCING again.

**⭐ PREVENTION RULE.** *A fault test proves the arms you thought of; it does not prove the property you
claimed. When a gate's ENFORCING status rests on a property — "fails safe", "cannot false-positive",
"is monotone" — write an arm that ATTACKS THE PROPERTY, and if you cannot construct such an arm, ship
ADVISORY.*
**⭐ SECOND RULE, cheaper and more general.** *Before claiming a check "cannot" do something, spend one
attempt trying to make it do that thing. The reviewer needed a single constructed example; so would I
have, had I looked for one instead of for confirmation.*

## 2026-09-17 (late) — ⛔ A REVIEW SUBAGENT DESTROYED UNCOMMITTED WORK WITH `git checkout --`

**Symptom.** A Tier 1 reviewer, asked to fault-test a gate by reproducing a historical defect, edited
`PROJECT KNOWLEDGE/04-HANDOFF.md` in place and then "restored" it with
`git checkout -- "PROJECT KNOWLEDGE/04-HANDOFF.md"`. That file had **real uncommitted changes**, and
the command reverts the whole file to `HEAD` — so it discarded the work-item diff along with the test
injection. `git reflog`, `git fsck` dangling blobs and editor local history all failed to recover it.

**Why it was survivable this time, and the number that made it so.** The loss was bounded to **three
lines** (the gate-count updates at `04-HANDOFF.md:676/:718/:722`) because the rest of that file had been
committed ~40 minutes earlier under the per-item Definition of Done. ⇒ **committing per item is not
bookkeeping; it is the blast radius.** Had the session batched its doc work to the end, an entire
session of handoff edits would have gone.

**Root cause.** The reviewer prompt told the agent to "restore any file you touch and verify with
`git diff`" — which it did, and the verification passed, because `git diff` shows a reverted file as
clean. **The instruction named the wrong safety check.** `git checkout --` is indistinguishable from a
correct restore when you only look at whether the file is now unmodified.

**⭐ PREVENTION RULE.** *Never instruct a subagent to mutate a file with uncommitted changes. If a
review needs fault injection, tell it to copy the tree (or the file) to the scratchpad and inject
there — and state explicitly: ⛔ `git checkout --`, `git restore`, `git stash`, `git reset` and
`git clean` are FORBIDDEN to reviewers, because a reverted file looks identical to a restored one.*
**⭐ COROLLARY for me.** *Before handing a reviewer a package with uncommitted work, know which files
are dirty — and prefer reviewing a COMMITTED state, so the worst case is recoverable by `git`.*


## 2026-09-17 (late) — A SHELL ATE TWO SPANS OF A DOCUMENT AND LEFT AN INVISIBLE BYTE BEHIND

**Symptom.** A changelog entry was appended with `bash -c "python -c '...'"`. Bash performed **command
substitution on the backticks inside the Python string**, so two spans never reached Python: a
filename, and a regex escape. The only visible symptom was a stray
`probe_retraction_coverage.py: command not found` printed ABOVE a line reading `changelog appended` —
which read like success.

**‼ AND THE FIRST DIAGNOSIS WAS WRONG, WHICH IS THE INTERESTING PART.** I recorded that the shell had
"deleted" the escape. Re-reading the file as BYTES showed it had not: the document contained
**`\x08`, a literal BACKSPACE control character**, between two backticks. Every terminal rendered it
as an empty pair of backticks. It was **present and invisible**, not absent. It surfaced only because
an assertion string failed to match and I inspected `repr()` instead of the rendering.

**‼‼ IT HAD HAPPENED BEFORE, TWICE.** A sweep found a second 0x08 in `28-HANDOFF-ARCHIVE.md:9918` —
*inside a sentence explaining that a control character in source is a hard failure "because `\b`
compiled to a BACKSPACE twice in one day and the gate still passed."* A Tier 1 reviewer then found a
**third**, older instance via `git log --all -S` in `03-PUNCH-LIST.md` (commit `5d91b279`,
2026-08-23). ⇒ **three independent sessions wrote a backspace byte into prose ABOUT the backspace
bug**, and nothing caught any of them.

**Root cause.** This project's prose is saturated with backticks — every symbol, file and flag is
inline code — so passing it through a shell-quoted string is a structural hazard, not an occasional
one. Escaping individual backticks is not a fix: it takes one miss.

**Why it is worse than the two loud quoting failures the same day.** Those died with `unexpected EOF`
and cost a retry. This one **partially succeeded** and produced a corrupted, committable document.
⇒ **a loud failure is a gift; a partial success is the hazard.**

**The fix that worked.** Write the script to a file and run the file — no shell parsing of content at
all. Both holes repaired, both historical bytes removed, and the class is now gated for docs by
`probe_doc_control_chars.py` (#64); it was already gated for `.py` source by `#24-p2headergate` (C).

**⭐ PREVENTION RULE.** *Never put backticks or `$` inside a shell-quoted string carrying prose or
code — write it to a file and execute the file.*
**⭐ SECOND RULE, the one that generalises.** *A document that looks right in a terminal has not been
checked. Control characters are invisible BY CONSTRUCTION — verify with `repr()` or a byte scan, and
